items.title: Can we trust a positive PSMA PET/CT before the Phoenix threshold? Positive predictive value after primary radiotherapy for prostate cancer. A retrospective cohort study.
items.journal: Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging
items.journal_full: European journal of nuclear medicine and molecular imaging
items.authors: van Altena EJE, Oprea-Lager DE, Scheltema MJV, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Restaging PSMA PET/CT reliably identifies recurrence after radiotherapy, even before the Phoenix threshold is met.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT is increasingly used after radiotherapy, even before the Phoenix threshold. We assessed the positive predictive value (PPV) of PET-positive findings in this setting.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Patients restaged with PSMA PET/CT after primary radiotherapy were classified as Phoenix-negative (PSA rise < 2.0 ng/mL above nadir) or Phoenix-positive. Local findings were verified by histopathology or MRI, metastases by histopathology or follow-up imaging. A sensitivity analysis was restricted to histopathology only. PPV was compared between Phoenix groups.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Of 833 patients, 724 were PET-positive; 263 local recurrences and 219 metastatic findings had a reference standard. PPV was 83.7% for local recurrence and 95.0% for metastases. Local PPV was lower in Phoenix-negative than Phoenix-positive patients (77.7% vs. 88.1%, p = 0.029), but not with histopathological verification (84.1% vs. 86.9%); metastatic PPV did not differ between groups (96.3% vs. 94.2%).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Restaging PSMA PET/CT reliably identifies recurrence after radiotherapy, even before the Phoenix threshold is met.

items.title: Preoperative prediction of microsatellite instability in rectal cancer using multiparametric MRI-derived intratumoral heterogeneity and exploration of biological mechanisms: a multicenter study.
items.authors: Li L, Yang D, Yan Y, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The model showed favorable training/internal performance but moderate external performance without clear incremental value. Larger prospective multicenter cohorts are needed. Transcriptomic and pilot IHC analyses suggest possible AKT1 expression differences between MSI-H and MSS rectal cancers.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To develop a machine-learning model combining multiparametric MRI-derived intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) scores with clinical features for preoperative prediction of microsatellite instability (MSI) in rectal cancer and to explore MSI-associated molecular features.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective study enrolled 464 rectal cancer patients from three centers, including training (n = 198; MSI-H, 26), internal validation (n = 110; MSI-H, 12), and external validation (n = 156; MSI-H, 23) cohorts. Three-dimensional ITH scores were derived from T2WI and DWI. Logistic regression identified independent clinical predictors. Six machine-learning algorithms were used to construct clinical, ITH, and combined models. Performance was assessed using AUCs with 95% confidence intervals, calibration curves, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP. TCGA transcriptomics, PPI analysis, and immunohistochemistry in 10 local samples were used for molecular exploration.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Age, tumor length, location, and N stage were independent predictors. The combined model achieved AUCs of 0.865 (95% CI, 0.828-0.899), 0.839 (95% CI, 0.775-0.895), and 0.785 (95% CI, 0.729-0.835) in training, internal, and external cohorts, respectively. In external validation, it was comparable to the clinical model (AUC = 0.790; BH-adjusted P = 0.076), and the ITH-only model performed poorly (AUC = 0.548). SHAP identified tumor location, T stage, and ITH features as major contributors. Transcriptomics identified 378 differentially expressed genes, and PPI analysis suggested AKT1 as a hub candidate. IHC showed higher AKT1 H-scores in MSS tumors (143.60 ± 26.14 vs. 76.74 ± 38.43; P = 0.008).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The model showed favorable training/internal performance but moderate external performance without clear incremental value. Larger prospective multicenter cohorts are needed. Transcriptomic and pilot IHC analyses suggest possible AKT1 expression differences between MSI-H and MSS rectal cancers.

items.authors: Rahmatullah ZF, Woronko AE, Hruban RH, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Pancreatoblastoma is a malignant tumor, which accounts for less than 1% of all pancreatic neoplasms. Further, it is rarely seen in adults and has a poor prognosis with metastasis or local invasion is present in nearly half of adult patients at diagnosis, most often involving the liver.

sections.text: Pancreatoblastoma is a malignant tumor, which accounts for less than 1% of all pancreatic neoplasms. Further, it is rarely seen in adults and has a poor prognosis with metastasis or local invasion is present in nearly half of adult patients at diagnosis, most often involving the liver. CT is the first-line modality for detection and surgical planning, yet the findings overlap those of more common pancreatic tumors. Pancreatoblastoma typically presents as a large exophytic mass in the pancreatic head with well-defined margins and an enhancing capsule. However, the capsule is often incomplete, and advanced tumors may show infiltrative borders. The mass is heterogeneous and may be solid or mixed solid and cystic, with calcification, enhancing internal septations, necrosis, hemorrhage, or potentially even internal vascularity. Pancreatoblastoma is mostly hypoattenuating relative to normal pancreatic parenchyma and shows progressive enhancement. Large tumors may cause biliary or main pancreatic ductal dilatation, tumor thrombus, or invasion of adjacent organs. Using pathologically proven adult cases, this pictorial review illustrates the spectrum of CT appearances of pancreatoblastoma and highlights the imaging characteristics of this rarely encountered tumor.

items.title: Enhanced prognosis stratification following surgery for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to optimize clinical decisions by reflecting tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment.
items.authors: Wu J, Fu X, Wu H, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: IPSS-PDAC is a non-invasive and robust prognostic stratification system that integrates imaging features and clinicopathological features. By sensitively reflecting tumor heterogeneity and TME, it provides references for clinical decision-making in the postoperative management of PDAC patients.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question This study constructs an integrated prognostic model combining imaging signatures and guideline-recommended clinicopathological variables to address unmet clinical challenges in postoperative risk stratification for PDAC patients. Findings A multi-planar Swin Transformer-based deep learning model (IPSS-PDAC) achieves a C-index of 0.836-0.871 for disease-free survival prediction. sections.label: Objective
sections.text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has an extremely dismal postoperative prognosis. Conventional TNM staging cannot adequately characterize tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment, leading to suboptimal risk stratification. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an integrated prognostic system for PDAC by combining deep learning (DL)-based radiomic features with guideline‑recommended clinicopathological variables.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This multicenter retrospective study included 592 patients with PDAC who underwent R0 surgical resection. A Swin Transformer-assisted DL classifier (Outcome Prediction for PDAC, OP-PDAC) was built using multi-planar contrast-enhanced CT scans (axial, coronal, and sagittal planes). Radiogenomic analysis was conducted in 41 patients to elucidate the biological underpinnings of the OP-PDAC. Furthermore, the Intelligent Prognosis Stratification System (IPSS-PDAC) was developed by incorporating clinicopathological variables into the OP-PDAC framework.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: In the derivation and test cohorts, the C‑index of OP-PDAC for predicting 1‑year disease‑free survival (DFS) ranged from 0.807 to 0.844, which was significantly higher than that of the clinicopathological model (CP-PDAC; C‑index, 0.631-0.656). The IPSS-PDAC further enhanced predictive performance, yielding a C‑index of 0.836-0.871, and enabled effective stratification for both DFS and overall survival (all log‑rank p < 0.01). Radiogenomic analysis revealed that high‑risk patients exhibited an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, elevated stromal scores, activated oncogenic pathways, and reduced CD8+ T‑cell infiltration.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: IPSS-PDAC is a non-invasive and robust prognostic stratification system that integrates imaging features and clinicopathological features. By sensitively reflecting tumor heterogeneity and TME, it provides references for clinical decision-making in the postoperative management of PDAC patients.

items.title: The toothless molar tooth malformation: exploratory fetal MRI-based phenotypical assessment of cases with suspected Joubert syndrome.
items.authors: Stuempflen M, Weber M, Schmidbauer VU, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: This study provides novel insights into the prenatal presentation of molar tooth malformations and accompanying anomalies commonly observed in patients with a suspected diagnosis of JS. JS can be suspected on fetal MRI even in the absence of classical MTS based on characteristic anomalies of the SCPs, brainstem, and cerebellum in combination with extracerebral anomalies supporting this diagnosis.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: QuestionWhat are phenotypical presentations of patients with suspected Joubert syndrome (JS) in fetal MRI and can JS be suspected in absence of molar tooth sign? FindingsJS can be suspected in fetal MRI without MTS based on characteristic changes in superior cerebellar peduncles, brainstem, and cerebellum and co-occurring extracerebral anomalies. Clinical relevanceThis exploratory study provides novel insights into the prenatal presentation of molar tooth malformations and associated anomalies commonly observed in cases with suspected JS. These findings may aid counseling physicians in selecting appropriate pregnancy management for patients with suspected JS.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: The molar tooth sign (MTS) is based on maloriented superior cerebellar peduncles (SCPs), a deepened interpeduncular fossa, and vermian hypoplasia, which may be less clearly delineable prenatally. Phenotypic assessment of patients with suspected Joubert syndrome (JS) was conducted, and additional morphological characteristics of JS on fetal MRI were defined.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: In this retrospective study, phenotypic assessment was performed for patients with a fetal MRI-based suspected diagnosis of JS. Analysis of the fetal brain included detection of MTS, brainstem anomalies, elevation of the fastigium in the midsagittal plane, thickened SCP with a course parallel to the anterior/middle cerebral fossa in the parasagittal plane, cerebellar dysplasia, cephaloceles, and extracerebral ciliopathic manifestations.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Eleven patients were identified and analyzed-three cases with genetic confirmation of JS, three with incomplete genetic testing, five without confirmatory genetic testing. Classical MTS was present in 55% of cases. Pathological appearance of the SCPs was observed in 73%, and dysplastic cerebellum and brainstem hypo- or dysplasia in 100%. Elevation of the fastigium was observed in 91%, cephaloceles in 46%, and extracerebral anomalies, especially renal, in 64%. All cases showed a hypo- and dysplastic vermis.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: This study provides novel insights into the prenatal presentation of molar tooth malformations and accompanying anomalies commonly observed in patients with a suspected diagnosis of JS. JS can be suspected on fetal MRI even in the absence of classical MTS based on characteristic anomalies of the SCPs, brainstem, and cerebellum in combination with extracerebral anomalies supporting this diagnosis.

items.title: Five-compartment restriction spectrum imaging for noninvasive assessment of liver fibrosis in chronic liver disease.
items.authors: Chen H, Zhan S, Qin Z, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Five-compartment RSI provides diffusion metrics associated with histologic fibrosis stage, and RSI-LF showed diagnostic performance numerically comparable to that of MRE. RSI is a promising microstructure-sensitive biomarker for liver fibrosis staging that warrants multicenter validation.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Noninvasive staging of liver fibrosis is essential in chronic liver disease (CLD). Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) is well validated but requires dedicated hardware, whereas the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) derived from conventional diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) lacks specificity. Restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) decomposes the diffusion signal into multiple compartments and may capture fibrosis-related microstructural changes.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To investigate the feasibility of RSI for noninvasive liver fibrosis staging in CLD and to compare its diagnostic performance with that of MRE, using liver biopsy as the reference standard.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective study included 100 consecutive patients with CLD who underwent liver biopsy, 3.0-T multi-b-value DWI (nine b values, 0-1500 s/mm²), and MRE within 6 months. Multi-compartment RSI models (K = 2-5) were fitted to region-of-interest-averaged signals, and the optimal model was selected using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). An RSI liver fibrosis index (RSI-LF) was derived from compartment fractions using ordinal logistic regression and internally validated with 1000 bootstrap resamples. AUCs of RSI-LF were compared with those of MRE and ADC using the paired DeLong test.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The five-compartment RSI model (RSI5) showed the lowest BIC. The second and fourth fractions, K5C2 and K5C4, correlated positively (ρ = 0.53) and negatively (ρ = -0.55) with fibrosis stage (both false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p < 0.001). RSI-LF yielded AUCs of 0.774 (95% CI: 0.651-0.898), 0.863 (0.793-0.933), and 0.911 (0.842-0.981) for ≥F2, ≥F3, and F4, respectively, with negligible bootstrap optimism. AUCs did not differ significantly from those of MRE at any threshold (all p > 0.05). RSI-LF also outperformed ADC at the ≥F3 and F4 thresholds (both p < 0.001).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Five-compartment RSI provides diffusion metrics associated with histologic fibrosis stage, and RSI-LF showed diagnostic performance numerically comparable to that of MRE. RSI is a promising microstructure-sensitive biomarker for liver fibrosis staging that warrants multicenter validation.

items.title: Diagnostic performance of liver virtual non-contrast and virtual unenhanced reconstructions derived from photon-counting detector CT of the upper abdomen.
items.authors: Gnasso C, Marras G, Piccinni G, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: VUE reconstructions showed good agreement with TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen in both contrast phases, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs and was closer to TNC than VUE only in subcutaneous fat and venous-phase muscle. Substantial bias in vascular and bone structures limits the interchangeability of both algorithms with TNC imaging. VNC may support a potential reduction in radiation dose when replacing a planned TNC acquisition; since lesion detection and characterization were not evaluated, the safe omission of TNC was not demonstrated.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) enables native spectral imaging with the generation of virtual non-contrast (VNC) images from contrast-enhanced acquisitions. Two reconstruction algorithms are currently available, Virtual Unenhanced (VUE) and Liver Virtual Non-Contrast (LVNC), but their reliability compared with True Non-Contrast (TNC) imaging in abdominal applications remains incompletely established. This study evaluated the quantitative accuracy, image quality, and potential clinical impact of VNC reconstructions derived from PCD-CT.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: In this retrospective single-center study, 150 patients, of whom 140 were included for the analyses, underwent multiphasic PCD-CT including TNC, arterial, and portal venous phases. VNC datasets were generated from arterial and venous acquisitions using the VUE and LVNC algorithms. Tissue attenuation, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were compared with TNC images. The agreement of VNC reconstructions with TNC-based classification criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis, and osteoporosis was also evaluated.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Significant attenuation differences were observed between TNC and VNC reconstructions across most tissues. The smallest errors were found in soft tissues, particularly the liver and spleen, whereas the largest discrepancies occurred in vascular and osseous structures. SNR was higher on VNC than on TNC images in the liver, spleen and paravertebral muscle but lower in several other tissues, whereas CNR was higher with LVNCa and lower with VUEv than with TNC. VUE most closely reproduced TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs. Agreement with TNC-based criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis and osteoporosis required reconstruction-specific cut-offs, which should be considered exploratory. Omitting TNC could potentially reduce radiation exposure by 16.5% for upper abdomen and 21.2% for total abdominal examinations.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: VUE reconstructions showed good agreement with TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen in both contrast phases, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs and was closer to TNC than VUE only in subcutaneous fat and venous-phase muscle. Substantial bias in vascular and bone structures limits the interchangeability of both algorithms with TNC imaging. VNC may support a potential reduction in radiation dose when replacing a planned TNC acquisition; since lesion detection and characterization were not evaluated, the safe omission of TNC was not demonstrated.

items.title: Robust visualization of the right adrenal vein using photon-counting CT across all BMI groups.
items.authors: Xu M, Liu L, Song R, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: PCCT provides favorable RAV visualization across the investigated BMI groups, with low-keV imaging and smoother reconstruction kernels associated with improved visualization quality.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate the robust visualization of photon-counting CT (PCCT) for right adrenal vein (RAV) across body mass index (BMI) groups with respect to virtual monochromatic imaging (VMI) energy levels and reconstruction kernels.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: A total of 302 patients who underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal PCCT were enrolled and stratified into non-obese, overweight, and obese groups based on Asian-specific BMI criteria. VMIs were reconstructed at 40, 55, and 70 keV with three vascular‑specific reconstruction kernels (Bv40, Bv48, Bv60). For quantitative evaluation, two radiologists assessed image metrics, including CT attenuation, image noise (standard deviation [SD]), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). Separately, another pair of radiologists independently evaluated qualitative image quality (encompassing both overall image quality and RAV visualization quality) using a 5-point Likert scale.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Quantitative evaluation showed that VMI energy level and reconstruction kernel were associated with changes in quantitative image quality metrics, with significant interactions between energy level and reconstruction kernel for all four quantitative metrics (all P < 0.001). Exploratory analyses suggested BMI-related interactions in RAV attenuation and subjective visualization quality. Lower keV increased RAV CT attenuation and CNR, with the highest values at 40 keV across all BMI groups. Qualitative evaluation demonstrated a 100% RAV visualization rate across all reconstruction settings and BMI groups, with median visualization scores ranging from 3.0 to 5.0. Inter-reader agreement was excellent (weighted κ = 0.82).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: PCCT provides favorable RAV visualization across the investigated BMI groups, with low-keV imaging and smoother reconstruction kernels associated with improved visualization quality.

items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Uribe C, Kurkowska S, Brosch-Lenz J, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Under more standardized conditions, organ absorbed dose estimates showed markedly lower variability, with QCD values as low as 3%. These results support implementation of standardized VOI segmentation rules, time-activity curve modeling conventions, and auditable quality control and reporting procedures to improve reproducibility in both clinical trials and routine practice.

sections.text: Personalized radiopharmaceutical therapies rely on accurate and reproducible absorbed dose estimates. However, substantial variability persists because of differences in imaging protocols, segmentation, time-activity curve fitting and integration, and dose calculation implementation. The Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging 177Lu Dosimetry Challenge was a 5-task international study designed to isolate sources of variability in image-based dosimetry workflows. In this final publication, we integrate findings across the series and perform a retrospective analysis of the original full-workflow submissions to estimate the reduction in variability achievable through methodologic consistency and quality assurance. Methods: In this final analysis, the original task 1 end-to-end SPECT/CT workflow submissions were reevaluated to generate a refined task 1 dataset by excluding previously identified processing or reporting mistakes, as well as submissions with methodologic choices inconsistent with the recommendations derived from the challenge. Exclusion criteria included nonstandard volume-of-interest (VOI) definitions, inconsistent VOI handling, inappropriate time-activity curve fitting and integration, and omission of required mass scaling. Variability was quantified using the interquartile range and quartile coefficient of dispersion (QCD). Results: The refined task 1 analysis showed that a substantial fraction of the observed variability is potentially avoidable. Exclusions reduced the analyzed dataset by approximately 50% and narrowed absorbed dose distributions for most organs and lesions. For patient A, QCD decreased for total kidney (23.1% to 3.0%), spleen (24.2% to 7.8%), and lesion 1 (22.8% to 13.3%). For patient B, organ variability also decreased (12.6% to 8.2% in the liver and 15.3% to 10.9% in the left kidney), although variability for some lesions decreased less substantially. Findings across the challenge indicated that, among the workflow steps evaluated, segmentation and time-activity curve fitting/integration were the dominant contributors to variability, whereas variability from the absorbed dose calculation step alone was generally small once upstream inputs were standardized. Conclusion: A substantial portion of variability in radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry is potentially avoidable through standardization and quality assurance. Under more standardized conditions, organ absorbed dose estimates showed markedly lower variability, with QCD values as low as 3%. These results support implementation of standardized VOI segmentation rules, time-activity curve modeling conventions, and auditable quality control and reporting procedures to improve reproducibility in both clinical trials and routine practice.

items.title: Efficacy of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 With and Without Androgen Receptor Pathway Inhibitors for mAPM-R Prostate Cancer: Secondary Analysis of VISION.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Yazdanpanah O, Calais J, Chi KN, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: The clinical benefits of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 were similar with and without concomitant ARPIs. The addition of concomitant ARPIs to [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 provided a numerically higher PSA response and a numerically greater median PSA-PFS and median OS.

sections.text: The potential clinical benefit and impact on tolerability of combining androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 remain uncertain and were not evaluated in the primary analysis of VISION (NCT03511664). In this secondary analysis, we assessed efficacy and safety of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 with and without concomitant ARPIs in previously treated patients (≥1 ARPI and 1 or 2 taxanes) with metastatic androgen pathway modulator-resistant prostate cancer (formerly metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer). Methods: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response, duration of PSA response, PSA progression-free survival (PSA-PFS), radiographic progression-free survival, overall survival (OS), and adverse events were explored in this post hoc analysis. For OS, a time-adjusted multivariate analysis was performed to control for biases. Results: Among patients randomized to [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617, 289 versus 262 in the full analysis set and 283 versus 246 patients in the safety analysis set received treatment with and without concomitant ARPIs, respectively. Among patients treated with versus without ARPIs, 49.7% versus 42.2% had a PSA response (≥50% reduction in PSA level) (odds ratio, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.93-2.13; nominal 2-sided P = 0.103), with a median response duration of 9.4 mo versus 8.8 mo, respectively. The median PSA-PFS was 8.6 mo versus 7.3 mo (hazard ratio, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.70-1.09; P = 0.120 [nominal 1-sided stratified log-rank test]). A time-adjusted multivariate analysis showed a median OS of 16.6 versus 13.3 mo (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.56-1.10; 2-sided P = 0.160). The frequency, nature, and severity of adverse events were similar between groups. Conclusion: The clinical benefits of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 were similar with and without concomitant ARPIs. The addition of concomitant ARPIs to [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 provided a numerically higher PSA response and a numerically greater median PSA-PFS and median OS.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Female infertility affects approximately 15% of couples of reproductive age, with tubal disease responsible for up to one-third of cases. Therefore, accurate, minimally invasive evaluation of tubal patency is a cornerstone of fertility assessment.

sections.text: Female infertility affects approximately 15% of couples of reproductive age, with tubal disease responsible for up to one-third of cases. Therefore, accurate, minimally invasive evaluation of tubal patency is a cornerstone of fertility assessment. Among the available modalities, including hysterosalpingography (HSG), MR HSG, and laparoscopic chromopertubation, hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography (HyCoSy) has gained prominence as a valuable alternative to conventional methods due to its safety, accessibility, and diagnostic reliability. Recent advances in contrast-enhanced US involving the use of second-generation microbubble agents combined with three-dimensional (3D) and four-dimensional (4D) acquisition technologies have significantly improved the performance of HyCoSy. These developments enable real-time volumetric visualization of the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes, enhancing both anatomic delineation and functional assessment of tubal patency. In addition, combined 3D and 4D (3D-4D) HyCoSy enables complementary evaluation of uterine morphology, adnexal structures, and associated infertility-related disorders such as endometriosis and adhesions, facilitating a comprehensive "one-stop" reproductive imaging approach. This article is intended to serve as a practical guide to performing 3D-4D HyCoSy with microbubble contrast agents, including preparation, technical parameters, and findings interpretation. In addition, the authors compare HyCoSy with conventional techniques, review characteristic imaging patterns of tubal patency and occlusion, and discuss potential pitfalls and preventive strategies. As an advanced US technology combined with a dynamic functional perspective, 3D-4D HyCoSy represents a powerful, cost-effective, and patient-friendly tool for integrated fertility evaluation in modern radiology practices.

sections.text: Yttrium 90 transarterial radioembolization has evolved from a palliative lobar therapy for advanced liver malignancies into a versatile potentially curative treatment across hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) stages, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), and liver metastases. Central to this evolution is the shift from empirical population-based activity prescriptions to personalized dosimetry, tailoring administered activity to each patient's anatomy, tumor biology, treatment intent, and microsphere distribution to optimize tumor absorbed dose while constraining normal tissue exposure. Prospective studies have demonstrated that personalized dosimetry significantly improves tumor response and overall survival compared with conventional dosing. Despite this evidence, clinical adoption remains inconsistent. In this review, the authors aim to address that gap by providing a practical intent-based framework for implementation. They present dosimetric principles, activity prescription methods, and dose-response evidence across HCC, iCCA, and liver metastases, with practical recommendations organized by treatment intent. Treatment intent, whether curative or palliative, is the primary determinant of dosimetric strategy, guiding selection of the dosimetry model, target dose, and normal liver dose constraints. The authors review pretreatment planning work flows and posttreatment verification and present a practical decision algorithm integrating clinical intent, imaging, and dosimetry modeling.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Chronic Liver Disease: 2026 Update.
items.journal_full: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
items.authors: Expert Panel on Gastrointestinal Imaging, Fung A, El Khouli RH, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: The guideline development and revision include an extensive analysis of current medical literature from peer reviewed journals and the application of well-established methodologies (RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE) to rate the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where evidence is lacking or equivocal, expert opinion may supplement the available evidence to recommend imaging or treatment.

sections.text: Chronic liver disease, caused by a range of etiologies, can lead to progressive liver function deterioration, hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, and, ultimately, end-stage liver disease. With cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease, complications include portal hypertension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, refractory ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and primary hepatocellular carcinoma. Imaging plays an important role in the diagnosis, treatment response assessment, and surveillance of chronic liver disease, specifically of hepatic hemochromatosis, steatosis, and fibrosis, in an effort to prevent progression to cirrhosis. This document reviews the imaging modalities best suited for these clinical scenarios, and a summary of current evidence is provided to support the use of various modalities for each of the clinical contexts. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision include an extensive analysis of current medical literature from peer reviewed journals and the application of well-established methodologies (RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE) to rate the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where evidence is lacking or equivocal, expert opinion may supplement the available evidence to recommend imaging or treatment.

items.title: Diagnostic performance and interobserver agreement of MRI for pancreatic cystic lesions: a multi-reader study with surgical histopathologic correlation.
items.authors: Elsherif SB, Saba B, Kim J, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: In this surgically selected cohort, consensus MRI differentiates mucinous from nonmucinous PCLs with high sensitivity. Detection of advanced neoplasia, particularly noninvasive high-grade dysplasia, remains challenging because of overlap with low-grade lesions. Fair-to-moderate interobserver agreement highlights the challenges of MRI-based risk stratification. The surgically selected cohort provides histopathologic confirmation but should be considered when interpreting performance estimates in the broader surveillance population.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To determine the diagnostic performance and interobserver agreement of MRI for differentiating mucinous from non-mucinous pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) and identifying advanced neoplasia using surgical pathology as the reference standard.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective single-center study included surgically resected PCLs with preoperative MRI (2019-2025). Three independent readers blindly assessed cyst subtype and imaging features, including worrisome features (WF) and high-risk stigmata (HRS) according to the 2024 Kyoto guideline. Consensus interpretation was established with a fourth senior abdominal radiologist. Diagnostic performance for mucinous lesion characterization and advanced neoplasia (high-grade dysplasia and invasive carcinoma) was evaluated. Interobserver agreement was assessed using Fleiss κ and Gwet AC1. Logistic regression and ROC analyses identified imaging predictors of advanced neoplasia.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 85 patients were included (mean age, 66.8 ± 12.5 years; 50.6 % female). At pathology, 70/85 lesions (82.4 %) were mucinous and 23/85 (27.1 %) represented advanced neoplasia, including 21 high-grade dysplasia and two IPMN-derived PDAC. MRI consensus interpretation achieved 100 % sensitivity, 80 % specificity, and 96.5 % accuracy for identifying mucinous lesions. MRI demonstrated 52.2 % sensitivity and 67.7 % specificity for advanced neoplasia using WF or HRS, whereas HRS alone improved specificity (95.2 %) at the expense of sensitivity (21.7 %). All readers correctly identified both cases of IPMN-derived PDAC. Interobserver agreement for cyst subtype classification was fair by Fleiss κ but substantial by Gwet AC1, whereas agreement for detecting advanced neoplasia was moderate. Main pancreatic duct diameter independently predicted advanced neoplasia (OR, 1.18; 95 % CI, 1.01-1.38; p = 0.042) and outperformed cyst size (AUC, 0.69 vs 0.56).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: In this surgically selected cohort, consensus MRI differentiates mucinous from nonmucinous PCLs with high sensitivity. Detection of advanced neoplasia, particularly noninvasive high-grade dysplasia, remains challenging because of overlap with low-grade lesions. Fair-to-moderate interobserver agreement highlights the challenges of MRI-based risk stratification. The surgically selected cohort provides histopathologic confirmation but should be considered when interpreting performance estimates in the broader surveillance population.

items.title: Single-Time-Point Time-integrated Activity Estimation for Dosimetry in 177Lu-PSMA Therapy: Evaluation of Analytical and Machine Learning Methods.
items.authors: Mansouri Z, Fitzpatrick K, Fredericks M, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: Analytical STP methods yield accurate TIA estimates when applied at appropriate imaging TPs. ML models that integrate analytical estimates with imaging features provide modest improvements in accuracy with less sensitivity to TP selection. However, optimal timing remained structure-dependent, requiring a compromise when a single acquisition is used. These findings support the potential of ML-driven STP dosimetry in 177Lu-PSMA-617 radiopharmaceutical therapy to enable more flexible and clinically feasible workflows, pending further validation with larger and more diverse data sets.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: The routine clinical implementation of patient-specific dosimetry in 177Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy can be challenging due to the need for multiple-time-point posttherapy SPECT/CT imaging to estimate time-integrated activity (TIA). Single-time-point (STP) approaches offer a more practical alternative, although their accuracy has yet to be fully established. This study aimed to evaluate existing analytical STP methods and to assess the feasibility and performance of a machine learning (ML) framework.

sections.label: Patients and methods
sections.text: Thirty-four patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer undergoing 177Lu-PSMA-617 therapy were retrospectively analyzed. Reference TIAs were derived from multiple-time-point 177Lu SPECT/CT imaging at 3 or 4 time points (TPs) postinjection (TP1: 0.7-2.1 h, TP2: day 1-2, TP3: day 3-4, TP4: day 5-7) in cycle 1 for 147 tumors, 64 kidneys, and 65 parotid glands using monoexponential or biexponential fitting. Analytical STP methods, proposed by Hänscheid and Madsen, were evaluated across different TPs. For each organ, a ML model was developed using a residual learning approach, in which the log-transformed ratio between reference TIAs and analytical STP TIA estimates was modeled. Input features included combinations of STP SPECT-derived parameters, baseline 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET-derived biomarkers (for individual structures and whole-body tumor volume), and clinical variables. Model performance was evaluated by using multiple quantitative metrics within a 10-times repeated 5-fold nested cross-validation framework and compared with purely analytic STP approaches. Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Analytical methods showed strong performance at optimal imaging TPs (TP2 for kidney/parotid, and TP3 for tumor), with the largest errors observed at early imaging (TP1). Overall, ML models provided modest improvement over analytical methods across structures at most TPs. The best performance was achieved using a ML model combining PET/SPECT imaging features with analytical TIA estimates. The mean percentage errors of the models, across TPs, ranged from -1.7 ± 17.9% (TP2) to 7.4 ± 65.3% (TP1) for kidneys, -0.4 ± 12.1% (TP2) to 4.5 ± 26.7% (TP4) for parotid glands, and 1.4 ± 14.8% (TP3) to -4.1 ± 100.5% (TP1) for tumors. Within the present cohort and modeling framework, the inclusion of clinical variables did not significantly improve model performance. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis showed that the ML models applied a positive correction to the analytical TIA estimates at early imaging TPs and a negative correction at late TPs.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: Analytical STP methods yield accurate TIA estimates when applied at appropriate imaging TPs. ML models that integrate analytical estimates with imaging features provide modest improvements in accuracy with less sensitivity to TP selection. However, optimal timing remained structure-dependent, requiring a compromise when a single acquisition is used. These findings support the potential of ML-driven STP dosimetry in 177Lu-PSMA-617 radiopharmaceutical therapy to enable more flexible and clinically feasible workflows, pending further validation with larger and more diverse data sets.

items.title: Advancing placenta accreta spectrum diagnosis: is 3-T MRI or combined MRI with ultrasound the answer?
items.authors: Tan S, Richmond D, Mil M, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Both US and 3-T MRIdemonstrated strong diagnostic performances for detecting PAS, with 3-T MRIdemonstrating stronger performance in this selective cohort, and not further improved by including US data. The continued use of US, MRI and clinical data for evaluating PAS disorder treatment options is recommended.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question No dedicated study has evaluated the diagnostic performance of 3-T MRIor the combined use of MRI with US in PAS. Findings 3-T MRIdemonstrates high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing PAS. The combined MRI and US assessment does not further improve diagnostic performance for PAS. Critical relevance statement 3-T MRImay be particularly useful as an adjunct in selected high-risk patients, equivocal ultrasound cases, or cases requiring assessment of myoinvasive disease and multidisciplinary surgical planning.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: This study compares the diagnostic performance of US and 3-T MRIin diagnosing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorder using final histopathological and surgical findings and explores the benefit of using a combined MRI and US approach to diagnose PAS.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of all patients undergoing 3-T MRIplacenta at our institution between January 2020 and November 2023. The gold standard for PAS outcome was histopathology, and where unavailable, we referred to the operative notes. Patients without surgical or histopathologic data, and non-diagnostic MRI studies were excluded. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), confidence intervals, and p-values were generated for MRI, US, and combined MRI + US to detect PAS with subgroup analysis for placenta accreta/increta and percreta.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Eighty-eight patients met the inclusion criteria. The sensitivity and specificity of MRI for all PAS was 100.0% and 80.0% (p < 0.001), compared to US 89.5% and 62.0% (p < 0.001), and combined MRI + US 100.0% and 56.0% (p < 0.001), respectively. For diagnosing placenta percreta, MRI had a sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% and 94.3% (p < 0.001), compared to US 55.6% and 94.3% (p < 0.001) and combined MRI + US 83.3% and 92.9% (p < 0.001).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Both US and 3-T MRIdemonstrated strong diagnostic performances for detecting PAS, with 3-T MRIdemonstrating stronger performance in this selective cohort, and not further improved by including US data. The continued use of US, MRI and clinical data for evaluating PAS disorder treatment options is recommended.

items.title: Penile inversion vaginoplasty: embryologic map, institutional technique, expected neoanatomy, and imaging of complications.
items.authors: Furlan V, Kampalath R, Chang O

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: It is important to understand the surgical steps involved in the creation of the external genitalia to effectively evaluate pelvic imaging in transgender individuals after penile inversion vaginoplasty (PIV). This review provides an overview of PIV, correlates neoanatomy with imaging, and discusses imaging evaluation of postoperative complications to guide clinical practice.

sections.text: It is important to understand the surgical steps involved in the creation of the external genitalia to effectively evaluate pelvic imaging in transgender individuals after penile inversion vaginoplasty (PIV). This review provides an overview of PIV, correlates neoanatomy with imaging, and discusses imaging evaluation of postoperative complications to guide clinical practice. During embryonic development of external genitalia, the genital tubercle differentiates into the glans penis and the clitoris in the male and female, respectively. The urogenital sinus differentiates into the lining of the male urethra and the lining of the vestibule in females. Importantly, embryologic homology provides a framework for understanding postoperative neoanatomy. Our institutional approach to PIV surgery utilizes the glans penis to construct the neoclitoris, the lining of the urethra to construct the neovestibule, and the penile and scrotal skin to line the neovagina. After surgery, contrast-enhanced CT is generally the first-line imaging modality for suspected acute deep postoperative complications, while MRI is preferred for detailed evaluation of neoanatomy and chronic postoperative complications. Correlating embryologic development, surgical technique, and imaging may improve clinician understanding of neoanatomy after PIV. This may facilitate accurate imaging evaluation of pelvic pathology in transgender individuals after PIV and promote timely diagnosis.

items.title: Integrated radiomics-deep learning modeling of hepatic vasculature for enhanced noninvasive prediction of portal hypertension and high-risk gastroesophageal varices.
items.authors: Qiu Q, Zheng R, Wang C, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A dual-path model integrating multi-vessel radiomics and deep learning features demonstrates robust predictive performance for CSPH and HRVs in cirrhotic patients. This approach may provide a new non-invasive alternative for risk stratification and clinical management of portal hypertension-related complications.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To evaluate whether CT-derived radiomics and deep learning features can improve non-invasive risk stratification of clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) and high-risk gastroesophageal varices (HRVs) in cirrhotic patients.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective study included 454 cirrhotic patients from center A and 77 from center B. CSPH labels were available only for patients from center A. Patients in both centers with available endoscopic findings were classified as HRVs or non-HRVs. A dual-path modeling framework integrating radiomics and deep learning-derived features extracted from multiple major hepatic vessels was developed, and was compared with single-path (radiomics-only and deep learning-only), single-vessel, vascular geometric, and clinical-feature-based models. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: For CSPH prediction, the dual-path model achieved the highest AUC (0.892 vs. 0.678-0.870 for the other models; P < 0.05 for most comparisons). For HRVs prediction, the proposed model achieved AUCs of 0.790 and 0.782 in the internal and external test set, respectively. The proposed model consistently outperformed the single-path models (0.625-0.648; all P < 0.05), single-vessel models (0.526-0.642; all P < 0.05), the vascular geometric model (0.528; P < 0.01), and the clinical-feature-based models (0.327-0.728; P < 0.001 for the APRI-based model) in the external test set.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: A dual-path model integrating multi-vessel radiomics and deep learning features demonstrates robust predictive performance for CSPH and HRVs in cirrhotic patients. This approach may provide a new non-invasive alternative for risk stratification and clinical management of portal hypertension-related complications.

items.title: Detection versus grading on prostate MRI: a multi-cohort study of diffusion, perfusion and implications for biparametric protocols.
items.authors: García-Hidalgo C, Consentino Hernández JA, Cayuela Espí JV

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Diffusion localized significant cancer, but mean ADC did not separate grade in detected lesions; perfusion timing was associated with grade, yet predicted it poorly and has not been externally validated. Whether omitting contrast forfeits clinically useful grading information therefore remains an open question, to be tested before contrast-free protocols are adopted where grade estimation matters.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: Prostate MRI is shifting toward biparametric protocols that omit the gadolinium-based dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) sequence - a decision validated entirely on cancer detection. Whether these protocols preserve the ability to estimate tumor grade, the quantity that drives management, has rarely been tested. Using unsupervised MRI "habitats" as a transferable probe, we asked whether the diagnostic contribution of MRI dissociates between detecting and grading prostate cancer.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Unsupervised k-means habitats of within-patient-normalized T2 and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), plus semi-quantitative DCE maps where available, were defined on PROSTATEx (training), frozen, and transferred unchanged to Prostate-MRI-US-Biopsy (external; 614 MRI targets and 12,809 biopsy cores with per-core Gleason) and QIN-Repeatability (test-retest). Under patient-grouped nested cross-validation we compared habitat, whole-lesion and clinical models, benchmarked habitats against ADC, validated habitat-pathology concordance against these cores, and tested whether the contribution of MRI dissociated between detection and grading.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Low-ADC habitats localized clinically significant cancer across the gland (odds ratio up to 3.05; two lowest-ADC habitats captured significant cancer at twice the random-sampling rate) - but did not exceed whole-lesion radiomics or the ADC value itself (area under the curve 0.69 versus 0.69, cross-validated in the external cohort; cores 0.58 versus 0.62). In 107 MRI-detected lesions, ADC no longer separated grade groups (p = 0.79), whereas DCE time-to-peak did, remaining associated with grade after adjustment for ADC, zone and volume (adjusted p = 0.006; likelihood-ratio p = 0.026), although out-of-sample prediction was weak (cross-validated κ 0.05).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Diffusion localized significant cancer, but mean ADC did not separate grade in detected lesions; perfusion timing was associated with grade, yet predicted it poorly and has not been externally validated. Whether omitting contrast forfeits clinically useful grading information therefore remains an open question, to be tested before contrast-free protocols are adopted where grade estimation matters.

items.title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in surgically resectable hepatocellular carcinoma (PRIME-HCC): a prospective, phase 1b, single-arm trial and translational analyses.
items.authors: D'Alessio A, Fulgenzi CAM, Pai M, et al.

conclusion.label: Interpretation
conclusion.text: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab is feasible in early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, and later-phase randomised trials are needed to confirm the efficacy of this treatment strategy. Longitudinal ctDNA monitoring could support detection of minimal residual disease and warrants further prospective validation.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab improves survival in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. We evaluated this combination as neoadjuvant therapy and investigated its effect on peripheral immunity and the tumour microenvironment.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: PRIME-HCC is a single-arm, phase 1b trial in adults (aged ≥18 years) with early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, Child-Pugh A liver function, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1. Patients received nivolumab (3 mg/kg intravenously on days 1 and 22 of the first and second cycle) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg intravenously on day 1 of the first cycle only) before liver resection. The primary endpoint was safety, assessed by treatment-related delays to surgery and adverse events in the intention-to-treat population. Translational analyses included imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics on paired tumour samples, peripheral immunophenotyping, T-cell receptor (TCR) β sequencing, and longitudinal tumour-agnostic circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) profiling. This trial was registered with EudraCT (2018-000987-27) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03682276); follow-up is currently ongoing.

sections.label: Findings
sections.text: Between Sept 18, 2019, and Sept 28, 2023, of 43 patients assessed for eligibility, 33 patients were enrolled (25 [76%] male and 8 [24%] female; median age 68 years [range 38-80; IQR 63-73]); median follow-up was 25·7 months (95% CI 21·2-30·1). Any-grade adverse events occurred in 31 (94%) of patients, with treatment-related adverse events (trAEs) in 25 (76%) patients. Grade 3 trAEs occurred in three (9%) patients (transaminase elevation, anaemia, and dyspnoea). Serious adverse events were recorded in three (9%) patients, and no grade 4-5 events or treatment-related deaths occurred. 30 (91%) patients underwent surgery, including two (6%) who had immune checkpoint inhibitor-related surgical delays. Objective response rate by RECIST 1.1 was noted in eight (25%; 95% CI 13-42) patients (one complete response and seven partial responses), with 31 (97%; 84-100) patients achieving disease control. The absence of ctDNA after surgery was associated with improved 2-year recurrence-free survival (nine [82%] of 11 patients vs two [29%] of seven; p=0·049), as was at least 50% ctDNA reduction (median not reached [95% CI not reached] vs 20·9 months [95% CI 16·3-25·4]; HR 0·14 [95% CI 0·02-0·91]; p=0·039). Patients with objective responses showed expansion of peripheral PD-1-positive, Ki-67-positive, CD8-positive T cells (T-responding exhausted cells [Tresp]), associated with higher baseline intratumoral progenitor-exhausted T cells (Tpex) and increased Tresp infiltration. Patients whose disease did not respond to treatment exhibited enrichment of terminally exhausted CD8-positive T cells (Tex-term; CD8-positive PD-1-positive TOX-positive cells) and regulatory T cells.

sections.label: Interpretation
sections.text: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab is feasible in early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, and later-phase randomised trials are needed to confirm the efficacy of this treatment strategy. Longitudinal ctDNA monitoring could support detection of minimal residual disease and warrants further prospective validation.

items.authors: Thanapirom K, Ngampimonsri J, Thaimai P, et al.

conclusion.text: LSM and SSM using 2D-SWE may help reduce the need for screening EGD in patients with cirrhosis, with observed missed-HRV rates of 4.8% and 4.0%, respectively.
