sections.text: For active surveillance assessment, 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT was performed in a 73-year-old man with Gleason 3+3 prostate adenocarcinoma. PET/CT showed a markedly enlarged prostate indenting the bladder base, with focal midline activity suggestive of prostatic urethral urinary retention. Intravenous furosemide was administered before 120-minute delayed imaging, which showed complete resolution of the activity and excluded pathologic uptake. After discharge, he developed urinary urgency and incomplete emptying, progressing to lower abdominal and pelvic pain with elevated creatinine. Postrenal acute kidney injury from acute urinary retention was diagnosed. Catheterization and inpatient monitoring normalized renal function, highlighting an underrecognized risk of forced diuresis.

items.title: Can CT Phantoms Produce Realistic CT Images of Human Anatomy? Physics-Based Evaluation of Multimaterial 3D-Printed CT Phantoms From CT Data.
items.authors: Jasper S, Jeukens C, Flohr T, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: CT phantoms generated from CT image volumes using 3D printing with multimaterial mapping on a voxel level accurately reproduce the template images in terms of image sharpness, noise characteristics, and attenuation properties of tissues with positive CT values not exceeding 1000 HU. The achievable spatial resolution is limited to medium-sharp levels and does not improve by using sharper template images. These findings support the use of image-based multimaterial 3D printing to produce realistic anthropomorphic phantoms for advanced CT image-quality assessment and optimization, and for validation of reconstruction algorithms and quantitative CT imaging methods.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: Patient-specific computed tomography (CT) phantoms can be produced using a novel 3D-printing technique that aims at replicating measured CT image volumes with high anatomic fidelity and accurate CT values. The purpose of this study is a comprehensive physics-based evaluation of both technical phantoms and a full-size adult abdominal phantom with regard to image-quality metrics and the reproducibility of CT values. In addition, the visualization of abdominal pathologies will be assessed.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: The study was conducted in 3 steps. First, a geometric reference disc phantom (40 mm thickness, 150 mm diameter) was 3D-printed using multimaterial jetting and scanned on a commercial photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) to assess the CT values of the base materials used for printing and to evaluate the influence of the printing process on spatial resolution and noise properties. Second, CT images of the reference phantom reconstructed with a medium-sharp and a sharp kernel were used as templates to print 2 CT-derived disc phantoms using multimaterial jetting with voxel-based material mapping. These phantoms were then scanned to assess how template image sharpness propagates into the image-quality properties of the final printed phantoms. Spatial resolution was evaluated using edge spread function (ESF) analysis and edge rise distance (ERD), whereas noise characteristics were assessed using noise power spectrum (NPS) analysis. Third, as a proof of concept, a full-size adult abdominal phantom was 3D-printed with a patient CT data set as template. Phantom images were compared with patient images regarding CT values, spatial resolution, noise properties, and the depiction of pathologic structures.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Evaluation of the CT attenuation of the base materials showed that CT values ranging from -37 HU to 995 HU in virtual monoenergetic images at 60 keV can be printed.For the reference disc, measured ESF curves showed close agreement with theoretical expectations across all reconstruction kernels, indicating preservation of spatial resolution by the printing process. CT-derived discs showed minor edge smoothing compared with the reference for smooth and medium-sharp reconstructions. For sharp reconstructions, edge smoothing was severe, with an ERD increase of up to 32% compared with the reference. Edge smoothing was more pronounced for the disc based on a sharp template. NPS were highly consistent across all discs, with only minor differences in peak amplitude. In the abdominal phantom images ESF and NPS closely matched those of the patient CT images. Measured attenuation agreed well for tissues with positive CT values up to 1000 HU. Fat was represented with increased CT values because of print material limitations. Clinically relevant pathologic structures, including a large hepatocellular carcinoma and a smaller focal liver lesion, were displayed comparably in the phantom images.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: CT phantoms generated from CT image volumes using 3D printing with multimaterial mapping on a voxel level accurately reproduce the template images in terms of image sharpness, noise characteristics, and attenuation properties of tissues with positive CT values not exceeding 1000 HU. The achievable spatial resolution is limited to medium-sharp levels and does not improve by using sharper template images. These findings support the use of image-based multimaterial 3D printing to produce realistic anthropomorphic phantoms for advanced CT image-quality assessment and optimization, and for validation of reconstruction algorithms and quantitative CT imaging methods.

items.title: Targeting PDGFRβ from radiopharmacy to nuclear medicine: Translational implementation of [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 PET/CT at an academic center.
items.authors: Ferrat M, Tzorzakakis A, Lindvall A, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: GMP-compliant production enabled the first reported oncology application of [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 in patients with liver tumours. The ongoing phase 1 IMAGINE-1 study will further evaluate its clinical potential.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Positron emission tomography (PET) enables non-invasive whole-body assessment of molecular biomarkers and is particularly valuable for evaluating heterogeneous diseases such as cancer. Platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta (PDGFRβ) is a stromal biomarker expressed on activated pericytes and fibroblasts that contributes to tumour remodelling, vascular regulation and therapeutic resistance. This study describes the translational implementation of the PDGFRβ-targeting PET tracer [68Ga]Ga-ATH001, from GMP-compliant radiopharmaceutical development to its first reported oncology application in patients with liver tumours.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: A GMP-compliant automated synthesis of [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 was established using a ModularLab PharmTracer synthesizer and validated for clinical use. The tracer was prospectively implemented in the IMAGINE-1 study (EU CT 2025-522290-11-00). PET imaging included dynamic liver acquisition immediately after injection, followed by whole-body PET/CT imaging and delayed liver scans to assess tracer biodistribution, tumour uptake and tracer kinetics.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 was successfully translated into clinical production using an automated in-house synthesis process, achieving a decay-corrected radiochemical yield of 51.9 ± 0.7 %, radiochemical purity of 97 %, radiochemical stability of 96.3 ± 0.5 % after 2 h at room temperature and apparent molar activity of 47.2 ± 1.6 GBq/µmol at EOS. Three consecutive production runs assessed reproducibility; a fourth batch served as a microbiological worst-case challenge and was excluded from the assessment. PET/CT imaging in three patients with colorectal liver metastases showed SUVpeak tumour-to-background ratios of 1.5 to 1.8 at 60 min after injection.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: GMP-compliant production enabled the first reported oncology application of [68Ga]Ga-ATH001 in patients with liver tumours. The ongoing phase 1 IMAGINE-1 study will further evaluate its clinical potential.

sections.label: Eu trial registration
sections.text: Clinical Trials Information system: CTIS, EU CT 2025-522290-11-00, Registered 29 September 2025, IMAGINE-1 | 2025-522290-11-00 | CTIS.eu.

items.title: Virtual liver biopsy for detecting steatohepatitis in chemotherapy-treated patients: comparison with whole-liver radiomics and external validation.
items.authors: Ammirabile A, Mastroleo F, De Martino R, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Virtual biopsy provides a reproducible, non-invasive radiomic sampling strategy for CASH prediction. Combined with liver volume metrics, it achieves performance comparable to whole-liver analysis, supporting its potential clinical application.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Despite its association with postoperative morbidity, the non-invasive preoperative assessment of CASH remains challenging in patients undergoing liver surgery. Findings Radiomic analysis based on a virtual liver biopsy, combined with volumetric measurements, showed excellent performance in predicting CASH, comparable to whole-liver analysis, with liver volume emerging as a key predictor. Critical Relevance Statement A standardized virtual biopsy-based radiomic analysis represents a promising non-invasive approach for evaluating liver parenchymal injury, as demonstrated in preoperative assessment of CASH and identification of high-risk surgical patients.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: Chemotherapy-associated steatohepatitis (CASH) increases the risk of postoperative liver failure and mortality in patients undergoing liver surgery. However, non-invasive diagnosis remains an unmet need. Radiomics has potential for characterizing liver parenchyma. This study evaluated the performance of a virtual liver biopsy for CASH prediction, comparing it with whole-liver radiomic analysis.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Two retrospective series of patients undergoing hepatectomy for colorectal liver metastases were analyzed: the public "Colorectal-Liver-Metastases" dataset (training and internal validation) and a monocenter series from Humanitas Research Hospital (external validation). Inclusion criteria were preoperative chemotherapy (≥ 2 months) and post-chemotherapy CT (thickness ≤ 5 mm). IBSI-compliant radiomic features were extracted from whole-liver parenchyma and from a virtual biopsy (manually segmented 2-mL cylinder of non-tumoral liver parenchyma). Estimated liver volume (eLV) was computed using three orthogonal diameters. Four XGBoost models were developed (70/30 split, 5-fold cross-validation): clinical; clinical + VB-radiomics (ViB); clinical + VB-radiomics + eLV (ViBE+); clinical + whole-liver radiomics (WholeLiver).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: One hundred eighty patients were included: 105 internal (63 males, mean age 58.9 years, 38% CASH+) and 75 external (44 males, mean age 62.4 years, 19% CASH+). WholeLiver and ViBE+ models achieved excellent and comparable performance in internal validation (WholeLiver: AUC = 0.857 (95% BS-CI: 0.676-0.954), accuracy = 0.774 (95% BS-CI: 0.613-0.903); ViBE + : AUC = 0.831 (95% BS-CI: 0.549-0.956), accuracy = 0.839 (95% BS-CI: 0.710-0.935); p = 0.814), outperforming ViB model (AUC = 0.724 (95% BS-CI: 0.483-0.896), accuracy = 0.774 (95% BS-CI: 0.613-0.903)). SHAP analysis confirmed liver volume metrics as key predictors. In external validation, the ViBE+ model achieved AUC = 0.745 (95% BS-CI: 0.604-0.886) and accuracy = 0.680 (95% BS-CI: 0.562-0.783).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Virtual biopsy provides a reproducible, non-invasive radiomic sampling strategy for CASH prediction. Combined with liver volume metrics, it achieves performance comparable to whole-liver analysis, supporting its potential clinical application.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Despite its association with postoperative morbidity, the non-invasive preoperative assessment of CASH remains challenging in patients undergoing liver surgery. Findings Radiomic analysis based on a virtual liver biopsy, combined with volumetric measurements, showed excellent performance in predicting CASH, comparable to whole-liver analysis, with liver volume emerging as a key predictor. Critical Relevance Statement A standardized virtual biopsy-based radiomic analysis represents a promising non-invasive approach for evaluating liver parenchymal injury, as demonstrated in preoperative assessment of CASH and identification of high-risk surgical patients.

items.title: Endovascular treatment of hepatic artery bleeding and pseudoaneurysms using stent-grafts: a retrospective single-centre analysis.
items.authors: Mathy RM, Da Florencia Ricardo D, Sedaghat S, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Stent-grafting is effective for managing hepatic artery bleeding, but precise sizing is crucial, as undersizing and small diameters increase the risk of inadequate haemostasis and occlusion.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question What are the technical and clinical outcomes of stent-graft treatment for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm, and which factors influence these outcomes? Findings Stent-graft treatment achieved high technical and clinical success rates. Stent-graft undersizing and smaller stent-graft diameters were associated with inadequate haemostasis and occlusion. Clinical relevance Stent-graft treatment is an effective option for managing hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm in critically ill patients. Accurate stent-graft sizing is a key determinant of clinical success.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To evaluate technical and clinical success rates and complications of stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysms.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This single-centre retrospective study consecutively included 58 patients who underwent attempted stent-grafting for hepatic artery bleeding (n = 40) or pseudoaneurysm (n = 18) between January 2010 and June 2021.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Technical success was achieved in 97% (56/58) of cases. Insufficient haemostasis after technical success was present in five cases (88% primary clinical success), decreasing to three cases after reintervention. In 3/5 cases, it was due to undersizing of the stent-graft, which occurred frequently, especially in vessel sizes ≥ 6 mm (n = 19, compared to the non-acute vessel diameter; n = 11, compared to the acute one). Median occlusion-free survival was 763 days. Patency rates were 81 ± 6% at 30 days and 56 ± 10% at two years. Early occlusion (≤ 30 days) was associated with significantly smaller stent-graft diameters (4.7 ± 0.7 mm vs 5.4 ± 0.7 mm; p = 0.014). In multivariate Cox regression analysis, a small diameter (4 mm) was confirmed as a risk factor for stent-graft occlusion (HR = 8.59, p = 0.006). Liver necrosis or liver failure due to insufficient collateralization occurred only in early occlusions. Median overall survival was 714 days. In 6/29 documented deaths, mortality was procedure-related (four because of insufficient haemostasis, with two after technical failure and two after technical success, and two because of fatal liver failure after stent-graft occlusion).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Stent-grafting is effective for managing hepatic artery bleeding, but precise sizing is crucial, as undersizing and small diameters increase the risk of inadequate haemostasis and occlusion.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question What are the technical and clinical outcomes of stent-graft treatment for hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm, and which factors influence these outcomes? Findings Stent-graft treatment achieved high technical and clinical success rates. Stent-graft undersizing and smaller stent-graft diameters were associated with inadequate haemostasis and occlusion. Clinical relevance Stent-graft treatment is an effective option for managing hepatic artery bleeding or pseudoaneurysm in critically ill patients. Accurate stent-graft sizing is a key determinant of clinical success.

items.title: Photon-counting detector CT for gastric cancer T staging: a comparative assessment with conventional energy integrating detector CT.
items.authors: Ji C, Li L, Li Y, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: PCD-CT demonstrated significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory retrospective comparison. The potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging warrants further validation.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question The diagnostic performance and potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging are still unclear. Findings PCD-CT showed significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory comparison. Clinical relevance PCD-CT may offer potential value in gastric cancer T staging.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) for gastric cancer T staging compared with conventional energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Fifty-three patients with preoperative PCD-CT and 54 patients with preoperative EID-CT were retrospectively enrolled. Two radiologists independently assessed the visibility and T stages using all available sequences, including virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs) from PCD-CT at 40, 50, 60, and 70 kiloelectron volt (keV) levels. The lesion detectability and diagnostic accuracy of the two CT systems were analyzed and compared. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of gastric cancer lesions were also measured.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Five lesions in the PCD-CT group and 12 lesions in the EID-CT group could not be confidently identified. For visible lesions, the overall T staging accuracies were 85.4% (95% CI: 72.8-92.8%) for Reader 1 and 83.3% (95% CI: 70.4-91.3%) for Reader 2 on PCD-CT, compared with 73.8% (95% CI: 58.9-84.7%) for Reader 1 and 78.6% (95% CI: 64.1-88.3%) for Reader 2 on EID-CT. The interobserver agreement for both CT systems was excellent, with weighted kappa values of 0.807 (95% CI: 0.693-0.921) for PCD-CT and 0.832 (95% CI: 0.720-0.943) for EID-CT. Quantitative analysis showed significantly higher SNR and CNR on PCD-CT than EID-CT (both p < 0.05).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: PCD-CT demonstrated significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory retrospective comparison. The potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging warrants further validation.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question The diagnostic performance and potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging are still unclear. Findings PCD-CT showed significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory comparison. Clinical relevance PCD-CT may offer potential value in gastric cancer T staging.

items.title: Ultrasound-derived fat fraction and shear wave elastography for liver assessment in bariatric surgery candidates: diagnostic performance and longitudinal changes.
items.authors: Zhang YL, Jin WK, Lee JM, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: UDFF provides accurate assessment of steatosis and shows potential for postoperative monitoring, whereas Auto-pSWE demonstrates moderate performance for significant fibrosis and transient postoperative changes, supporting its complementary rather than standalone role.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of ultrasound-derived fat fraction (UDFF) and auto-point shear wave elastography (Auto-pSWE) in bariatric surgery candidates, identify biological variables independently associated with their values and monitor postoperative changes in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) patients.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent UDFF and Auto-pSWE examinations within 3 days before bariatric surgery (October 2023-February 2025), with intraoperative biopsy as reference. Diagnostic performance of UDFF and Auto-pSWE (which measured shear wave velocity, SWV) were analyzed by receiver operating characteristic analysis. Multivariable generalized linear models identified variables independently associated with UDFF and SWV. Postoperative follow-ups were conducted at 3 and 6 months in MASLD patients.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 237 patients (mean age, 29.42 ± 9.37; 98 men) were included. UDFF showed excellent diagnostic performance for steatosis grades (AUCs: 0.991 for ≥S1, 0.911 for ≥S2, and 0.831 for ≥S3), with steatosis percentage as the strongest independent correlate (partial R2=0.302). SWV exhibited moderate diagnostic performance for significant fibrosis (AUC = 0.752), with fibrosis stages and alanine aminotransferase showing similar independent explanatory power (partial R2=0.067 and 0.063, respectively). In 104 MASLD patients, median UDFF decreased substantially by approximately 80% at 6 months while SWV transiently rose at 3 months before returning to a level comparable to baseline at 6 months.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: UDFF provides accurate assessment of steatosis and shows potential for postoperative monitoring, whereas Auto-pSWE demonstrates moderate performance for significant fibrosis and transient postoperative changes, supporting its complementary rather than standalone role.

items.title: Enhanced image quality and interpretation efficiency of voxelwise-computed diffusion-weighted imaging for bladder cancer VI-RADS assessment.
items.authors: Zhang M, Chen C, Zhao Q, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: vcDWI improved tumor conspicuity and background suppression, was compatible with non-inferiority to aDWI in an exploratory analysis, and reduced interpretation time in VI-RADS assessment, with good-to-excellent inter-observer agreement.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is central to bladder cancer assessment with the Vesical Imaging-Reporting and Data System (VI-RADS). Computed diffusion-weighted imaging (cDWI) reduces scan time but has limited signal-to-noise ratio (SNR); its voxelwise variant, voxelwise-computed diffusion-weighted imaging (vcDWI), may overcome this limitation. We evaluated whether vcDWI provides better image quality and shorter interpretation time while maintaining diagnostic accuracy compared with acquired DWI (aDWI) in VI-RADS assessment.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This single-center study included 111 consecutive patients with bladder cancer who underwent magnetic resonance imaging between October 2019 and October 2024. Two radiologists (2 and 5 years' experience) assessed image quality and objective metrics: tumor SNR (SNRtumor), urine-referenced SNR, contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and urine-referenced contrast ratio (CR, the ratio of tumor to urine signal intensity); they performed VI-RADS scoring and recorded interpretation times. Diagnostic performance for muscle invasion (VI-RADS ≥ 4) was evaluated against histopathology.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: vcDWI showed higher urine-referenced SNR and contrast ratio than all aDWI sequences (all p < 0.001), with CNR comparable to b = 1400 s/mm², whereas lesion-only SNRtumor was lower than at b = 700 and b = 1400 s/mm². It received superior subjective scores for lesion clarity and overall image quality (all p < 0.001). Diagnostic performance was comparable, with the difference in area under the curve (AUC) within a 0.10 non-inferiority margin in an exploratory post hoc analysis (AUCs, vcDWI vs. aDWI: 0.86 vs. 0.85 and 0.90 vs. 0.91; one-sided 95% upper bounds 0.030 and 0.054). vcDWI reduced interpretation time (median times 16.0% and 28.6% lower; p < 0.001), and inter-observer agreement was good for aDWI and excellent for vcDWI (weighted κ = 0.797 vs. 0.895).

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: vcDWI improved tumor conspicuity and background suppression, was compatible with non-inferiority to aDWI in an exploratory analysis, and reduced interpretation time in VI-RADS assessment, with good-to-excellent inter-observer agreement.

items.title: ESOI-ESUR multicentre validation of a structured MRI report for cervical cancer staging.
items.authors: Russo L, Pintican R, Woitek R, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A structured MRI report for cervical cancer staging significantly outperformed narrative reporting across all quality domains in a multicentre crossover design.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Cervical cancer management is highly stage-dependent, yet evidence on clinician-centred benefit of structured vs narrative MRI staging reports in routine practice is scarce. Findings In a multicentre crossover study, a FIGO-anchored structured MRI report significantly outperformed narrative reporting on all five general quality domains. Clinical relevance A structured MRI report standardises the communication of staging features that drive cervical cancer management and is preferred by referring clinicians over narrative reporting across specialties, disease stages, and European centres.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To compare an International Federation of Gyneology and Obstetrics (FIGO)-anchored structured MRI report with conventional narrative reporting for cervical cancer staging by evaluating referring clinicians' satisfaction.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: In this prospective multicentre crossover study (January-June 2024), consecutive patients with biopsy-proven cervical cancer at any FIGO stage underwent staging MRI at five European centres. For each patient, one narrative and one structured report were produced and independently evaluated by gynaecologists and radiation oncologists using a 12-item questionnaire (5-point Likert scale): five general items (Q1-Q5) for both formats and seven feature-specific items (Q6-Q12) for structured reports only. The primary endpoint was the proportion of structured-report evaluations with an overall score ≥ 20 (target ≥ 80%). Paired comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation (r) as effect size.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: One hundred patients were evaluated, yielding 200 report evaluations. Of 100 structured report evaluations, 98.0% (95% Clopper-Pearson CI: 93.0-99.8%) achieved an overall score ≥ 20, exceeding the 80% threshold, vs 78.0% (95% CI: 68.6-85.7%) for narrative reports. Structured reports scored significantly higher on all five general items and on the overall score (all p < 0.05), with the largest effects for readability (r = 0.95) and brevity (r = 0.85). The advantage was consistent across reader type, disease stage, and centre, with the strongest effect in locally advanced disease. Q6 (cervical stromal invasion) had the lowest feature-specific satisfaction (73.7% scoring ≥ 4), prompting template revision.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: A structured MRI report for cervical cancer staging significantly outperformed narrative reporting across all quality domains in a multicentre crossover design.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Cervical cancer management is highly stage-dependent, yet evidence on clinician-centred benefit of structured vs narrative MRI staging reports in routine practice is scarce. Findings In a multicentre crossover study, a FIGO-anchored structured MRI report significantly outperformed narrative reporting on all five general quality domains. Clinical relevance A structured MRI report standardises the communication of staging features that drive cervical cancer management and is preferred by referring clinicians over narrative reporting across specialties, disease stages, and European centres.

items.title: Diffusion-weighted MRI-derived μDiff index and extracellular volume fraction for severity classification of acute pancreatitis.
items.authors: Song X, Chen Y, Xiong Y, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: The DWI-derived μDiff index showed good discrimination of Atlanta-defined AP severity, with performance statistically comparable to MRSI. Their combination improved discrimination and retained high performance after internal validation, supporting their complementary value for severity classification.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To evaluate the diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)-derived quantitative index (μDiff) and T1 mapping-derived extracellular volume (ECV) fraction for distinguishing mild acute pancreatitis (AP) from the combined moderately severe or severe category, and to compare their discrimination with magnetic resonance severity index (MRSI) and clinical scores.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective study enrolled patients with AP who underwent abdominal MRI early after admission between 2024 and 2025. MRI protocols included conventional imaging, DWI, and pre- and postcontrast T1 mapping. The DWI-derived μDiff index was calculated from signal intensities at b values of 200 and 1500 s/mm2, whereas ECV was derived from pancreatic and blood-pool T1 values. AP severity was classified according to the 2012 revised Atlanta classification. Five single-predictor and four two-predictor logistic models were evaluated using AUCs with 95% confidence intervals, paired DeLong comparisons, and 2,000-resample bootstrap internal validation; calibration and exploratory decision-curve analyses were also performed.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Among 140 patients with AP, 99 had mild AP and 41 had moderately severe or severe AP. Both μDiff and ECV increased with severity. μDiff showed an AUC of 0.896 (95% CI, 0.836-0.956), with no statistically significant difference from MRSI (0.878; 95% CI, 0.811-0.946; DeLong p = 0.720). The μDiff + MRSI model achieved an apparent AUC of 0.972 (95% CI, 0.948-0.996) and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.969, with improved discrimination over μDiff and MRSI alone (Holm-adjusted p = 0.019 and p = 0.003, respectively). Its corrected calibration slope and Brier score were 0.911 and 0.067.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: The DWI-derived μDiff index showed good discrimination of Atlanta-defined AP severity, with performance statistically comparable to MRSI. Their combination improved discrimination and retained high performance after internal validation, supporting their complementary value for severity classification.

items.title: MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram for differentiating FIGO 2023 stage I from stage II-IV endometrial cancer: a multicenter study.
items.authors: Chu X, Gao L, Wang X, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The MRI-based DLRN showed robust discrimination between FIGO 2023 stage I and stage II-IV EC across test sets, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification and decision support.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question The introduction of the FIGO 2023 staging system has made the differentiation between stages more challenging, highlighting the need for better tools. Findings A new MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) accurately identifies high-risk patients, significantly outperforming traditional and individual clinical prediction methods. Critical relevance statement This tool helps doctors make better preoperative treatment plans, potentially improving patient outcomes in endometrial cancer.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: Preoperative identification of FIGO 2023 stage I endometrial cancer (EC) is important for treatment planning. We aimed to develop and validate a deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) based on multiparametric MRI to distinguish stage I EC from stage II-IV disease.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This study retrospectively enrolled patients from three centers. Patients from Centers 1 and 2 were randomly split into a training set (n = 616), and an internal test set (n = 158), and Center 3 served as an external test set (n = 232). The DLRN integrated deep-learning features, intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics features, and clinical characteristics. The DLRN was compared with clinical, radiomics, and deep-learning models. Discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with AUCs compared using DeLong's test.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 1006 patients (mean age, 56.5 ± 9.7 years) were analyzed. In the internal test set, the DLRN achieved an AUC of 0.852, higher than the clinical (0.673; p = 0.001), original radiomics (0.765; p = 0.030), and combined radiomics (0.793; p = 0.050) models. In the external test set, the DLRN remained robust (AUC = 0.829) and outperformed the clinical, original radiomics, and combined radiomics models (AUC = 0.680, 0.681, and 0.743; all p < 0.005). With DLRN assistance, radiologists showed improved diagnostic performance.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The MRI-based DLRN showed robust discrimination between FIGO 2023 stage I and stage II-IV EC across test sets, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification and decision support.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question The introduction of the FIGO 2023 staging system has made the differentiation between stages more challenging, highlighting the need for better tools. Findings A new MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) accurately identifies high-risk patients, significantly outperforming traditional and individual clinical prediction methods. Critical relevance statement This tool helps doctors make better preoperative treatment plans, potentially improving patient outcomes in endometrial cancer.

items.title: AASLD EXPO: Diagnosis and management of hepatitis delta virus (HDV) infection.
items.authors: Lim JK, Debes JD, Feld JJ, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: All HBsAg positive individuals should be screened for HDV. All adults with chronic HDV and compensated liver disease are candidates for HDV therapy. Recent advances in HDV treatment offer hope for meaningful improvement in clinical outcomes.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: HDV infection represents a rare co-infection or super-infection among persons with HBV infection and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to an increased risk of liver events such as hepatic decompensation and HCC.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: The Expert Practice Opinion (EXPO) document was developed by subject matter experts and commissioned by the AASLD Practice Guidelines Committee to provide timely guidance on the screening, diagnosis, and management of HDV infection. Writing group members performed a targeted literature review and generated EXPO statements which were agreed upon by group consensus.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: All individuals who are HBsAg positive should be tested at least once for HDV infection with HDV antibody. HDV antibody positive individuals should undergo HDV RNA testing to confirm active infection. All individuals with chronic HDV should undergo further evaluation including non-invasive fibrosis testing, preferably with elastography. Lab monitoring and HCC surveillance imaging is suggested every 6 months. All adults with chronic HDV viremia and compensated liver disease should be considered candidates for HDV therapy with bulevirtide for chronic virologic suppression, or alternatively bulevirtide plus peg-IFN alfa-2a for individuals without contraindications to peg-IFN and who desire a finite duration regimen. Considerations for patient selection, treatment regimen, monitoring, assessment of response, and care of patients in special populations are summarized in the document.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: All HBsAg positive individuals should be screened for HDV. All adults with chronic HDV and compensated liver disease are candidates for HDV therapy. Recent advances in HDV treatment offer hope for meaningful improvement in clinical outcomes.

items.title: Fetal Liver Volume and Morphology in Growth-Restricted Fetuses and Their Association With Neonatal Morbidity: An MRI Study.
items.journal_full: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
items.authors: Misochnik M, Olender A, Schonberger D, et al.

conclusion.label: Data conclusion
conclusion.text: FGR was associated with reduced fetal liver size and altered geometry, which were associated with neonatal morbidity.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) may induce redistribution of the fetal circulation to preserve perfusion of vital organs. Reduced hepatic delivery of oxygen- and nutrient-rich blood may cause volumetric and morphological remodeling.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To quantify fetal liver volume and morphology in FGR and assess associations with adverse neonatal outcomes.

sections.label: Study type
sections.text: Single-center, prospective and retrospective.

sections.label: Population
sections.text: Ninety-two singleton pregnancies: 36 FGR cases (prospective) and 56 appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) controls (retrospective).

sections.label: Field strength/sequence
sections.text: 3-T, True Fast Imaging with Steady-State Free Precession (TrueFISP) for fetal liver and body imaging, and TrueFISP or Half-Fourier Acquisition Single-shot Turbo Spin-Echo for brain imaging.

sections.label: Assessment
sections.text: The fetal liver, body, and brain were segmented using deep learning tools. Liver volume, liver-to-body and brain-to-liver volume ratios, and 12 liver PyRadiomics shape features were assessed. Neonates were followed for composite adverse neonatal outcomes (CANO) until discharge.

sections.label: Statistical tests
sections.text: Linear regression assessed associations with gestational age in AGA fetuses. Linear mixed-effects models compared groups, adjusting for gestational age and fetal sex. Univariable logistic regression assessed associations with CANO. Benjamini-Hochberg correction controlled the false discovery rate at 0.05.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: FGR fetuses had significantly lower liver volume than AGA fetuses (74.95 ± 1.76 vs. 114.89 ± 2.18 cm3), lower liver-to-body ratio (0.053 ± 0.001 vs. 0.057 ± 0.001), and higher brain-to-liver ratio (2.637 ± 0.085 vs. 1.978 ± 0.047). FGR fetuses demonstrated significantly less elongated liver geometry, (10.7% higher PyRadiomics elongation values) and had a significantly higher surface-to-volume ratio (11.9%). CANO occurred in 30/92 neonates (27 FGR, 3 AGA). Higher brain-to-liver ratio (OR = 4.12, 95% CI: 1.93-8.77), PyRadiomics elongation values (less elongated geometry; OR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.26-3.30), PyRadiomics flatness values (less flattened geometry; OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.07-2.65), and surface-to-volume ratio (OR = 3.26, 95% CI: 1.80-5.90) were significantly associated with CANO.

sections.label: Data conclusion
sections.text: FGR was associated with reduced fetal liver size and altered geometry, which were associated with neonatal morbidity.

items.title: PDGFRβ-Targeting VHH Tracer Enables Noninvasive PET Imaging of Kidney Fibrosis.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Caspers T, Kulkarni V, Florea A, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Tracer signal correlated with PDGFRβ expression, confirming the specificity of the approach. Conclusion: We provide the first proof of concept for noninvasive PET imaging of PDGFRβ-expressing fibrogenic cells in kidney disease, supporting further development of this approach for specific, noninvasive assessment of kidney fibrosis.

sections.text: With a prevalence above 10% worldwide, chronic kidney disease is one of the leading medical burdens. Independent of the underlying cause, kidney fibrosis emerges as the common final endpoint and serves as the most robust predictor of disease progression and long-term prognosis. Fibrosis is driven by extracellular matrix-producing mesenchymal cells, which are characterized by platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ) expression. PDGFRβ also mediates fibrogenesis in these cells and represents a potential therapeutic target for direct intervention or a potential anchor for selective delivery of antifibrotic drugs. Diagnostic approaches assessing PDGFRβ expression in kidneys are missing. Here, we developed and evaluated a novel tracer using a PDGFRβ-targeting biparatopic variable domain of a heavy-chain-only antibody construct, designated SP02SP26-ABD, for in vivo, noninvasive, molecular imaging of kidney fibrosis. Methods: PDGFRβ expression was assessed in human kidney biopsies and publicly available transcriptomic datasets. In vivo imaging studies were performed in 2 distinct murine models of kidney fibrosis using fluorescence imaging and 89Zr-labeled PET. Specificity and dose dependency were evaluated using a nonspecific control variable domain of a heavy-chain-only antibody construct, R2R2-ABD, and coinjection of increasing amounts of unlabeled SP02SP26-ABD. Ex vivo biodistribution and correlation with histologic and molecular markers of fibrosis were performed. Results: PDGFRβ was increased in fibrotic human kidneys across multiple disease entities, predominantly localized to pericytes and fibroblasts, supporting its relevance as a translational imaging target. In vivo imaging demonstrated significantly higher tracer accumulation in fibrotic compared with nonfibrotic kidneys across both models, whereas tracer accumulation in nonrenal organs was low, with minimal uptake in the spleen. We found no difference between fibrotic and nonfibrotic kidneys when using a nonspecific R2R2-ABD control construct, whereas increasing amounts of unlabeled SP02SP26-ABD led to a dose-dependent decrease in tracer accumulation, consistent with a saturation effect. Tracer signal correlated with PDGFRβ expression, confirming the specificity of the approach. Conclusion: We provide the first proof of concept for noninvasive PET imaging of PDGFRβ-expressing fibrogenic cells in kidney disease, supporting further development of this approach for specific, noninvasive assessment of kidney fibrosis.

items.title: Clinical Study Protocol for PENTILULA: A Phase 1/2 Study Assessing [177Lu]Lu-Pentixather for Relapsed or Refractory CXCR4-Positive Acute Leukemia.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Bodet-Milin C, Lelan F, François C, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: This first-in-human clinical study is ongoing, having reached the fifth and final activity level. [177Lu]Lu-pentixather is being used to definitively establish the MTD and preliminary efficacy of this CXCR4-targeted approach in this high-risk population with limited therapeutic options.

sections.text: C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 (CXCR4) inhibition may represent a new therapeutic strategy for patients with acute leukemia (AL), not only by increasing chemosensitivity but also by preventing relapse through disruption of residual leukemic cell interactions with the bone marrow niche. Radiolabeled CXCR4 ligands are available for PET imaging ([68Ga]Ga-pentixafor) and radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) ([177Lu]Lu-pentixather/[90Y]Y-pentixather). Early clinical experience with CXCR4-targeted RPT, together with the reported feasibility of CXCR4-targeted PET in acute myeloid leukemia, supports the development of theranostic approaches targeting the CXCR4/C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12-defined leukemia-initiating cell niche. The objective of this study is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of a single infusion of [177Lu]Lu-pentixather in patients with relapsed/refractory AL (including both acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia). Methods: PENTILULA is an investigator-initiated, first-in-human, prospective phase 1/2 study based on a standard 3 + 3 dose-escalation design with 5 levels and 3-6 patients per level. Key inclusion criteria include patients with relapsed/refractory AL with CXCR4-positive leukemic cells. The primary endpoint is the incidence and evaluation of dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) and determination of the MTD. DLTs will be assessed 4-6 wk after RPT and include grade 3 or higher nonhematologic toxicity, prolonged grade 4 pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow, and excessive renal or hepatic radiation absorbed dose. The MTD is defined as the highest level at which fewer than one third of patients experience a DLT. In a subset of patients, [68Ga]Ga-pentixafor PET/MRI will be performed to explore the predictive value of theranostic PET imaging on CXCR4 expression, dosimetry, and treatment response. Conclusion: This first-in-human clinical study is ongoing, having reached the fifth and final activity level. [177Lu]Lu-pentixather is being used to definitively establish the MTD and preliminary efficacy of this CXCR4-targeted approach in this high-risk population with limited therapeutic options.

items.title: Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor as a Radiotheranostic Target in Orthotopic Models of Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Lee W, King AP, Baidoo K, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: [89Zr]Zr-Pani and [225Ac]Ac-Pani represent a radiotheranostic pair that enables EGFR-specific imaging and targeted α-particle therapy in orthotopic HCC models. These findings establish EGFR as a promising radiotheranostic target in HCC, broadening the patient population eligible for image-guided radiopharmaceutical interventions for liver cancer.

sections.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, with a 5-y survival rate of approximately 20%. Although glypican-3-targeted radiotheranostics are under development, a plurality of patients with HCC lack glypican-3 expression, underscoring the need for alternative targetable antigens. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is overexpressed in 50%-70% of HCC tumors and represents a clinically validated therapeutic target. Here, we developed and evaluated a panitumumab-based EGFR-targeted radiotheranostic pair, [89Zr]Zr-desferrioxamine-panitumumab ([89Zr]Zr-Pani) for immuno-PET and [225Ac]Ac-Macropa-panitumumab ([225Ac]Ac-Pani) for targeted α-particle therapy, in clinically relevant orthotopic HCC models. Methods: Panitumumab was conjugated with desferrioxamine or Macropa chelators and radiolabeled with 89Zr or 225Ac, respectively. EGFR expression was characterized across a panel of HCC cell lines. Binding affinity, biodistribution, and tumor specificity were assessed in subcutaneous and orthotopic Huh-7 models, with EGFR-mediated targeting confirmed by blocking (200-fold molar excess of unlabeled panitumumab). Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in mice bearing orthotopic Huh-7-Luc+ tumors (n = 6 per group) after a single 9.3 kBq dose of [225Ac]Ac-Pani, with longitudinal monitoring by bioluminescence imaging, [89Zr]Zr-Pani immuno-PET, and blood chemistry. Results: [89Zr]Zr-Pani exhibited high-affinity binding to EGFR (dissociation constant, 0.35 nM) and demonstrated robust tumor accumulation in both subcutaneous Huh-7 (20.6 ± 2.6 %IA/g) and orthotopic Huh-7-Luc+ tumors (19.3 ± 2.0 %IA/g) at 120-192 h postinjection. Biodistribution of [225Ac]Ac-Pani closely mirrored that of [89Zr]Zr-Pani across organs and tumors, with tumor uptake reduced approximately 5-fold by blocking (21.7 ± 1.1 vs. 4.5 ± 0.6 %IA/g; P < 0.0001), confirming EGFR-specific targeting. A single 9.3 kBq administration of [225Ac]Ac-Pani induced substantial early tumor regression and significantly prolonged median survival (70 d) compared with vehicle (28 d) and blocking (35 d) groups (log-rank P < 0.0001), with no clinically meaningful hepatotoxicity or renal toxicity. However, tumor regrowth eventually occurred in all treated mice. Conclusion: [89Zr]Zr-Pani and [225Ac]Ac-Pani represent a radiotheranostic pair that enables EGFR-specific imaging and targeted α-particle therapy in orthotopic HCC models. These findings establish EGFR as a promising radiotheranostic target in HCC, broadening the patient population eligible for image-guided radiopharmaceutical interventions for liver cancer.

items.title: Patient Communication and Radiation Safety in [177Lu]Lu-PSMA Radiopharmaceutical Therapy: International Survey of 102 Theranostic Centers.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Zahner J, Unterrainer LM, Czernin J, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: This international survey demonstrated broad consensus for core clinical procedures but showed variability in posttreatment radiation precautions after RPT. sections.text: [177Lu]Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) is increasingly administered worldwide in both inpatient and outpatient settings. Despite its growing use, there is no harmonized international guidance on what patients should be told before, during, and after therapy. This study aimed to capture current clinical practice and expert opinion to identify areas of consensus and divergence to develop a patient information template. Methods: An international survey was conducted among theranostic centers performing [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT. The questionnaire covered pretreatment procedures, therapy procedures, radiation precautions guidance, and posttreatment procedures. Inpatient and outpatient settings were evaluated separately. Results: In total, 102 centers from 23 countries participated. High agreement was observed for most pretreatment procedures, core therapy aspects, and general posttreatment guidance. In contrast, substantial variability was identified in posttreatment radiation precautions, particularly regarding distancing measures, duration of precautions, transportation after discharge, household and hygiene recommendations, and guidance affecting social interactions. Conclusion: This international survey demonstrated broad consensus for core clinical procedures but showed variability in posttreatment radiation precautions after RPT. By summarizing current practice and translating it into a patient information template, this project supports more consistent patient guidance across diverse clinical settings.

items.title: Preclinical Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling of PSMA Radioligands: Demonstrating Nonspecific Retention and Reversible Albumin-Binding Effects.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Alvers A, Mapanao AK, Müller C, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: The models with reversible albumin-binding further improved the regressions for the albumin-binding radioligands but had limited impact on TIA estimates. By integrating these mechanisms, preclinical PBPK models provide novel insights into radioligand kinetics and can inform the refinement of clinical PBPK models toward safer and more individualized PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

sections.text: Radiopharmaceutical therapy with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) radioligands has emerged as a promising treatment modality for metastatic androgen pathway modulator-resistant prostate cancer (formerly metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer). Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling has been applied in clinical studies of PSMA radioligands. However, clinical models are necessarily simplified because of sparse patient data, which may mask important pharmacokinetic processes. The aim of this study was to perform PBPK modeling on comprehensive preclinical data and identify previously neglected dynamics of PSMA radioligands with translation relevance. Methods: Biodistribution and albumin-binding affinity data were previously obtained for the 2 PSMA radioligands [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 and [177Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T and the 3 albumin-binding PSMA radioligands [177Lu]Lu-SibuDAB, [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-ALB-53, and [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-ALB-56. A baseline, preclinical PBPK model was built using a widely studied radioligand PBPK model structure. Three types of modifications to the baseline model were developed: nonspecific retention in PSMA-negative tissues and kidneys, change from an irreversible to a reversible albumin-binding model, and albumin-bound fraction implementation. Models with modification combinations were built, and regressions were performed against the biodistribution data. The modifications were evaluated on the regression performances, and simulations of the fitted models were compared with clinically established baseline regressions through time-integrated activity (TIA) ratios. Results: For all radioligands, incorporating nonspecific retention markedly improved the corrected Akaike information criterion (AIC). The reversible albumin-binding model showed improved AIC for all albumin-binding radioligands. The implementation of albumin-bound fractions degraded the AIC but showed minor impact on fits. With nonspecific retention, substantial increases in TIAs were observed for PSMA-negative organs, particularly for the dose-limited organ red marrow where TIA ratios reached 3.0, 1.5, and 1.6 for [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617, [177Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T, and [177Lu]Lu-SibuDAB, respectively. TIAs for PSMA-positive tissues and kidneys remained relatively stable. Conclusion: This preclinical study demonstrated that disregarding nonspecific retention led to marked underestimation of doses to PSMA-negative tissues such as in the radiosensitive red marrow. The models with reversible albumin-binding further improved the regressions for the albumin-binding radioligands but had limited impact on TIA estimates. By integrating these mechanisms, preclinical PBPK models provide novel insights into radioligand kinetics and can inform the refinement of clinical PBPK models toward safer and more individualized PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

items.authors: Withey SJ, Gutierrez P, Ponsiglione AM, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The P-SMART approach, designed to align with the PI-RADS sector map, yielded significantly higher interobserver agreement for prostate lesion-level localisation than the PI-RADS method, across reader experience and gland size, though overall agreement was only moderate. Improved reproducibility may support biopsy targeting, active surveillance monitoring, and treatment planning.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: Precise lesion localisation on prostate MRI-specifically, identification of whether at the apex, mid-gland, or base-is essential for effective communication and clinical management. This study aimed to assess interobserver agreement of current practice using the Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) against a novel anatomy-based approach, P-SMART (Prostate Simplified MRI Anatomy Recognition and Training).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This multi-reader, two-phase agreement study, used axial and sagittal T2-weighted MRI from a publicly available dataset. Forty MRI cases were annotated with four regions of interest (ROIs). Readers were asked to document ROI location-apex, mid-gland, or base-first using the PI-RADS method, then following a 3-week washout period and short educational intervention, using the P-SMART method. Interobserver agreement was evaluated using Fleiss' kappa (κ) statistics and compared following bootstrap resampling using a paired t-test. Subgroup analyses were performed by reader expertise and prostate size.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Following quality assurance, 156 ROIs were evaluated by 43 readers in each phase of the study. Overall interobserver agreement improved with P-SMART vs PI-RADS (κ = 0.571 vs 0.399; p < 0.001). In subgroup analyses, improvements were consistent for experts (0.663 vs 0.435; p < 0.001), non-experts (0.530 vs 0.393; p < 0.001), large prostates (0.518 vs 0.325; p < 0.001), and small prostates (0.620 vs 0.461; p < 0.001).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The P-SMART approach, designed to align with the PI-RADS sector map, yielded significantly higher interobserver agreement for prostate lesion-level localisation than the PI-RADS method, across reader experience and gland size, though overall agreement was only moderate. Improved reproducibility may support biopsy targeting, active surveillance monitoring, and treatment planning.

items.title: Application of topological deep learning in staging liver fibrosis based on hepatobiliary phase MR images.
items.authors: Zhou X, Tang X, Zhao H, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The TopoEfficientViT model had high predictive performance for staging liver fibrosis by integrating multi-scale persistent homology topology with convolutional networks.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Early-stage liver fibrosis is reversible; thus, accurate staging of liver fibrosis is of great importance.. Liver biopsy is the gold standard for the diagnosis of liver fibrosis; however, its invasive nature limits its clinical application. Accurate noninvasive staging of liver fibrosis remains challenging. Thus, there is an urgent need for a precise and reliable noninvasive diagnostic approach.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: A topological deep learning model combining topological data analysis and EfficientViT framework (TopoEfficientViT) was developed to effectively capture global contextual relationships in hepatobiliary phase MR images for assessment of staging liver fibrosis.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Our retrospective study included patients with chronic liver diseases from June 2018 to July 2025, which was approved by our Institutional Review Board. Our data from a hospital site (Site A) in our institution were divided into a training set (n = 275) and a validation set (n = 75). The test set (n=65) was composed of data from a separate hospital site (Site B) in the same institution.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 415 patients (323 males, mean age 56.52±9.54 years; 92 females, mean age 58.86±9.68 years) were enrolled in the study. In the training set, the AUC and accuracy of TopoEfficientViT for staging liver fibrosis F1-2 vs. F3-4 were 0.942 and 0.906, respectively; for staging liver fibrosis F1-3 vs. F4 were 0.957 and 0.891, respectively. In the validation set, the AUC and accuracy for staging liver fibrosis F1-2 vs. F3-4 were 0.849 and 0.76, respectively; for staging liver fibrosis F1-3 vs. F4 were 0.861and 0.813, respectively. In the test set, the AUC and accuracy for staging liver fibrosis F1-2 vs. F3-4 were 0.829 and 0.769, respectively; for staging liver fibrosis F1-3 vs. F4 were 0.791 and 0.785, respectively.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The TopoEfficientViT model had high predictive performance for staging liver fibrosis by integrating multi-scale persistent homology topology with convolutional networks.

items.title: Noninvasive Diagnosis of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Outside Guideline-Defined High-Risk Populations: Evolving Perspectives in the Era of MASLD.
items.authors: Kang TW, Song BG

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Noninvasive imaging-based diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in high-risk patients currently relies on the radiological hallmark of arterial-phase hyperenhancement followed by delayed washout. These criteria were designed to achieve both a high positive predictive value and sufficient specificity when applied to well-defined target populations.

sections.text: Noninvasive imaging-based diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in high-risk patients currently relies on the radiological hallmark of arterial-phase hyperenhancement followed by delayed washout. These criteria were designed to achieve both a high positive predictive value and sufficient specificity when applied to well-defined target populations. However, the incidence of HCC is rising globally among individuals outside the traditional high-risk groups, including those with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease) and genetic predispositions. This shifting epidemiology poses challenges to the current noninvasive diagnostic strategies and the binary classification of patients as either "at high-risk" or "not at high-risk," which heavily depends on established risk factors such as chronic hepatitis B, chronic hepatitis C, and liver cirrhosis. Consequently, HCC in non-high-risk individuals is often diagnosed at more advanced stages, underscoring the urgent need for reliable and noninvasive diagnostic tools tailored to this demographic population. These challenges present opportunities for the radiology community to play a proactive role in addressing them. Given the heterogeneous risk factors among low- and intermediate-risk populations, integrated strategies incorporating imaging features, fibrosis stage, serum biomarkers, individualized risk models, and artificial intelligence-assisted cross-sectional imaging may help improve the noninvasive diagnosis of non-cirrhotic or metabolically driven HCC. This review summarizes the current performance and limitations of noninvasive diagnosis outside the conventional high-risk populations in the era of MASLD and highlights emerging diagnostic strategies that warrant further investigation as evidence continues to accumulate.

items.title: Multiphasic CT radiomics-clinical model for predicting acute pancreatitis recurrence: a multicenter survival analysis.
items.authors: Wu W, Rong C, Wang S, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: The combined model demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting recurrence within the first 24 months after first-episode AP and may facilitate individualized follow-up and secondary prevention strategies.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Can a multiphasic CT radiomics-clinical model improve prediction of AP recurrence over clinical factors alone in a multicenter setting? Findings The combined model demonstrated numerically higher predictive performance than the clinical model, though the incremental improvement was not statistically significant. Critical relevance statement This study critically evaluates the added value of multiphasic radiomics for recurrence prediction in AP, demonstrating that while radiomics captures baseline microenvironmental vulnerability, post-discharge clinical interventions remain the dominant dynamic drivers.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To develop and externally validate a predictive model integrating multiphasic CT radiomics and clinical variables to estimate recurrence risk after first-episode acute pancreatitis (AP).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This multicenter retrospective study included 548 patients with first-episode AP (training, n = 272; internal validation, n = 117; external validation, n = 159). Clinical and multiphasic CT data were collected, with recurrence as the primary endpoint. After stability-based feature selection, clinical, radiomics, and combined Cox models were constructed. Performance was evaluated using the C-index and time-dependent AUC, with SHAP for interpretability.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 548 patients were included (median age 42 years; 363 men). Recurrence rates were similar across cohorts (30.1%, 29.9%, and 28.3%; p = 0.702). The combined model achieved C-indices of 0.783 and 0.775 in the internal and external validation cohorts, respectively, numerically higher than those of the clinical model (0.748 and 0.750) and radiomics model (0.647 and 0.619), although the incremental improvement over the clinical model was not statistically significant. In the external validation cohort, time-dependent AUCs remained acceptable through 36 months but declined at 48 months. High-risk patients had lower 3-year recurrence-free survival than low-risk patients (37.4% vs 86.8%; log-rank p < 0.001). SHAP analysis identified the NC-3mm-Radscore as the most influential imaging-derived variable, whereas etiology-targeted prevention was the dominant protective factor.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: The combined model demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting recurrence within the first 24 months after first-episode AP and may facilitate individualized follow-up and secondary prevention strategies.

items.title: Can reduced tube voltage CT imaging obviate the need for the arterial phase in patients with undifferentiated acute abdominal pain?
items.authors: Cronenberg R, Röhrich S, Rabadi T, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: PVP-only imaging with low-kV technique reduced radiation exposure while providing sufficient diagnostic information, suggesting selective use of additional arterial phase for a specific patient group with suspicious vascular emergencies.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To evaluate the diagnostic performance in abdominal low-kV (kilo-voltage) contrast-enhanced CT (CE-CT) of patients from the emergency department (ED) between venous-phase-only reading sessions and arterial-venous-phase reading sessions.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: 96 patients (mean age 54 years, +/- 17, 49 men) who presented at the ED with undifferentiated abdominal pain underwent multiphasic low-kV CT including at least late arterial phase (LAP) and portal venous phase (PVP). Two reviewers, (Reader 1-board certified radiologist with subspecialization in gastrointestinal imaging and Reader 2-advanced resident with experience in gastrointestinal imaging), analyzed the PVP and LAP independently and determined the most appropriate diagnosis. LAP and PVP images were compared to a reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of the PVP for both readers were calculated. Incremental diagnostic value of the LAP was evaluated.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The PVP showed sensitivity, specificity and accuracy in detecting relevant pathology of 93.2%, 87.5% and 92.7% in Reader 1 and 89.8%, 75.0% and 88.5% in Reader 2, respectively with concordant results in 85.4%. There were no findings exclusively detectable in the LAP relevant for clinical management, however it caused approximately 40% of the radiation dose.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: PVP-only imaging with low-kV technique reduced radiation exposure while providing sufficient diagnostic information, suggesting selective use of additional arterial phase for a specific patient group with suspicious vascular emergencies.

items.title: Diagnostic performance benchmarks of MRI for prostate cancer: a large-scale cohort study of 33,759 patients.
items.authors: Bao J, Su M, Tu H, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: This large-scale real-world study provides critical multicenter evidence supporting the use of PI-RADS in clinical practice worldwide, while also revealing substantial variability in scoring and diagnostic performance across institutions. The findings offer an evidence-based overview of PI-RADS implementation in China and worldwide, highlighting both its utility and inconsistencies.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question What are the real-world PI-RADS diagnostic performance benchmarks for clinically significant prostate cancer detection across diverse Chinese multicenter institutions versus global data? Findings PI-RADS demonstrated good overall performance (SROC AUC 0.903 at a threshold of ≥ 3), with superior discriminatory ability in older patients, higher PSA levels, and v2.1 users. Critical relevance statement This article critically assesses substantial inter-institutional heterogeneity in PI-RADS performance, highlighting that pooled estimates should not replace local calibration and that regionally adapted implementation strategies are essential for advancing clinical radiology practice.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate the real-world diagnostic performance of PI-RADS for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) across large-scale worldwide cohorts.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This multicenter observational study included 20,429 patients from nine Chinese institutions and a published worldwide meta-analysis dataset comprising 13,330 patients for comparison. All PI-RADS assessments were extracted from original MRI reports produced by clinical radiologists as part of standard diagnostic workflows. Summary receiver operating characteristic curves were constructed using a bivariate random-effects model, and center-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled via random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: PI-RADS exhibited overall discriminatory performance for csPCa across nine Chinese cohorts comparable to the META results from 70 studies, though significant inter-center variation was observed. Using a PI-RADS ≥ 3 threshold, pooled sensitivity was 92.6% and specificity was 51.5%. At a PI-RADS ≥ 4 threshold, pooled specificity improved to 78.1%, with a sensitivity of 81.5%. The overall diagnostic performance was consistent across thresholds: The summary ROC (SROC) AUC was 0.903 for PI-RADS ≥ 3 and 0.826 for PI-RADS ≥ 4 in detecting csPCa at the meta-analysis level. Subgroup analyses indicated better performance among older patients (≥ 70 years) and those with higher PSA levels (> 20 ng/mL). PI-RADS v2.1 outperformed v2 or earlier versions in most clinical scenarios.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: This large-scale real-world study provides critical multicenter evidence supporting the use of PI-RADS in clinical practice worldwide, while also revealing substantial variability in scoring and diagnostic performance across institutions. The findings offer an evidence-based overview of PI-RADS implementation in China and worldwide, highlighting both its utility and inconsistencies.

items.authors: Lin H, Zhou J, Deng R, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: One-stop VP-PCCT delivers high-quality morphologic and perfusion evaluation in a single low-dose scan, with hemodynamic profiles that may be associated with histological grade and MVI status.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Clinical use of dynamic volume perfusion CT for comprehensively evaluating HCC without additional multiphase contrast-enhanced imaging remains limited. Findings Multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT provided high-quality morphologic imaging of HCC at a low dose, with perfusion parameters independently indicating poorly differentiated HCC and MVI. Critical relevance statement One-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT enables high-quality morphologic and functional assessment in a single low-dose scan, providing comprehensive HCC evaluation with hemodynamic profiling that may support the assessment of histological grade and MVI.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To assess the feasibility of one-stop multi-energy dynamic volume perfusion photon-counting CT (VP-PCCT) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) evaluation, including lesion detection and correlations with histopathology.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: From July 2024 to June 2025, 407 participants with suspected malignant liver lesions prospectively underwent VP-PCCT, and 177 patients with pathology-confirmed HCC who received three-phase energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) were retrospectively enrolled for comparisons of image quality and lesion detectability. Single-phase images reconstructed from VP-PCCT perfusion datasets were compared with EID-CT. Perfusion parameters were analyzed between groups stratified separately by histological grade and microvascular invasion (MVI), and logistic regression was employed to identify independent indicators.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Ninety-two participants [median age, 62 years (IQR, 53-69); 76 males] with pathology-confirmed HCC were included in the VP-PCCT group and matched with 92 in the EID-CT group. Compared with EID-CT, 40-keV VP-PCCT provided comparable image quality for HCC and vessels with a similar tumor detection rate but a lower radiation dose. Poorly-differentiated HCCs showed higher tumor hepatic perfusion index (HPItumor) and peritumoral blood flow (BFperitumor); MVI-positive HCCs exhibited lower tumor arterial liver perfusion (ALPtumor) and normalized blood flow of peritumoral region (BFnorm_peritumor) (all p < 0.05). HPItumor [odds ratio (OR): 1.06] and BFperitumor (OR: 1.04) were independent risk factors for poorly differentiated HCC, whereas decreased ALPtumor (OR: 0.97) and BFnorm_peritumor (OR: 0.25) were associated with MVI positivity (all p < 0.05).

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: One-stop VP-PCCT delivers high-quality morphologic and perfusion evaluation in a single low-dose scan, with hemodynamic profiles that may be associated with histological grade and MVI status.

sections.text: Question Clinical use of dynamic volume perfusion CT for comprehensively evaluating HCC without additional multiphase contrast-enhanced imaging remains limited. Findings Multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT provided high-quality morphologic imaging of HCC at a low dose, with perfusion parameters independently indicating poorly differentiated HCC and MVI. Critical relevance statement One-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT enables high-quality morphologic and functional assessment in a single low-dose scan, providing comprehensive HCC evaluation with hemodynamic profiling that may support the assessment of histological grade and MVI.
