items.title: AI-accelerated compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction for colon MRI: prospective validation of image quality and preliminary assessment of staging accuracy versus contrast-enhanced CT.
items.authors: Guan Z, Sun N, Chang TJ, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The AI-accelerated MRI protocol significantly outperformed CECT in image quality and preliminary staging accuracy for colon cancer evaluation while eliminating radiation exposure.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Can an AI-accelerated MRI protocol provide superior image quality and staging performance compared with contrast-enhanced CT, which has limited diagnostic accuracy for colon cancer staging? Findings AI-accelerated MRI using L₁-regularized compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction achieved superior image quality and higher preliminary staging accuracy than contrast-enhanced CT. Critical Relevance Statement AI-accelerated MRI improves image quality and staging confidence without radiation exposure, supporting its potential to enhance preoperative assessment and clinical decision-making in colon cancer.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To prospectively validate an AI-accelerated MRI protocol combining L₁-regularized compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction for colon cancer staging, compared with contrast-enhanced CT (CECT).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This single-center study (August 2022-April 2024) enrolled 132 patients with pathologically confirmed colon cancer who underwent both 3.0-T non-contrast MRI and CECT within 1 week. Patients unable to complete an MRI were excluded. MRI sequences included T1- and T2-weighted imaging and diffusion-weighted imaging. Image quality was assessed using a 4-point Likert scale, alongside quantitative analysis of contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) and edge rise distance (ERD). Surgical pathology correlation was available for 33 cases. Five radiologists independently reviewed the images.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Among 153 matched examination pairs from 132 patients (mean age, 58 ± 11 years), AI-MRI outperformed CECT in both qualitative and quantitative measures. MRI yielded higher image quality scores (4 [IQR 3-4] vs. 3 [IQR 3-3]), improved CNR (5.5 [IQR 4.2-7.0] vs. 1.3 [IQR 0.7-2.2]), and reduced ERD (1.6 mm [IQR 1.2-2.8] vs. 3.7 mm [IQR 2.8-5.0]). MRI provided superior peritoneal sharpness (75.8%) and colonic wall visualization (100%), and superior or equivalent tumor conspicuity (92.2%) and nodal assessment (86.9%), whereas CECT demonstrated better artifact control (45.1%). In preliminary analyses, MRI achieved higher T-staging accuracy (78.8% vs. 30.3%) and N-staging specificity (93.3% vs. 13.3%).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The AI-accelerated MRI protocol significantly outperformed CECT in image quality and preliminary staging accuracy for colon cancer evaluation while eliminating radiation exposure.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Can an AI-accelerated MRI protocol provide superior image quality and staging performance compared with contrast-enhanced CT, which has limited diagnostic accuracy for colon cancer staging? Findings AI-accelerated MRI using L₁-regularized compressed sensing and deep learning reconstruction achieved superior image quality and higher preliminary staging accuracy than contrast-enhanced CT. Critical Relevance Statement AI-accelerated MRI improves image quality and staging confidence without radiation exposure, supporting its potential to enhance preoperative assessment and clinical decision-making in colon cancer.

items.title: ESR Essentials: MRI of the scrotum-practice recommendations by the European Society of Urogenital Radiology.
items.authors: Tsili AC, Pasoglou V, Campo I, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: While conventional ultrasonography (US) remains the first-line imaging modality for scrotal pathology, multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has emerged as a valuable problem-solving tool for indeterminate US findings. Owing to its superior soft-tissue contrast, functional imaging capabilities, and operator independence, mpMRI allows for the precise localization and characterization of scrotal lesions.

sections.text: While conventional ultrasonography (US) remains the first-line imaging modality for scrotal pathology, multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has emerged as a valuable problem-solving tool for indeterminate US findings. Owing to its superior soft-tissue contrast, functional imaging capabilities, and operator independence, mpMRI allows for the precise localization and characterization of scrotal lesions. This paper from the European Society of Urogenital Radiology Scrotal and Penile Imaging Working Group provides a comprehensive, evidence-based overview of scrotal mpMRI for a general radiologist. It details optimized imaging protocols, recommending a standard sequence of T1-weighted, T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and subtracted dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging. The article highlights key clinical indications, including the characterization of intratesticular and paratesticular masses, local staging of testicular germ cell tumors, and differentiation between germ cell and sex cord-stromal neoplasms. This paper familiarizes radiologists with normal MRI appearances and MRI findings of common scrotal diseases. Evidence-based recommendations for reporting basic MRI examinations of the scrotum are also provided. The potential of advanced techniques, such as diffusion tensor imaging and proton MR spectroscopy, and the future integration of artificial intelligence and radiomics, are also discussed. We hope the implementation of these recommendations into radiological practice will enhance diagnostic confidence and promote standardized practice in scrotal MRI for radiologists. KEY POINTS: While conventional ultrasound is the first-line modality for scrotal pathology, it can yield inconclusive findings regarding complex mass characterization and local tumor staging. Multiparametric MRI combines anatomical and functional data to accurately characterize scrotal masses, localize impalpable, undescended testes, and provide precise local tumor staging. Scrotal multiparametric MRI serves as a valuable problem-solving tool that enhances diagnostic confidence in sonographically indeterminate cases, prevents unnecessary radical orchiectomies, supports testis-sparing surgery or active surveillance, and standardizes radiological reporting templates to optimize personalized patient management.

items.title: Reducing operator-dependent variability in liver shear wave elastography through an AI-guided region-of-interest placement pipeline.
items.authors: Ali AR, Prakash S, Wang S, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The proposed AI-driven pipeline significantly improved ROI placement consistency and reproducibility, highlighting its potential to enhance clinical reliability in liver fibrosis assessment.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Operator-dependent variability in region-of-interest (ROI) placement compromises measurement reproducibility in B-mode shear wave elastography. We developed an AI pipeline to place an optimal ROI. Findings The AI pipeline achieved liver segmentation performance of Dice 0.89 (AUC 0.94) and demonstrated higher AI-to-attending agreement (93.8%) than inter-attending agreement (81%) for ROI placement. Clinical relevance By standardizing ROI placement, elastogram box selection, and probe angle/contact guidance, the AI pipeline reduces operator-dependent variability in liver SWE acquisition, supporting more reproducible liver stiffness measurements that could improve fibrosis staging reliability.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline that automates optimal circular region-of-interest (ROI) placement and the surrounding elastogram box, provides probe-angle/contact guidance, and measures skin-to-capsule distance (SCD) to standardize liver SWE acquisition, aiming to reduce operator-dependent variability.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: A two-stage pipeline combined SimCLR self-supervised pretraining on 17,441 unlabeled ultrasound images, followed by ENet fine-tuning using 495 annotated images for liver segmentation and 1564 images for poor probe contact detection. Segmentation outputs were combined with constraints on valid liver tissue pixels, axial depth, lateral boundaries, and regions of poor acoustic coupling to generate masks for optimal ROI placement. A distance transformation algorithm then identified optimal ROI coordinates within these masks. An inter-observer reader study assessed AI performance by comparing automated ROI placement, SCD measurements, and probe-angle correction guidance with annotations from expert attending radiologists.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: 18,182 US images from 654 liver elastography examinations in 609 patients (mean age, 52.6 ± 12.95 years; 55.4% male) were acquired from three ultrasound systems. The AI pipeline achieved liver segmentation performance with a Dice coefficient of 0.89, sensitivity of 0.95, specificity of 0.93, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.94. The reader study demonstrated significantly higher AI-to-attending radiologist agreement (93.8%) compared to inter-attending agreement for ROI placement (81%). Cohen's kappa agreement between two attending radiologists was 0.25.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The proposed AI-driven pipeline significantly improved ROI placement consistency and reproducibility, highlighting its potential to enhance clinical reliability in liver fibrosis assessment.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Operator-dependent variability in region-of-interest (ROI) placement compromises measurement reproducibility in B-mode shear wave elastography. We developed an AI pipeline to place an optimal ROI. Findings The AI pipeline achieved liver segmentation performance of Dice 0.89 (AUC 0.94) and demonstrated higher AI-to-attending agreement (93.8%) than inter-attending agreement (81%) for ROI placement. Clinical relevance By standardizing ROI placement, elastogram box selection, and probe angle/contact guidance, the AI pipeline reduces operator-dependent variability in liver SWE acquisition, supporting more reproducible liver stiffness measurements that could improve fibrosis staging reliability.

items.title: An integrated MRI-pathology model for predicting response to TACE combined with targeted therapy and immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma.
items.authors: Ding W, Hua HJ, Shen X, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: IMPRESS model may provide a promising tool for pretreatment response prediction and survival risk stratification in unresectable HCC undergoing TACE-based combination therapy.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Reliable pretreatment tools are needed to identify unresectable HCC patients likely to benefit from TACE plus targeted therapy and immunotherapy. Findings An integrated MRI-pathology model combining habitat radiomics and deep-learning pathomics predicted treatment response, with validation and testing areas under the curve of 0.878 and 0.875. Clinical relevance The integrated model may support pretreatment response stratification for TACE-based triple therapy and help inform surveillance intensity or alternative treatment considerations, pending prospective validation.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: The efficacy of transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) plus targeted therapy and immunotherapy in unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is limited by variable responses. We aimed to develop and validate an integrated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-pathology model for response prediction and survival stratification (IMPRESS), which combines pretreatment MRI habitat radiomics and paired biopsy whole-slide images (WSIs) pathomics.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This multicenter, retrospective study enrolled patients with unresectable HCC receiving TACE plus targeted therapy and immunotherapy from January 2019 to December 2024. Eligibility required pretreatment MRI and paired biopsy WSIs within 1 month before therapy, Child-Pugh class A/B, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status ≤ 1, and at least one measurable intrahepatic lesion ≥ 1 cm. Patients with missing or poor-quality MRI or WSIs, prior locoregional or systemic HCC therapy, second malignancy, ECOG ≥ 2, or incomplete data were excluded. Habitat MRI radiomics, WSI pathomics, and clinical features were integrated into IMPRESS. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Single-cell analysis was performed to explore the biological basis of the IMPRESS predictions.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Among 231 patients, 94 (40.7%) achieved a treatment response. IMPRESS achieved AUCs of 0.957 (95% CI: 0.931-1.0), 0.878 (95% CI: 0.789-0.966), and 0.875 (95% CI: 0.782-0.966) in the training, validation, and test cohorts, respectively. Predicted responders and non-responders showed significantly different overall survival in all cohorts (all p < 0.001). Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed distinct immune and proliferative patterns consistent with model predictions.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: IMPRESS model may provide a promising tool for pretreatment response prediction and survival risk stratification in unresectable HCC undergoing TACE-based combination therapy.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Reliable pretreatment tools are needed to identify unresectable HCC patients likely to benefit from TACE plus targeted therapy and immunotherapy. Findings An integrated MRI-pathology model combining habitat radiomics and deep-learning pathomics predicted treatment response, with validation and testing areas under the curve of 0.878 and 0.875. Clinical relevance The integrated model may support pretreatment response stratification for TACE-based triple therapy and help inform surveillance intensity or alternative treatment considerations, pending prospective validation.

items.title: A fractal-integrated CT score predicts high-risk pathology and early recurrence in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.authors: Zhu J, Yu H, Ren W, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: This CT-based score, integrating fractal biomarkers, enables accurate, noninvasive preoperative prediction of aggressive pathological features in PDAC and provides incremental value for early recurrence risk stratification.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Can the fractal-based imaging features be used to predict high-risk pathological features and guide risk stratification for early recurrence in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)? Findings This CT-based score integrating fractal analysis predicted high-risk pathological features and was independent predictors of early recurrence and provided incremental prognostic value beyond pathologic factors. Clinical relevance This CT-based imaging score may help identify patients at high-risk of aggressive pathology before surgery and may further complement postoperative pathological risk stratification for early recurrence.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To develop and validate a noninvasive CT-based imaging score incorporating fractal analysis to predict high-risk pathological features in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and to assess its prognostic value for early recurrence.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective bicenter study included 514 patients with pathologically confirmed PDAC who underwent curative resection, divided into training (n = 219), internal validation (n = 94), external validation (n = 100) and outcome datasets (n = 101). The fractal dimension (FD) and lacunarity were extracted from portal venous-phase CT images via box-counting algorithms. Imaging predictors of high-risk pathological features, including high tumor grade, lymphovascular invasion (LVI) and perineural invasion (PNI), were identified by logistic regression and integrated into a comprehensive weighted imaging score. Cox regression analyses were performed to assess its prognostic value for early recurrence.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Patients with high-risk pathological features exhibited greater FD and lacunarity. The final score included six imaging features: necrosis, peripancreatic fat infiltration, venous involvement, regional lymphadenopathy, FD and lacunarity. For any high-risk pathology, the fractal-integrated score achieved AUC of 0.94, 0.88 and 0.84 in the training, internal validation and external validation datasets, respectively. For high pathological burden, the AUCs were 0.92, 0.80, and 0.77. In the outcome dataset, the score was an independent predictor of early recurrence (HR = 2.71; p = 0.004) and improved prognostic discrimination when combined with pathologic predictors.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: This CT-based score, integrating fractal biomarkers, enables accurate, noninvasive preoperative prediction of aggressive pathological features in PDAC and provides incremental value for early recurrence risk stratification.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Can the fractal-based imaging features be used to predict high-risk pathological features and guide risk stratification for early recurrence in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)? Findings This CT-based score integrating fractal analysis predicted high-risk pathological features and was independent predictors of early recurrence and provided incremental prognostic value beyond pathologic factors. Clinical relevance This CT-based imaging score may help identify patients at high-risk of aggressive pathology before surgery and may further complement postoperative pathological risk stratification for early recurrence.

items.title: Automatic generation of training data from dual-energy CT scans: a new approach to train renal vessel segmentation models.
items.authors: Zhang Y, Zhong H, Ma J, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: VNC and Iodine-density images can be utilized to automatically generate training data for segmentation models. This pipeline shows promise for training segmentation models on NECT images.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To investigate the feasibility of automatic training data generation using virtual non-contrast (VNC) images of dual-energy CT and to evaluate the performance of medical segmentation models trained on auto-generated data.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Training images were generated from contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) scans using VNC algorithm. Corresponding training labels were generated from iodine-density images via intensity thresholding. The paired VNC images and labels constituted the dataset (791 cases in total) for training non-enhanced CT (NECT) segmentation models. We attempted to train segmentation models with VNC images alone, as well as the combination of VNC and real NECT images.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Models trained with auto-generated data effectively performed renal vein segmentation on NECT images, achieving Dice score of 69.60%. It identified 100% (70/70) vein main trunks and 54.5% (6/11) accessory veins in the test set. The models' performance on artery segmentation was not satisfactory, with Dice score of 44.56%. It only identified 41.4% (29/70) artery main trunks and 4.54% (1/22) accessory arteries. However, the combination of generated data and labeled data greatly improved model's artery Dice to 71.23%. Combined model identified 100% (70/70) vein main trunks, 98.6% (69/70) artery main trunks, 68.2% (15/22) accessory arteries and 63.6% (7/11) accessory veins. Its accessory artery detection is significantly higher than the model trained with labeled data (15/22 vs. 5/22, p < 0.01), closing the gap with human radiologist (15/22 vs. 18/22, p = 0.250).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: VNC and Iodine-density images can be utilized to automatically generate training data for segmentation models. This pipeline shows promise for training segmentation models on NECT images.

items.title: T2-weighted MRI-based radiomics for preoperative prediction of homologous recombination deficiency status in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.
items.authors: Zhou J, Jiang X, Deng M, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: Our research demonstrated that the combined model achieved the optimal predictive performance. It is feasible to apply radiomics to predict HRD status of HGSOC patients, which can further assist clinicians in formulating individualized treatment strategies.

sections.label: Rationale and objectives
sections.text: The aim of this study was to explore the feasibility of T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) - based radiomics in preoperative prediction of homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) status in patients with high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), and to establish a non-invasive approach for guiding individualized treatment planning.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: A total of 133 patients with pathologically confirmed HGSOC who underwent MRI scan (T2WI, T1-contrast enhanced) were retrospectively enrolled in this study. All patients were stratified into HRD-positive and HRD-negative group. These 133 patients (41 in HRD-negative group and 92 in HRD-positive group) were randomly allocated to a training set (n = 93) and a validation set (n = 40) at a 7:3 ratio. Three different models were constructed and evaluated: clinical characteristics only (clinical model); T2WI-radiomics features only (radiomics model); and a combination of them all (combined model). The predictive performance was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and area under the curves (AUCs) were compared using the DeLong test. Calibration curves and decision curve analysis (DCA) were applied to validate the clinical-radiomic combined model.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: In the training set, the combined model achieved the best performance (AUC = 0.889; all P > 0.05). The radiomics model achieved predictive performance comparable to the clinical model (AUC of 0.762 vs. 0.790; P = 0.676). In the validation set, the combined model performed significantly better than the clinical or radiomics model (AUCs of 0.853 vs. 0.805 vs. 0.706; all P > 0.05). DCA demonstrated that the combined model achieved superior net benefit across a wide range of threshold probabilities compared with the clinical and radiomics models alone.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: Our research demonstrated that the combined model achieved the optimal predictive performance. It is feasible to apply radiomics to predict HRD status of HGSOC patients, which can further assist clinicians in formulating individualized treatment strategies.

items.title: CT-fibrosis score: development and internal validation for identifying advanced fibrosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
items.authors: Kokenberger G, Almetwali O, Yu T, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The CT-Fibrosis Score achieved moderate discrimination for advanced fibrosis but did not improve discrimination when added to FIB-4. External validation in an unselected population undergoing CT for non-hepatic indications is required before any opportunistic application.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: Advanced fibrosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) involves metabolic and anatomic remodeling beyond the liver. We developed and internally validated an interpretable CT-based score integrating abdominal body-composition and organ measurements and compared it with the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: We retrospectively studied 151 patients with biopsy-confirmed MASLD (86 advanced [F3-F4], 65 early-stage [F0-F2] fibrosis). Deep learning-based segmentation quantified abdominal adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, bone, liver, and spleen measurements. The CT-Fibrosis Score was developed using repeated (50×) stratified 5-fold cross-validation, with imputation, standardization, and feature selection confined to each training fold and inner 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter selection. Performance was based on out-of-fold predictions and compared with FIB-4 using the DeLong test. Sensitivity analyses addressed missing data, age dependence, and ascites.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Four features were consistently selected: age, bone-to-abdominal-cavity volume ratio, visceral adipose tissue (VAT) density, and spleen index. The CT-Fibrosis Score achieved an out-of-fold AUC of 0.77 (95% CI 0.69-0.85). Among 141 patients with an available FIB-4 score, no significant difference was detected between the CT-Fibrosis Score (AUC 0.76) and FIB-4 (AUC 0.79; difference - 0.03, 95% CI - 0.11 to + 0.04; p = 0.37); this comparison was not powered for non-inferiority. Adding the CT-Fibrosis Score to FIB-4 did not improve discrimination (AUC 0.80 vs. 0.79; difference + 0.003, 95% CI - 0.04 to + 0.05; p = 0.90), with the confidence interval excluding an improvement greater than approximately 0.05.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The CT-Fibrosis Score achieved moderate discrimination for advanced fibrosis but did not improve discrimination when added to FIB-4. External validation in an unselected population undergoing CT for non-hepatic indications is required before any opportunistic application.

items.title: Multimodality imaging of hepatic cystic echinococcosis: diagnostic approach, differential diagnosis, complications, and post-treatment assessment.
items.authors: Salahshour F, Navabakhsh B, Dadgar S, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Cystic echinococcosis (CE), caused by the metacestode of Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato, is a zoonosis that remains endemic across the Middle East, the Mediterranean basin, North Africa and South America, and the liver is the organ most frequently involved. Because serological assays are of limited sensitivity and specificity, imaging carries the diagnostic burden: ultrasonography (US) is the cornerstone for initial diagnosis, staging, treatment planning and longitudinal follow-up; computed tomography (CT) best defines anatomical location, vascular relationships, mural calcification and acute complications such as rupture and superinfection; and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) more faithfully reproduces US-defined staging morphology than CT and provides superior soft-tissue contrast for assessing biliary involvement and separating CE cysts from cystic neoplasms.

sections.text: Cystic echinococcosis (CE), caused by the metacestode of Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato, is a zoonosis that remains endemic across the Middle East, the Mediterranean basin, North Africa and South America, and the liver is the organ most frequently involved. Because serological assays are of limited sensitivity and specificity, imaging carries the diagnostic burden: ultrasonography (US) is the cornerstone for initial diagnosis, staging, treatment planning and longitudinal follow-up; computed tomography (CT) best defines anatomical location, vascular relationships, mural calcification and acute complications such as rupture and superinfection; and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) more faithfully reproduces US-defined staging morphology than CT and provides superior soft-tissue contrast for assessing biliary involvement and separating CE cysts from cystic neoplasms. The aim of this pictorial review is fourfold: to illustrate the US, CT and MRI appearance of each World Health Organization Informal Working Group on Echinococcosis (WHO-IWGE) stage of hepatic CE and to explain how stage assignment translates directly into a stage-specific treatment decision-anti-parasitic treatment, percutaneous treatment, surgery or watch-and-wait; to present, stage by stage, the hepatic lesions that mimic CE and the findings that discriminate them; to depict the wall signs of the CE cyst that become visible with high-frequency linear transducers, including the three-layered wall, adherent brood capsules and hydatid sand; and to review the imaging of complicated CE together with the expected post-treatment appearance, procedure-related complications and the imaging strategy for detecting recurrence.

items.title: Early Implementation Performance of the CMS Electronic Clinical Quality Measure for Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality in Diagnostic CT: An Evaluation of 254 Facilities.
items.journal_full: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
items.authors: Smith-Bindman R, Bindman AB, Kohli MD, et al.

conclusion.label: Discussion
conclusion.text: Early ExRad performance varied widely across facilities and across CT categories within the same facility. Most variation reflected particular facility-category combinations, so facilities need their own category-level results to identify which protocols to target.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate early facility performance on the CMS-adopted Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality for Diagnostic CT in Adults (ExRad) measure, the first automated radiology outcome measure in CMS payment programs, during the first 16 months of the measure's inclusion in CMS programs.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: ExRad evaluates each adult diagnostic CT examination in three steps: assignment to 1 of 19 CT categories defined by anatomic region and clinical indication; computation of size-adjusted radiation dose and image noise from the DICOM radiation dose-structured report and pixel data; and comparison of both against category-specific thresholds. Because the clinical and radiology data sit in separate systems, translation software inside the health system firewall may be used to perform the linkage. An examination is out of range if its dose or noise exceeds its category threshold; a facility's score is the percentage of eligible examinations out of range (lower is better). We analyzed all facilities reporting between May 2025 and August 2026.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Across 254 facilities and 783,634 examinations in 16 CT categories, 30.7% were out of range: 240,409 (30.7%) exceeded the dose threshold and 446 (0.06%) the noise threshold. Facility scores varied widely: median 29.5% (interquartile range [IQR] 18.4-44.7; range 1.8-82.4), with facilities at the 90th percentile scoring 4.6 times more out-of-range scans than those at the 10th percentile. Median out-of-range percentages by category ranged from 0% (routine and low-dose cardiac) to 82.6% (high-dose head; IQR 23.5-100.0); routine abdomen and pelvis, the highest-volume category, had a median of 43.9% (IQR 30.1-61.3). Within facilities, the median gap between best- and worst-performing category was 74 percentage points (IQR 49-89; intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.12).

sections.label: Discussion
sections.text: Early ExRad performance varied widely across facilities and across CT categories within the same facility. Most variation reflected particular facility-category combinations, so facilities need their own category-level results to identify which protocols to target.

items.title: Mapping Gadolinium-based Contrast Agent Residues in the Rat Kidney.
items.authors: Hummel L, Boyken J, Gladytz T, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: This study provides the first comprehensive spatially resolved characterization of renal GBCA residues at an early and a late time point. GBCA residues exhibited specific intrarenal distribution patterns and distinct changes in these patterns over the course of their elimination. Our findings of specific retention patterns suggest that renal microanatomy and local physicochemical conditions play critical roles in GBCA retention. These insights provide a foundation for future investigations into retention mechanisms and potential long-term tissue effects.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) are routinely used to enhance magnetic resonance (MR) imaging. In recent years, GBCA residues were detected in multiple organs, with the kidney as the primary organ of excretion showing the highest concentrations. This study aimed to map the intricate spatial distribution of GBCA residues in rat kidneys at an early and a late time point.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Rats received one of 6 marketed GBCAs [3 macrocyclic, 3 linear; cumulative dose 4.8 mmol gadolinium (Gd)/kg] or saline and were sacrificed at day 5 or week 14 post administration (n = 5 per GBCA and time point). In whole renal tissue slices, the distribution of elemental Gd was determined by laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry and the distribution of intact GBCA chelates by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-mass spectrometry imaging. In ex vivo kidneys, MR relaxometry was used to assess MR-detectable GBCA residues.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: At day 5, Gd was predominantly localized in the renal cortex across all GBCAs, with 10- to 100-fold lower medullary levels. Distribution patterns corresponded well with those of exemplary intact GBCA chelates. At week 14, Gd levels had decreased by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude. Distribution patterns from linear GBCAs showed Gd remaining predominantly in the cortex, while Gd from macrocyclic GBCAs was similar in cortex and medulla. Several GBCAs exhibited a prominent Gd presence at the transition zone between outer and inner medulla. Intact chelate was only detectable for the exemplary macrocyclic GBCA, with a spatial distribution pattern matching that of elemental Gd. MR relaxometry detected GBCA residues within ex vivo kidneys but also in the surrounding water-based fixative. This indicated the presence and washout of intact GBCAs, which was greater for macrocyclic versus linear GBCAs.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: This study provides the first comprehensive spatially resolved characterization of renal GBCA residues at an early and a late time point. GBCA residues exhibited specific intrarenal distribution patterns and distinct changes in these patterns over the course of their elimination. Our findings of specific retention patterns suggest that renal microanatomy and local physicochemical conditions play critical roles in GBCA retention. These insights provide a foundation for future investigations into retention mechanisms and potential long-term tissue effects.

items.title: Percutaneous and endovascular procedures in adrenal disease: indications, technique, and outcomes.
items.authors: Durmus MA, Taydas O, Arik E, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Adrenal masses are found on roughly 4-5% of abdominal imaging studies, and the proportion rises with age. Most are benign, non-functioning adenomas that need imaging characterization and hormonal screening but no intervention.

sections.text: Adrenal masses are found on roughly 4-5% of abdominal imaging studies, and the proportion rises with age. Most are benign, non-functioning adenomas that need imaging characterization and hormonal screening but no intervention. The remainder, comprising metastases, adrenocortical carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and hormonally active adenomas, raise questions that computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging cannot always settle; in these cases image-guided procedures can help. Percutaneous biopsy is reserved for hormonally inactive lesions whose benignity imaging has not established and whose histology would change management. Adrenal venous sampling remains the reference method for lateralizing aldosterone excess in primary aldosteronism and therefore decides who is offered adrenalectomy, although success depends heavily on operator experience and local protocol. Thermal ablation has produced biochemical and blood-pressure responses in selected aldosterone-producing adenomas and local control of limited metastases, but the evidence is largely nonrandomized and does not establish equivalence with surgery. Transarterial embolization serves three purposes: hemostasis in adrenal hemorrhage, devascularization before resection of hypervascular tumors, and functional treatment of aldosteronism, now supported by one small randomized trial. Each procedure carries hazards peculiar to the gland (catecholamine crisis, adrenal insufficiency after bilateral treatment, non-target embolization) that shape patient selection and periprocedural monitoring. This review covers indications, technique, outcomes and complications for each. Surgery remains the treatment of choice for most operable patients. Interventional radiology is most useful when the indications for sampling, ablation or embolization are recognized early and discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting, not only after surgery has been declined.

items.title: Clinical validation of Node-RADS for nodal staging in colon cancer: a retrospective study of 360 patients.
items.authors: Wu G, Xiao J, Wang D, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: In this large retrospective cohort, contrast-enhanced CT-based Node-RADS demonstrated reliable diagnostic performance for preoperative assessment of LNM in colon cancer and outperformed the conventional size-based criterion. The good inter-observer agreement further supports the reproducibility and clinical feasibility of Node-RADS in routine clinical practice.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Can CT-based Node-RADS overcome the low sensitivity and underestimation of nodal metastasis associated with the conventional 10-mm short-axis criterion in preoperative colon cancer staging? Findings In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases. Critical relevance statement In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of the Node Reporting and Data System version 1.0 (Node-RADS 1.0) for preoperative evaluation of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in colon cancer and to benchmark its diagnostic performance against conventional CT-based size criteria.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective study enrolled patients who underwent radical resection for colon cancer at Shantou Central Hospital between January 2015 and January 2019. All patients received radical resection followed by histopathological evaluation of regional lymph nodes. Preoperative computed tomography (CT) images were independently reviewed by two experienced radiologists using the Node-RADS scoring system. Inter-observer agreement was assessed, and diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 360 patients were included. Lymph node positivity was associated with several CT features, including nodal size, internal heterogeneity, necrosis, margin characteristics, fatty hilum status, and the Node-RADS score (all p < 0.05). The Node-RADS score demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.835, 95% CI: 0.792-0.871) with an optimal cutoff of ≥3, good inter-observer reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) = 0.962), and higher discriminative ability than the conventional 10-mm size criterion (AUC 0.546; p < 0.05).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: In this large retrospective cohort, contrast-enhanced CT-based Node-RADS demonstrated reliable diagnostic performance for preoperative assessment of LNM in colon cancer and outperformed the conventional size-based criterion. The good inter-observer agreement further supports the reproducibility and clinical feasibility of Node-RADS in routine clinical practice.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Can CT-based Node-RADS overcome the low sensitivity and underestimation of nodal metastasis associated with the conventional 10-mm short-axis criterion in preoperative colon cancer staging? Findings In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases. Critical relevance statement In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases.

items.title: MRI-based biomarkers for risk stratification and assessment of treatment response in Metabolic dysfunction-associated Steatotic liver disease.
items.authors: Mironova M, Taouli B, Ehman RL, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Artificial intelligence may broaden access by automating analysis and enabling PDFF from routine MRI. We review the evidence supporting these biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis and regulatory use, and their role in clinical trials and in treatment decisions for approved MASH therapies.

sections.text: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects up to 38% of the population globally. Liver biopsy, the historical reference standard, is invasive, subject to sampling error and not scalable. MRI-based biomarkers provide non-invasive, quantitative whole liver assessment. MRI proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) is the most accurate noninvasive measure of steatosis (thresholds of 6.4%, 17.4% and 22.1% for grades ≥1, ≥2 and 3), and a ≥30% relative reduction is associated with histologic response. Liver stiffness by magnetic resonance elastography (MRE-LS) is the most accurate imaging biomarker for fibrosis: MRE-LS of 3.1-4.4 kPa corresponds to F2-F3 and ≥5 kPa to cirrhosis, and each 1-kPa increase is associated with a 43% higher risk of hepatic decompensation. Iron-corrected T1 is a sensitive but nonspecific marker of disease activity whose prognostic value requires further study. Composite scores, MAST, MEFIB, and MASH Resolution Index, combine imaging and blood tests for advanced fibrosis diagnosis and response assessment. MRE is cost-effective compared with vibration-controlled transient elastography for detecting advanced fibrosis. Artificial intelligence may broaden access by automating analysis and enabling PDFF from routine MRI. We review the evidence supporting these biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis and regulatory use, and their role in clinical trials and in treatment decisions for approved MASH therapies.

items.title: Simplifying CT/MRI LI-RADS v2018 Maintains Diagnostic Performance: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis.
items.journal_full: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
items.authors: Lam E, Leeflang MMG, Adamo RG, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Simplifying LI-RADS v2018 by removing TG and using a 10-mm size cut-off preserved diagnostic table AUC while improving LR-5 sensitivity without loss of specificity or PPV.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) diagnostic algorithm assesses hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) probability of liver observations in high-risk individuals, but complexity may limit its adoption.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To evaluate whether LI-RADS v2018 can be simplified without impairing diagnostic performance by removing threshold growth (TG) and reducing size cut-offs.

sections.label: Study type
sections.text: Retrospective meta-analysis.

sections.label: Population
sections.text: Eight thousand five hundred eighty-two patients (mean age: 59 ± 11 years; 6610 male) at risk for HCC with CT/MRI (986 CT, 6554 MRI, and 1042 CT/MRI).

sections.label: Field strength/sequence
sections.text: Field strength: 1.5T and 3.0T; sequences varied by institution per LI-RADS technical requirements.

sections.label: Assessment
sections.text: LI-RADS v2018 using major features only was compared with seven simplifications removing TG and/or applying single size cut-offs (≥ 10, ≥ 15, and ≥ 20 mm) in individual participant data (IPD) of 64 studies (29 institutions, 11 countries) from the LI-RADS Living Systematic Review and IPD Meta-analysis Project. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2.

sections.label: Statistical tests
sections.text: Summary receiver operating characteristic curves estimated area under the curve (AUC) across LR-3 to LR-5; LR-5 sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value (PPV) were estimated using a one-step bivariate mixed-effects model. Differences were assessed by cluster bootstrap. p < 0.05 indicated significance, uncorrected for multiple comparisons.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Nine thousand four hundred six observations were included. Excluding TG with a 10-mm cut-off showed AUC similar to LI-RADS v2018 (0.80 vs. 0.81, p = 0.44) and significantly higher LR-5 sensitivity (73.8% vs. 71.8%) with similar specificity (72.5% vs. 73.7%, p = 0.13) and PPV (97.8% vs. 97.8%, p = 0.73). Removing TG with 15-mm and 20-mm cut-offs had significantly lower AUC than v2018 (-0.03 [95% CI: -0.041, -0.019]; -0.043 [-0.054, -0.032], respectively) and sensitivity (-13.2% [95% CI: -14.5%, -12.0%]; -30.1% [-31.7%, -28.5%], respectively). Of the 64 studies, 17 had low-risk of bias, and 56 had low applicability concerns.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Simplifying LI-RADS v2018 by removing TG and using a 10-mm size cut-off preserved diagnostic table AUC while improving LR-5 sensitivity without loss of specificity or PPV.

sections.label: Protocol registration
sections.text: Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/cjwgp).

sections.label: Technical efficiency
sections.text: Stage 2.

items.title: CT-based adaptation of the Vizzielli laparoscopic risk-adjusted score in advanced ovarian cancer: Agreement and inter-reader reproducibility.
items.authors: Versienti E, Arcieri M, De Martino M, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Proposed CT-based variants showed agreement with the Vizzielli laparoscopic risk-adjusted score. The PCI-based ECOG-PS variant showed the highest agreement metrics, suggesting that structured CT assessment may help approximate laparoscopic risk categories before invasive evaluation.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To evaluate agreement of proposed CT-based variants with the Vizzielli laparoscopic risk-adjusted score in suspected advanced ovarian cancer and assess inter-reader agreement of CT-derived components.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective single-center study included consecutive adults evaluated between January 2021 and November 2025 for suspected advanced ovarian cancer who underwent contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT and staging laparoscopy. Proposed CT-based modifications were operationalized as six score variants combining CT-derived peritoneal tumor burden, CT-estimated ascites, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), and either Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG-PS) or CT-derived body composition parameters. Agreement with the laparoscopic risk-adjusted score was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), Spearman correlation coefficient, and weighted Cohen's kappa.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The final cohort included 80 patients. All CT-based variants showed agreement with the laparoscopic risk-adjusted score. For the variant combining CT-derived PCI, CT-estimated ascites, ECOG-PS, and CA-125, the consistency ICC was 0.76, Spearman's ρ was 0.806, and weighted Cohen's kappa was 0.76. This variant showed 70.0% agreement across the three risk categories and 83.8% agreement for high-risk versus non-high-risk classification, classifying 20 of 22 laparoscopic high-risk patients as high risk. The PCI-based skeletal muscle index (SMI) variant maintained substantial agreement: ICC, 0.73; Spearman correlation coefficient, 0.742; weighted Cohen's kappa, 0.74. Inter-reader agreement was high for CT-derived PCI, with an ICC of 0.91.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Proposed CT-based variants showed agreement with the Vizzielli laparoscopic risk-adjusted score. The PCI-based ECOG-PS variant showed the highest agreement metrics, suggesting that structured CT assessment may help approximate laparoscopic risk categories before invasive evaluation.

items.title: Node-RADS outperforms dual-energy CT-derived quantifications for distinguishing metastatic from non-metastatic regional lymph nodes in resectable gastric cancer.
items.authors: Yao DX, Lin XX, Bei TX, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Node-RADS demonstrates superior diagnostic performance compared with DECT-derived quantitative parameters for identifying metastatic regional LNs in resectable GC, and can be reliably applied in the DECT settings.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Preoperative differentiation of metastatic from non-metastatic regional lymph nodes in resectable gastric cancer remains inaccurate using conventional size criteria. Findings Node-RADS (AUC = 0.859) outperformed SD diameter (continuous: AUC = 0.780; its > 8 mm dichotomized counterpart: AUC = 0.748) and ICDP (AUC = 0.612) for metastatic LN discrimination. Clinical relevance Node-RADS is a standardized and reproducible criterion that can be applied in dual-energy CT scenarios to effectively identify regional lymph node metastasis in resectable gastric cancer.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate and compare the diagnostic performance of Node-RADS, dual-energy CT (DECT)-derived quantitative parameters, and their combination for distinguishing metastatic from non-metastatic regional lymph nodes (LNs) in patients with resectable gastric cancer (GC).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Between Jan 2022 and Oct 2025, 115 consecutive patients with resectable GC who underwent preoperative triple-phase enhanced DECT scans and radical gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy were retrospectively enrolled. A total of 151 regional LNs (70 metastatic, 81 non-metastatic) with region-level pathological confirmation were selected for node-level comparison. Two radiologists independently assessed Node-RADS scores for each LN. LN short diameter (SD) was measured at the venous phase on the maximal axial slice. DECT-derived parameters (CT attenuation at 40 keV, iodine concentration (IC), and effective atomic number (Zeff) across arterial, venous, and delayed phases) were analyzed using a freehand region of interest on the maximal axial slice of the LN. Diagnostic performances were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis and compared using the DeLong test.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: IC at delayed phase (ICDP) was the sole parameter associated with LN involvement. The initial Node-RADS score (cut-off ≥ 3) achieved an AUC of 0.859 (95% CI: 0.793-0.910), significantly outperforming SD (AUC: 0.780, p < 0.05) and ICDP (AUC: 0.612, p < 0.05). Two modified Node-RADS algorithms incorporating ICDP under different rule-in and rule-out criteria were established, but did not improve diagnostic performance beyond the initial Node-RADS scores.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Node-RADS demonstrates superior diagnostic performance compared with DECT-derived quantitative parameters for identifying metastatic regional LNs in resectable GC, and can be reliably applied in the DECT settings.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Preoperative differentiation of metastatic from non-metastatic regional lymph nodes in resectable gastric cancer remains inaccurate using conventional size criteria. Findings Node-RADS (AUC = 0.859) outperformed SD diameter (continuous: AUC = 0.780; its > 8 mm dichotomized counterpart: AUC = 0.748) and ICDP (AUC = 0.612) for metastatic LN discrimination. Clinical relevance Node-RADS is a standardized and reproducible criterion that can be applied in dual-energy CT scenarios to effectively identify regional lymph node metastasis in resectable gastric cancer.

items.title: Treatment Effect of Perioperative (Neoadjuvant and Adjuvant) Apalutamide plus Androgen-deprivation Therapy Versus Radical Prostatectomy Alone in Patients with High-risk Localized or Locally Advanced Prostate Cancer from the PROTEUS Substudy.
items.authors: Briganti A, Steuber T, Shore ND, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: Perioperative apalutamide plus ADT improved EFS and delayed subsequent therapy compared with SOC. Together with the blinded PROTEUS main study, these results support perioperative apalutamide plus ADT as a new therapeutic option for selected patients with HR-LPC/LAPC who are fit for surgery and 1-yr systemic therapy.

extras.label: Results and limitations
extras.text: In total, 408 patients (median age 66 yr [interquartile range 62-71]) were randomized: perioperative apalutamide plus ADT, n = 102; RP, n = 306. Median follow-up was 37.4 mo in patients without EFS events. Perioperative apalutamide plus ADT significantly improved EFS compared with RP alone (median not reached vs 19.1 mo; estimated 3-yr event-free rates 63% vs 41%; HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.26-0.55; p < 0.001). Because of the nonconstant HR over time, indicating that the proportional hazards assumption was not met, a post hoc restricted mean survival time analysis was performed. This analysis estimated that the average event-free time during the first 36 mo was 31.7 mo (95% CI 30.3-33.1) with perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus 20.7 mo (95% CI 19.1-22.4) with RP alone, a difference of 11.0 mo (95% CI 8.8-13.1; p < 0.001). MFS by conventional or PSMA PET imaging favored perioperative apalutamide plus ADT over RP alone (estimated 3-yr event-free rates 87% vs 78%; HR 0.49; 95% CI 0.26-0.90; p = 0.019), and the hazard of subsequent therapy was reduced by 71% (HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.20-0.43; p < 0.001). MFS by conventional imaging showed no difference between study groups (estimated 3-yr event-free rates 94% vs 92%; HR 0.74; 95% CI 0.30-1.82; p = 0.5). Grade 3-4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 31 patients (31%) receiving perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus 62 patients (22%) receiving RP.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: The blinded placebo-controlled PROTEUS (Perioperative Treatment with Erleada United with Surgery) study demonstrated that adding 1-yr perioperative apalutamide plus androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) benefited patients with high-risk localized prostate cancer or locally advanced prostate cancer (HR-LPC/LAPC) who were undergoing radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection (RP).

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: This substudy evaluated 1-yr perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus standard-of-care (SOC) RP.

sections.label: Design, setting, and participants
sections.text: Patients with newly diagnosed HR-LPC/LAPC were randomized 1:3 to open-label perioperative apalutamide (240 mg/d) plus ADT (six 28-d cycles before and after RP) or RP.

sections.label: Outcomes measurements and statistical analysis
sections.text: The primary end point was event-free survival (EFS), defined as time to biochemical failure, local/regional recurrence, distant metastasis, or death. Secondary/other end points included metastasis-free survival (MFS) by conventional or prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA PET) imaging, MFS by conventional imaging, and time to first subsequent therapy; p values were nominal. Time-to-event end points were analyzed with the Kaplan-Meier method and stratified Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for the randomization stratification factors to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

sections.label: Results and limitations
sections.text: In total, 408 patients (median age 66 yr [interquartile range 62-71]) were randomized: perioperative apalutamide plus ADT, n = 102; RP, n = 306. Median follow-up was 37.4 mo in patients without EFS events. Perioperative apalutamide plus ADT significantly improved EFS compared with RP alone (median not reached vs 19.1 mo; estimated 3-yr event-free rates 63% vs 41%; HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.26-0.55; p < 0.001). This analysis estimated that the average event-free time during the first 36 mo was 31.7 mo (95% CI 30.3-33.1) with perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus 20.7 mo (95% CI 19.1-22.4) with RP alone, a difference of 11.0 mo (95% CI 8.8-13.1; p < 0.001). MFS by conventional or PSMA PET imaging favored perioperative apalutamide plus ADT over RP alone (estimated 3-yr event-free rates 87% vs 78%; HR 0.49; 95% CI 0.26-0.90; p = 0.019), and the hazard of subsequent therapy was reduced by 71% (HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.20-0.43; p < 0.001). Grade 3-4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 31 patients (31%) receiving perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus 62 patients (22%) receiving RP.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: Perioperative apalutamide plus ADT improved EFS and delayed subsequent therapy compared with SOC. Together with the blinded PROTEUS main study, these results support perioperative apalutamide plus ADT as a new therapeutic option for selected patients with HR-LPC/LAPC who are fit for surgery and 1-yr systemic therapy.

items.title: After-hours on-site radiologist availability and emergency CT reporting: a roster-based cohort with staffing-boundary analysis.
items.authors: Konieczka P, Kłosiewicz T, Al-Hosam K

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: During comparable after-hours periods, roster-recorded absence of an on-site CT radiologist was associated with longer complete-report TAT, particularly for abdominopelvic CT. Downstream stay differences were exploratory and may reflect broader hospital processes.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To compare after-hours emergency CT report turnaround during periods with versus without roster-recorded on-site CT radiologist availability.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective roster-based cohort included emergency-department CT examinations from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. The common-support cohort comprised non-holiday weekdays from 15:00 to 06:59 and all weekends and public holidays. Components within 15 min were grouped into packages. The exposure was on-site CT radiologist availability recorded in the final as-worked duty roster; actual reporting route was secondary. The primary outcome was scan-to-complete-report turnaround time (TAT). Models used duty-date-clustered standard errors and adjusted for patient, temporal, workload, and examination characteristics.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The cohort contained 13,533 CT packages; 13,270 had usable TAT and 12,333 index encounters were clinically linked. Median TAT was 81 min without and 58 min with an on-site radiologist. Absence of an on-site radiologist was associated with 33.9% longer adjusted TAT (95% CI 25.4-43.0). The association was 28.4% for routine non-contrast head CT and 45.5% for abdominopelvic CT (interaction + 15.1%; p = 0.001). A ± 120-minute staffing-boundary analysis estimated 45.7% longer TAT (16.3-82.5), with positive estimates across ± 60- to ± 180-minute bandwidths and no detected covariate discontinuities. Actual-route TAT was 47.7% longer amid 34.5% route discordance.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: During comparable after-hours periods, roster-recorded absence of an on-site CT radiologist was associated with longer complete-report TAT, particularly for abdominopelvic CT. Downstream stay differences were exploratory and may reflect broader hospital processes.

items.authors: Parillo M, Deistung A, Vaccarino F, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
