sections.text: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is a high-resolution 3D gradient-echo (GRE) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique that combines magnitude and phase information to increase sensitivity to blood products, iron, calcification, thrombus, and venous structures. In routine practice, SWI should be interpreted together with source magnitude images, filtered phase images, processed SWI images, and minimum-intensity projection (minIP) images, keeping in mind blooming and other artefacts, as well as vendor-dependent phase conventions. Its most established role is in brain MRI, particularly in: suspected cerebral amyloid angiopathy; baseline and follow-up assessment of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with haemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H) during anti-amyloid therapy; traumatic brain injury; multiple sclerosis work-up, when assessment of the central vein sign or paramagnetic rim lesions is clinically relevant; neuro-oncology; and vascular malformations. Overall, these constitute the core recommended brain scenarios for SWI supported by moderate to high levels of evidence. Outside neuroradiology (e.g., musculoskeletal, abdominal, breast, pelvic, and cardiac imaging), SWI remains promising but less standardised and should currently be reserved for selected problem-solving indications. KEY POINTS: SWI should be acquired as a high-resolution 3D GRE sequence and interpreted together with source magnitude images, filtered phase images, and post-processed minIP images, keeping in mind blooming and other artefacts, as well as vendor-specific phase conventions. SWI should be included in brain MRI protocols when haemorrhagic or microvascular susceptibility findings are expected to affect diagnosis or management, especially in cerebral amyloid angiopathy, anti-amyloid therapy monitoring, traumatic brain injury, and neuro-oncology or multiple sclerosis work-up. Outside neuroradiology, SWI can be used as a targeted problem-solving adjunct rather than as a routine sequence.

items.title: Transfemoral transcaval adrenal biopsy: a technical report and review of adrenal biopsy approaches.
items.authors: Rubinov Y, Lubat A, Katz R, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Despite advances in cross-sectional imaging, adrenal biopsy plays a role in a small subset of lesions that remain indeterminate after complete imaging work-up or in which tissue diagnosis would alter management. Anatomic constraints around the adrenal glands can make safe percutaneous access technically challenging.

sections.text: Despite advances in cross-sectional imaging, adrenal biopsy plays a role in a small subset of lesions that remain indeterminate after complete imaging work-up or in which tissue diagnosis would alter management. Anatomic constraints around the adrenal glands can make safe percutaneous access technically challenging. This technical report describes a transfemoral transcaval approach to biopsy of a right adrenal mass directly abutting the inferior vena cava (IVC) that was not safely accessible by conventional percutaneous routes. Additionally, a concise review of contemporary adrenal biopsy indications and access routes is performed. Adapted from transfemoral transcaval liver biopsy, the technique uses right common femoral venous access, positioning of a reshaped metal guide cannula within the IVC at the level of the lesion adjacent to the right renal vein, and deployment of a core biopsy needle across the caval wall under combined fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance, with cone-beam CT confirmation of needle position and completion venography to exclude caval injury. Diagnostic tissue was obtained without periprocedural complication; histopathology demonstrated an unexpected pheochromocytoma, a finding discussed here in detail due to its implications for pre-procedure biochemical evaluation. This limited experience demonstrates technical feasibility in carefully selected patients. The safety and comparative effectiveness of the technique require evaluation in larger series.

items.title: MRI-based deep learning model for prediction of Ki-67 expression level in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
items.authors: Wang C, Jin M, Zhang Y, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: We developed and validated a non-invasive DL model integrating contrast-enhanced MRI and clinical parameters that accurately predicts Ki-67 expression in iCCA, demonstrating superior diagnostic performance.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Ki-67 expression is a valuable prognostic indicator in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA). This study aimed to develop a non-invasive Deep learning (DL) model based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical data to predict Ki-67 expression preoperatively.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Patients with iCCA between January 2020 and January 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Based on immunohistochemistry, patients were classified into high-expression group (Ki-67 > 50%) and low-expression group (Ki-67 ≤ 50%). After image acquisition, tumor segmentation, and preprocessing, a 3D-ResNet10 network was utilized for MRI feature extraction. A feed-forward neural network (FFN) was used for clinical feature extraction. Subsequently, the extracted image and clinical features were fused and fed into a lightweight classifier to perform Ki-67 level prediction. The performance of the DL models was evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation using accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, and the area under the curve (AUC).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 117 patients were ultimately included (30 cases in the high-expression group and 87 cases in the low-expression group). The model based solely on clinical variables demonstrated limited predictive efficacy (mean AUC: 53.18 ± 14.60%). The model utilizing MRI features alone exhibited high specificity (86.14 ± 10.25%) but modest sensitivity. In contrast, the fused DL model significantly outperformed both individual models, attaining a mean AUC of 84.24 ± 8.82%, an accuracy of 87.17 ± 5.95%, a specificity of 93.07 ± 9.35%, and a markedly improved sensitivity of 70.00 ± 19.44%, yielding a robust F1-score of 73.42 ± 12.28%.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: We developed and validated a non-invasive DL model integrating contrast-enhanced MRI and clinical parameters that accurately predicts Ki-67 expression in iCCA, demonstrating superior diagnostic performance.

items.title: Pretreatment prediction of neoadjuvant therapy response in locally advanced gastric cancer using an additive ctSLEP score and spectral CT.
items.authors: Peng Y, Guo X, Ren T, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The combined model showed reasonable predictive performance in internal validation. These findings support further external evaluation of a low-dimensional, clinically interpretable strategy integrating morphologic invasion burden, spectral enhancement, and systemic inflammation for pretreatment NAT response stratification.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To develop an additive ctSLEP score from routine CT morphologic invasion signs and evaluate the complementary value of morphologic CT, quantitative spectral CT, and systemic inflammation for pretreatment prediction of neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) response in locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC).

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective study included 158 patients with LAGC who underwent NAT and radical gastrectomy and were randomly divided into training and internal validation cohorts (7:3). Becker tumor regression grade 1a/1b defined response and 2/3 nonresponse. Additive ctSLEP summed four pretreatment CT signs: serosal invasion, extramural venous invasion, subtle signs of occult peritoneal/omental involvement, and lymphovascular invasion. Five hierarchical models combined additive ctSLEP, venous-phase iodine concentration (ICVP), arterial enhancement fraction (AEF), and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR). Performance was assessed using AUC, Brier score, calibration, and prespecified paired DeLong comparisons. A chemotherapy-only sensitivity analysis was performed.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Sixty-five patients (41.1%) were responders and ninety-three (58.9%) nonresponders. In the internal validation cohort, AUCs for the Morphology, Spectral, Imaging, Clinical-spectral, and Combined models were 0.642, 0.741, 0.725, 0.713, and 0.754, respectively. The Combined model had the highest AUC and lowest Brier score (0.200). Adding spectral CT to morphology increased AUC by 0.083 (P=0.129), and adding additive ctSLEP to the Clinical-spectral model increased AUC by 0.041 (P=0.558). In 51 patients receiving chemotherapy alone, higher additive ctSLEP was associated with greater odds of nonresponse (OR=2.15, 95% CI 1.35-3.88), whereas higher ICVP was associated with lower odds (OR=0.83, 95% CI 0.69-0.96).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The combined model showed reasonable predictive performance in internal validation. These findings support further external evaluation of a low-dimensional, clinically interpretable strategy integrating morphologic invasion burden, spectral enhancement, and systemic inflammation for pretreatment NAT response stratification.

items.title: CT-based multimodal fusion model for preoperative clear cell renal cell carcinoma grading: A multicenter study.
items.authors: Wu Y, Wang H, Liu C, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The multimodal fusion framework demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance across the internal validation and external test cohorts. These findings could be regarded as an exploratory study rather than evidence of established clinical superiority. The framework may provide complementary information for preoperative ccRCC grading.

extras.label: Critical relevance statement
extras.text: This study evaluates an exploratory multimodal fusion framework for preoperative ccRCC grading by combining clinical data, deep learning, and multiscale radiomic features. The framework may provide complementary non-invasive information for risk stratification.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To develop and evaluate a multimodal fusion framework for the preoperative World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) low- and high-grade classification of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), integrating clinical characteristics, deep learning (DL), and radiomic signatures extracted from corticomedullary phase (CMP) contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) images.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: In this retrospective multicenter study, we evaluated a cohort of 1,052 patients with histologically verified ccRCC across four institutions. The data of the primary cohort (Center A, n = 665) were randomly divided into a training dataset (n = 465) and an internal validation dataset (n = 200). The data of 387 additional patients from three institutions (Centers B-D) constituted the independent external test set. Initial single-modality classifiers were developed via ensemble machine learning, utilizing clinical variables, multiscale radiomic data (capturing intratumoral, habitat, and peritumoral regions), and DL representations (2D, 2.5D, and 3D). A soft voting mechanism was subsequently applied to integrate the top-performing base models. Model interpretability was determined using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, and overall diagnostic efficacy was quantified through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The weighted soft voting model (SoftVote-Opt) showed the numerically highest AUC among the evaluated fusion strategies and single-modality models. This model yielded AUCs of 0.761 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.839) and 0.745 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.813), with corresponding MCCs of 0.347 (95 % CI: 0.217-0.475) and 0.302(95 % CI: 0.205 -0.387), within the internal validation and external test sets, respectively. SHAP analysis revealed peritumoral 5 mm radiomic features as the primary determinants of the model's output, followed by intratumoral radiomic features, whereas deep learning and clinical features offered lower relative contributions.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The multimodal fusion framework demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance across the internal validation and external test cohorts. These findings could be regarded as an exploratory study rather than evidence of established clinical superiority. The framework may provide complementary information for preoperative ccRCC grading.

sections.label: Critical relevance statement
sections.text: This study evaluates an exploratory multimodal fusion framework for preoperative ccRCC grading by combining clinical data, deep learning, and multiscale radiomic features. The framework may provide complementary non-invasive information for risk stratification.

items.title: Long-term MRI surveillance of hepatocellular adenomas selected for conservative management: time to regression after oral contraceptive cessation.
items.authors: Jain N, Kim TK, Khalili K, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: In this selected surveillance cohort, most HCAs managed without intervention remained stable or decreased in size during long-term MRI follow-up. After OCP cessation, regression was gradual, with modest reduction often apparent within the first year but larger reductions frequently requiring several years; findings in the small ≥ 5 cm subgroup were exploratory. Limited early size reduction should therefore not, in isolation, be interpreted as failure of conservative management.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To describe the long-term MRI evolution of hepatocellular adenomas (HCAs) selected for conservative management and to quantify the time to predefined degrees of lesion size reduction after oral contraceptive pill (OCP) cessation.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: In this retrospective study, adults with pathologically proven or imaging-typical HCA who underwent serial liver MRI between January 2010 and December 2024 were reviewed. Up to three indexed lesions per patient were tracked, and lesion evolution was categorized using predefined lesion-level size-change thresholds derived from RECIST 1.1 conventions. In lesions from patients with documented post-diagnosis OCP cessation, time to ≥ 10%, ≥ 20%, and ≥ 30% diameter reduction was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Primary outcomes were repeated in one-lesion-per-patient sensitivity analyses (largest lesion per patient).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: 116 patients (110 women; mean age 38 ± 10 years) with 269 HCAs; median follow-up 6.5 years. Among 174 lesions selected for continued conservative management, 166 (95.4%) were stable or regressed. In an exploratory subgroup of 17 lesions with baseline diameter ≥ 5 cm, all were stable or regressive and 11 (64.7%) measured below 5 cm at last imaging. Among 81 lesions after OCP cessation, median times to ≥ 10%, ≥ 20%, and ≥ 30% diameter reduction were 8.6, 24.3, and 49.9 months (95% CI for ≥ 30%, 36.2-75.1). Findings were similar in sensitivity analyses. Both observed malignant transformations occurred in β-catenin-activated HCA, with no surveillance hemorrhage.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: In this selected surveillance cohort, most HCAs managed without intervention remained stable or decreased in size during long-term MRI follow-up. After OCP cessation, regression was gradual, with modest reduction often apparent within the first year but larger reductions frequently requiring several years; findings in the small ≥ 5 cm subgroup were exploratory. Limited early size reduction should therefore not, in isolation, be interpreted as failure of conservative management.

items.title: Reassessing the diagnostic value of spectral CT-derived parameters for pathological grading of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder.
items.authors: Wang X, Du S, Hu J, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Spectral CT-derived parameters are associated with pathologic grade in UCB but demonstrate only moderate discriminatory performance.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of spectral CT-derived quantitative parameters for preoperative prediction of pathologic grade in urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UCB) and to assess their incremental value over clinical variables and model robustness.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: In this retrospective study, patients with pathologically confirmed UCB who underwent preoperative contrast-enhanced spectral CT were included. Quantitative spectral parameters were extracted. Inter-reader agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Variables with P < 0.10 on univariable analysis were entered into multivariable logistic regression to construct clinical, imaging and combined models. Model robustness was evaluated using penalized regression (LASSO and elastic net) as sensitivity analyses. Model performance and clinical net benefit were assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, DeLong testing, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 120 patients were included (65 high-grade tumours and 55 low-grade tumours). Spectral parameters showed good to excellent inter-reader agreement. Several imaging features were associated with tumor grade on univariable analysis (P < 0.05). After inclusion of calcification in the clinical analysis, age remained independently associated with tumor grade, whereas tumor size, tumor number, and calcification were not statistically significant in the multivariable clinical model. AEF remained the only independent imaging predictor. The AUC was 0.743 for the imaging model, 0.746 for the clinical model and 0.772 for the combined model. The incremental improvement of the combined model over the clinical model was small (ΔAUC = 0.027) and not statistically significant (DeLong P = 0.563). DCA showed limited additional net benefit of the combined model at intermediate risk thresholds.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Spectral CT-derived parameters are associated with pathologic grade in UCB but demonstrate only moderate discriminatory performance.

items.title: CT imaging features in prognostic risk stratification compared to clinical staging in resectable gastric cancer: a multicenter study.
items.authors: Zhang R, Tang L, Liu Y, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Integrating visually assessable CT imaging features with conventional cStage improved DFS prognostic discrimination in the development cohort, while the derived CIS further refined risk stratification within preoperative cStage groups.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To evaluate the incremental prognostic value of visually assessable CT features beyond clinical stage (cStage) for disease-free survival (DFS) risk stratification in gastric cancer.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Patients undergoing curative gastrectomy were retrospectively included in development and external cohorts. Clinical and pathological stages were reconstructed according to the AJCC 8th edition and simplified to three tiers. Clinical Stage, CT Imaging, and Combined models were evaluated for discrimination, calibration, bootstrap-corrected performance, and external validation. Incremental prognostic value was assessed using changes in the C-index and time-dependent AUCs. A development-derived CT Imaging Score (CIS) cutoff was locked for exploratory risk refinement within preoperative cStage strata.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Among 886 patients (development, n = 698; external, n = 188), cStage-pStage concordance was 51.0% and 61.2%, respectively (linear-weighted κ = 0.387 and 0.513). In the development cohort, adding CIS to cStage increased the C-index from 0.648 to 0.805 (ΔC-index = 0.160, P = 0.002) and the 1-, 3-, and 5-year AUCs by 0.159, 0.184, and 0.193, respectively (all P = 0.001). The optimism-corrected C-index was 0.797 for the Combined model. External C-indices were 0.676, 0.694, and 0.695 for the Clinical Stage, CT Imaging, and Combined models, respectively. In the development cohort, CIS-high status was associated with worse DFS within cStage II (HR = 8.66, 95% CI: 5.59-13.42) and cStage III (HR = 5.78, 95% CI: 3.74-8.92), with associations retained after adjustment for postoperative pStage.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Integrating visually assessable CT imaging features with conventional cStage improved DFS prognostic discrimination in the development cohort, while the derived CIS further refined risk stratification within preoperative cStage groups.

conclusion.label: Conclusion

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question MASH is a critical histological endpoint of MASLD, but reliable non-invasive tools for its assessment remain inadequate. Findings The MR-PAT model integrating MRI-based PDFF and adipose tissue quantification demonstrates robust and excellent diagnostic performance for identifying MASH. Critical Relevance Statement The MR-PAT model leverages hepatic steatosis and the adipose tissue burden to elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms driving steatohepatitis. sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To develop a non-invasive diagnostic model combining magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived proton density fat fraction (PDFF) and adipose tissue for identifying metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: A total of 197 consecutive patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) who underwent liver biopsy, MRI-PDFF, and transient elastography (TE) were retrospectively enrolled. Independent predictors of MASH were identified using univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses. A combined model was constructed and internally validated via 1000 bootstrap resamples. The diagnostic performance was compared with that of established non-invasive tests (NITs).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Multivariable logistic regression analyses demonstrated that the PDFF and total adipose tissue index (TATI) were independent risk factors for MASH. The MRI-based PDFF-adipose tissue (MR-PAT) model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.866 for MASH identification. Bootstrap internal validation yielded an AUC of 0.870. The performance of the models was consistent across clinically relevant subgroups. The diagnostic performance of the MR-PAT model for MASH identification was significantly better than that of all the established NITs (all p < 0.05).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The MR-PAT model, combining MRI-derived PDFF and TATI, provides an accurate and robust non-invasive tool for identifying MASH. It outperforms widely recognized NITs and holds promise for risk stratification in patients with MASLD.

It can serve as an accurate, non-invasive tool for identifying MASH and holds promise for risk stratification in patients with MASLD.

items.authors: Xu L, Wang X, Liu Y, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A structured PI-QUAL v2 lecture improved both the accuracy and inter-reader agreement of prostate MRI image-quality assessments among diverse evaluators. Incorporating QA/QC further enhanced institutional image quality. PI-QUAL v2 training is a feasible strategy for standardizing prostate MRI quality.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Does a structured PI-QUAL v2 lecture for radiologists and technologists improve prostate MRI quality assessment performance and institutional imaging practice across institutions? Findings PI-QUAL v2 training improved accuracy (66.7% to 76.7%) and inter-reader agreement in prostate MRI quality assessment, while QA/QC feedback enhanced institutional imaging quality. Clinical relevance statement Structured PI-QUAL v2 education combined with quality assurance and quality control feedback improves evaluator consistency and institutional prostate MRI quality, facilitating standardized image-quality assessment and broader implementation of high-quality prostate MRI in clinical radiology.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate the impact of a prostate imaging quality (PI-QUAL) v2 lecture on the accuracy and inter-reader agreement of prostate MRI image-quality assessment among radiologists and technologists from diverse professional backgrounds and institutions, and to evaluate its role in institutional-level quality improvement through a quality control (QC) process.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Ten participants (five radiologists and five technologists) from five different hospitals independently evaluated 15 prostate MRIs before and after a standardized PI-QUAL v2 lecture. Reference scores were established by two experienced radiologists. Concordance with reference was assessed using accuracy and balanced accuracy. Inter-reader agreement was measured using percent agreement (PA) and Gwet's AC1. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on participant characteristics. For the quality assurance and QC (QA/QC), each center submitted 15 prostate MRIs before and after the lecture. Image quality was evaluated centrally to assess institutional improvement.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Overall accuracy increased from 66.7% to 76.7%, and balanced accuracy increased from 62.9% to 84.2%; the mixed-effects model indicated significantly higher post-lecture accuracy (p = 0.038). Accuracy was also higher across all subgroups. Inter-reader agreement improved from PA 57.6% to 72.6% and Gwet's AC1 from 0.214 to 0.466. Through the QA/QC process, three centers initially failed to meet PI-QUAL v2 technical criteria. After feedback, all post-intervention scans achieved PI-QUAL v2 scores > 1.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: A structured PI-QUAL v2 lecture improved both the accuracy and inter-reader agreement of prostate MRI image-quality assessments among diverse evaluators. Incorporating QA/QC further enhanced institutional image quality. PI-QUAL v2 training is a feasible strategy for standardizing prostate MRI quality.

items.title: Generating patient-friendly radiology reports with a local large language model: expert evaluation of quality and readability.
items.authors: van der Mee FAM, Broos R, Ottenheijm RPG, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Can a locally hosted LLM generate patient-friendly radiology reports while preserving data privacy and maintaining acceptable accuracy, completeness, and readability? Findings A locally hosted LLM generated patient-friendly report conclusions with higher quality scores than main reports, while clinically relevant hallucinations remained an important safety concern. Clinical relevance A locally hosted LLM has potential to generate patient-friendly radiology report translations without external cloud data transfer. Report conclusions appear to be the most promising initial application, although clinician oversight and further patient-centered validation remain essential before clinical implementation.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections (n = 359) and conclusion sections (n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch-Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t-tests.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1-Q3 5-5] vs 4 [3-5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5-5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48-84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation.

items.title: Patterns of Progression on Posttreatment Imaging During [177Lu]Lu-PSMA Radiopharmaceutical Therapy.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Yadav S, Khan S, Moradi Tuchayi A, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: PSMA-negative progression is uncommon and tends to emerge early. PSA-imaging discordance is frequent, underscoring the need for integrated imaging assessment throughout treatment.

sections.text: We characterized patterns of treatment response and progression during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) using serial posttreatment SPECT/CT and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET imaging and evaluated cycle-by-cycle prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-imaging concordance. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 361 patients from 2 academic centers who received at least 2 cycles of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT between May 2017 and March 2025. Posttreatment SPECT/CT scans were qualitatively evaluated to determine the site and pattern of response and progression, including PSMA low-avidity and PSMA-negative disease. Progression was defined by the appearance of new lesions or at least a 2-fold growth in preexisting lesions on SPECT/CT. PSA response was defined per Prostate Cancer Clinical Trials Working Group 3 criteria as at least a 50% decline from baseline. For cycle-by-cycle concordance analysis, PSA change was classified directionally as rising or falling relative to the prior cycle. In patients who paused or completed RPT after response, progression imaging was compared with the final on-treatment SPECT/CT scan. Results: Overall, 290 of 361 (80%) patients demonstrated a decrease in lesion size or number on posttreatment imaging. Of 312 patients with baseline bone disease, 81% demonstrated a response on posttreatment imaging. In total, 156 of 361 patients (43%) demonstrated progression during treatment. New osseous lesions developed in 132 patients, of whom 89 (67%) had PSMA low-avidity disease. At cycle 2, 64% of new lesions were osseous, increasing to at least 90% by cycles 4-6. PSMA-negative progression occurred in 22 patients (6%), predominantly in the liver (n = 11) and lymph nodes (n = 8), with 59% detected at cycle 2. Among 81 patients with imaging available at PSA progression after treatment completion or pause, 74 (91%) had imaging progression; of these, 69 (93%) demonstrated osseous and 13 (18%) nodal progression. PSA and imaging were discordant in 25%-43% of patients across cycles, with discordance increasing from cycle 2 to cycle 6. Conclusion: Progression during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT occurs most frequently in bone, with 67% of patients with new osseous lesions demonstrating a PSMA low-avidity disease component. PSMA-negative progression is uncommon and tends to emerge early. PSA-imaging discordance is frequent, underscoring the need for integrated imaging assessment throughout treatment.

items.authors: Esmaeilzadeh Asl S, Hoberück S, Sonnenfeld A, et al.

These results support a potential role for PSMA PET/CT in improving patient selection and detecting oligometastatic disease, enabling higher precision in treatment planning.

sections.text: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT has become the gold standard for staging and restaging prostate cancer, with superior diagnostic accuracy over conventional imaging and established prognostic value. However, there are limited data on whether PSMA PET/CT-improved staging accuracy is associated with improved long-term patient outcomes. This study analyzes the association between PSMA PET/CT at primary staging and overall survival (OS), biochemical recurrence (BCR), and cancer-specific survival (CSS) in a large university hospital cohort at a center where PSMA PET/CT has been clinically available for over 13 y. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included all 11,146 patients with prostate cancer diagnosed between 2013 and 2023. The final analysis cohort consisted of 6999 patients, of whom 505 (7.2%) underwent PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. We classified patients into 3 groups using D'Amico risk classification. Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier methods and adjusted Cox regression models. To control for selection bias, propensity score matching and overlap weighting were applied. Landmark analysis addressed selection and immortal time biases, and Fine-Gray models accounted for competing risk of death in a BCR analysis. Results: PSMA PET/CT was associated with a longer time to BCR (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.51; 95% CI, 0.38-0.68; P < 0.001), longer CSS (HR = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.61; P < 0.001), and longer OS (HR = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; P < 0.001). PSMA PET imaging was associated with particularly better outcomes in high-risk patients, especially those treated with radiotherapy. In the radiotherapy group, the HRs were 0.42 for OS, 0.42 for BCR, and 0.25 for CSS (all P < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant association was observed in patients undergoing radical prostatectomy. As the formal interaction test between PSMA PET/CT and treatment modality was not statistically significant, this differential finding should be considered exploratory. Across all 9 sensitivity analyses, HRs were consistently below 1, indicating a uniform direction of benefit. Conclusion: The association observed in this large real-world cohort supports the clinical value of PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. Findings were particularly favorable among high-risk patients undergoing radiotherapy, although this subgroup difference should be interpreted as exploratory given the nonsignificant interaction test. These results support a potential role for PSMA PET/CT in improving patient selection and detecting oligometastatic disease, enabling higher precision in treatment planning.

items.title: Role of [18F]F-Fluciclovine PET/CT in Patients with Biochemical Recurrence of Prostate Cancer and Negative PSMA PET Results: A Single-Center Study.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Szidonya L, Obrzut S, Lim JY, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Among patients with an available reference standard (n = 14), all positive findings were confirmed to be true-positive. Conclusion: [18F]F-fluciclovine PET detected recurrent disease in over half of patients with negative PSMA PET findings and frequently altered management, supporting its complementary role in selected patients with BCR.

sections.text: Our purpose was to evaluate whether [18F]F-fluciclovine PET/CT detects sites of disease in patients with biochemical recurrence (BCR) of prostate cancer and negative findings on prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET and to assess its impact on intended management. Methods: In this prospective single-arm study (NCT05722925), 50 patients with BCR (prostate-specific antigen [PSA] ≥ 0.2 ng/mL) and negative findings on PSMA PET underwent [18F]F-fluciclovine PET/CT within 30 d of the previous imaging. Detection rate, distribution of disease, PSA-stratified analysis, management impact, and correct localization rate were assessed using descriptive statistics and exact CI. Results: [18F]F-fluciclovine PET had positive findings in 28 of 50 patients (56%; 95% CI, 41%-70%). Disease was confined to the prostate bed in 14 patients (50%), whereas 14 (50%) demonstrated nodal or distant metastases. Detection rate increased with PSA, from 44% at a PSA of 0.2-0.5 ng/mL to 100% at a PSA of 5 ng/mL or higher. The intended management changed in 71% of patients after the [18F]F-fluciclovine PET: 87% of patients with positive findings and 54% with negative findings. Among patients with an available reference standard (n = 14), all positive findings were confirmed to be true-positive. Conclusion: [18F]F-fluciclovine PET detected recurrent disease in over half of patients with negative PSMA PET findings and frequently altered management, supporting its complementary role in selected patients with BCR.

items.title: Botulinum Toxin Plus Transdermal Scopolamine Reduces Salivary Gland Uptake in Patients Undergoing Tandem Radiopharmaceutical Therapy with [225Ac]Ac- and [177Lu]Lu-PSMA Radioligands.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Mueller J, Zhao T, Jakobsson V, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: BTX plus transdermal scopolamine is a promising strategy to reduce salivary gland uptake during PSMA RPT. This approach enhances patient quality of life after PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy, particularly with α-emitting radionuclides, while preserving its excellent therapeutic efficacy.

sections.text: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has shown remarkable efficacy in advanced metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. However, salivary gland toxicity is a major dose-limiting adverse effect, particularly with α-emitting radionuclides such as 225Ac. Although tandem therapy with combined [225Ac]Ac- and [177Lu]Lu-labeled PSMA-targeted RPT in a single low-activity cycle may address certain challenges, effective salivary gland protection remains crucial. In this study, we explored the use of botulinum toxin (BTX) type A (incobotulinumtoxinA) plus transdermal scopolamine as a protective strategy to mitigate salivary gland uptake of PSMA radioligands. Methods: IncobotulinumtoxinA was injected percutaneously, with increasing dosages of up to 300 units distributed into the parotid and submandibular glands under ultrasound guidance, a mean of 24 d before scheduled tandem PSMA RPT. Transdermal scopolamine was applied from 72 h before RPT until 2 h after RPT. Molecular imaging was conducted as per PSMA RPT protocol, with pretreatment PSMA PET/CT to confirm ligand uptake and follow-up PET/CT for restaging. SPECT/CT was conducted as imaging after RPT. PET SUVmean or SPECT counts were measured, and ratios of injected-to-noninjected contralateral glands were calculated and compared before and after BTX. Results: Fourteen patients (mean age, 68.0 ± 8.1 y) were included; 1 patient received 2 injections before his treatment, and another underwent 2 tandem RPT cycles, with BTX administered before each cycle. Mean cumulative administered activity was 5.05 ± 1.09 GBq for 177Lu and 6.87 ± 3.14 MBq for 225Ac. Combination therapy with incobotulinumtoxinA plus transdermal scopolamine was associated with lower PSMA radioligand uptake in BTX-treated salivary glands relative to untreated contralateral glands, with mean reductions of approximately 30% in parotid glands and 17% in submandibular glands compared with untreated glands. Up to 300 units of incobotulinumtoxinA distributed among the major salivary glands was safe. No patient discontinued tandem PSMA therapy because of xerostomia, and no grade 3 or 4 toxicities were observed during PSMA RPT. Conclusion: BTX plus transdermal scopolamine is a promising strategy to reduce salivary gland uptake during PSMA RPT. This approach enhances patient quality of life after PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy, particularly with α-emitting radionuclides, while preserving its excellent therapeutic efficacy.

items.title: Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen PET/CT Complements MRI for Focal Therapy Selection in Prostate Cancer: A Whole-Mount Histopathologic Study.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Sonni I, Mohammadigoldar Z, Furey G, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: Adding PSMA PET/CT to mpMRI significantly improves sensitivity for exclusionary features, reflecting complementary molecular and anatomic information. However, combined imaging still misses a substantial proportion of adverse pathology, so imaging alone should not determine eligibility.

sections.text: The incremental value of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT over multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) for selecting patients for prostate cancer focal therapy is undefined. Unlike lesion-detection studies, we evaluated whether PSMA PET/CT, mpMRI, and their combination correctly determine focal therapy eligibility when validated against whole-mount histopathology (WMHP). Methods: We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing radical prostatectomy (RP) at UCLA (2017-2024) with preoperative PSMA PET/CT and mpMRI, a biopsy grade group (GG) of 3 or less, unilateral disease, and a prostate-specific antigen level of less than 20 ng/mL. Two blinded readers per modality assessed extraprostatic extension (EPE), seminal vesicle invasion (SVI), bilateral disease, and multifocality; a third adjudicated discordances. Eligibility required the absence of all 4. On WMHP, ineligibility was EPE, SVI, multifocal or bilateral disease with a contralateral or secondary GG of at least 2 nodules, or any GG greater than 3 focus at RP. Modalities were compared by McNemar tests. Results: Of 112 patients, 77 (69%) were ineligible on WMHP, including 19 (17%) with a GG greater than 3 focus at RP. Sensitivity and specificity were 53% and 54% for PET and 70% and 49% for mpMRI. Combined imaging improved sensitivity to 83% (P < 0.001 vs. PET; P = 0.002 vs. MRI) but reduced specificity to 26%. Per 100 patients at this prevalence, this would correctly identify approximately 9 additional ineligible patients while falsely excluding approximately 7 true candidates. mpMRI was more sensitive than PET for EPE (77% vs. 32%, P < 0.001), whereas PET was more specific (90% vs. 58%, P < 0.001). Combined imaging improved detection of multifocal (44% vs. 23%, P = 0.001) and bilateral disease (45% vs. 23%, P = 0.002) versus MRI alone. Conclusion: Adding PSMA PET/CT to mpMRI significantly improves sensitivity for exclusionary features, reflecting complementary molecular and anatomic information. However, combined imaging still misses a substantial proportion of adverse pathology, so imaging alone should not determine eligibility.

items.title: Symptomatic Hyperkinetic Gallbladder: An Unrecognized Indication for Cholecystectomy.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Graham MM, Mohamed MK, Samuel I

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: The high percentage of patients with a GBEF exceeding 79% has not been appreciated, as most of the previous studies evaluated healthy subjects and did not examine outcomes. These results should shift how we think about GBEF studies and how the results are reported.

sections.text: For decades, low gallbladder ejection fraction (GBEF), measured with hepatobiliary scintigraphy after infusion of sincalide, has been used to diagnose symptomatic biliary hypokinesia and as a predictor of the necessity for cholecystectomy. Recently, gallbladder hypercontractility (GBEF > 79%) has been recognized as a cause of right upper quadrant pain, and cholecystectomy has often resulted in symptom relief. This retrospective study evaluated follow-up data collected after GBEF studies to determine the incidence of cholecystectomy or persistence of symptoms. Methods: We evaluated all GBEF biliary studies performed at our institution between January 1, 2012, and December 31, 2025. Study reports containing "ejection fraction" and "sincalide" were identified to establish the study population. All patients presented with right upper quadrant pain. They received 185 MBq (range, 111-259 MBq) of 99mTc-mebrofenin intravenously and were imaged in a 20° left anterior oblique position for 60 min. Once the gallbladder was clearly seen, the patients were given a 30-min intravenous infusion of sincalide (0.02 μg/kg), and imaging was continued for a total of 45 min. Patients were categorized as having probable gallbladder disease (cholecystectomy and resolution of symptoms or no cholecystectomy and persistent symptoms) or unlikely gallbladder disease (cholecystectomy and persistent symptoms or no cholecystectomy and resolved symptoms or other diagnosis). Results: In total, 1775 patients were included in the final analysis. Forty percent of patients had a GBEF of greater than 79%, and 27% had a GBEF of less than 39%. Of those who underwent cholecystectomy, 90% of those with a GBEF of less than 39% and 94% of those with a GBEF of greater than 79% experienced symptom relief. The incidence of probable biliary disease was 61% in patients with a low GBEF and 44% in patients with a high GBEF and was lowest in the group with a GBEF of 60%-69% (24% of patients). Conclusion: Our study found that hepatobiliary GBEF is not as accurate as we have assumed. Additional clinical criteria are needed to improve patient selection and positive outcomes. The high percentage of patients with a GBEF exceeding 79% has not been appreciated, as most of the previous studies evaluated healthy subjects and did not examine outcomes. These results should shift how we think about GBEF studies and how the results are reported.

sections.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic fibroinflammatory cholangiopathy characterized by multifocal biliary strictures, cholestasis, and an increased risk of hepatobiliary malignancy and liver failure. MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) are central to diagnosis, surveillance, and risk stratification. Recent consensus guidelines from the International PSC Study Group emphasize standardized reporting for PSC with MRI and MRCP. Beyond anatomic assessment, established and emerging quantitative and functional imaging biomarkers include liver stiffness measurements, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction, and relative hepatobiliary phase enhancement. Imaging-based scoring systems such as Assessment of Noncontrast MRI for Advanced Liver Imaging (ANALI) scores provide additional prognostic information and correlate with clinical outcomes and established risk models. Hepatocyte-specific contrast-enhanced MRI allows evaluation of biliary excretion and regional liver function, facilitating identification of functional strictures and parenchymal dysfunction. The authors review current MRI and MRCP reporting standards, prognostic scoring systems, and evolving functional MRI techniques, with an emphasis on practical implementation in clinical radiology practice.

items.journal_full: Radiographics : a review publication of the Radiological Society of North America, Inc
items.authors: Panda A, Farah A, Itani M, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, yet it is frequently asymptomatic. Meckel diverticulum poses unique diagnostic challenges due to its variable manifestation and infrequent visualization at imaging.

sections.text: Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, yet it is frequently asymptomatic. Meckel diverticulum poses unique diagnostic challenges due to its variable manifestation and infrequent visualization at imaging. The authors review the embryology and anatomy of Meckel diverticulum, its normal radiologic appearances, and its complications and their management. Complications of Meckel diverticulum occur in up to 4%-9% of patients. Symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is more common in children but can also be seen in adults. A giant Meckel diverticulum, presence of ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue, or adjacent adhesions and bands are associated with a higher likelihood of a symptomatic manifestation. The most common complications include small-bowel obstruction, gastrointestinal bleeding, and diverticulitis. Children more commonly present with gastrointestinal bleeding, while diverticulitis is more common in adults. Small-bowel obstruction can occur at any age and can be secondary to inversion of Meckel diverticulum, intussusception, volvulus, internal or external hernias, neoplasms, enteroliths, congenital bands, or postinflammatory changes. When a patient presents with acute abdomen or gastrointestinal bleeding, the choice of imaging modalities includes CT or US, with the latter preferred in the pediatric population. Technetium 99m-pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel scan) can be additionally performed to evaluate rectal bleeding in younger patients. MRI is reserved as a problem-solving tool. Meckel diverticulum should be differentiated from its common imaging mimics (eg, the appendix, ileal duplication cyst, and mesenteric small-bowel diverticulum). When Meckel diverticulum is not visualized at imaging, the radiologist still plays a key role by raising suspicion for an underlying Meckel diverticulum and identifying other critical imaging findings that can inform clinical management. An understanding of the common clinical manifestations associated with Meckel diverticulum and a systematic imaging approach can improve preoperative diagnosis and patient management.

items.title: CT-based deep learning integrating pancreatic imaging and body composition for severity prediction in acute pancreatitis.
items.authors: Zeng D, He M, Lin B, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: A CT-based DL model integrating pancreatic imaging, body composition, and clinical variables demonstrated good performance for AP severity prediction.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Early severity stratification in AP remains challenging because conventional clinical and imaging assessments may not fully capture pancreatic injury and systemic disease status. Findings A CT-based DL model integrating pancreatic imaging, body composition, and clinical variables demonstrated good performance for severity prediction in AP. Critical Relevance Statement This study evaluates the value of integrating pancreatic imaging and CT-derived body composition information and supports the use of routinely acquired CT data for early risk stratification, potentially facilitating more individualized monitoring and management of AP.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To develop and validate a deep learning (DL)-based CT model integrating pancreatic imaging and CT-derived body composition for severity prediction in acute pancreatitis (AP).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: In this retrospective dual-center study, patients with AP who underwent CT within 72 h of symptom onset were enrolled from January 2021 to September 2025 at Center 1 and January 2023 to September 2024 at Center 2. The primary dataset (n = 426) was randomly divided into a training set (n = 298) and an internal test set (n = 128), while 110 patients from Center 2 served as the external test set. A three-dimensional DL model was developed for pancreatic imaging, and two-dimensional DL models were constructed for L3-level visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and skeletal muscle (SM). Six predictive models were constructed: clinical, pancreas, VAT, SM, pancreas-clinical (PC), and combined. Performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis, DeLong testing, calibration, decision curve analysis, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The combined model achieved area under the curve (AUCs) of 0.897 (95% CI: 0.862-0.932), 0.909 (95% CI: 0.861-0.958), and 0.910 (95% CI: 0.856-0.964) in the training, internal test, and external test sets, respectively. The combined model outperformed the PC model in the training set (p = 0.002) and external test set (p = 0.020). NRI and IDI analyses confirmed the incremental predictive value of body composition features.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: A CT-based DL model integrating pancreatic imaging, body composition, and clinical variables demonstrated good performance for AP severity prediction.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Early severity stratification in AP remains challenging because conventional clinical and imaging assessments may not fully capture pancreatic injury and systemic disease status. Findings A CT-based DL model integrating pancreatic imaging, body composition, and clinical variables demonstrated good performance for severity prediction in AP. Critical Relevance Statement This study evaluates the value of integrating pancreatic imaging and CT-derived body composition information and supports the use of routinely acquired CT data for early risk stratification, potentially facilitating more individualized monitoring and management of AP.

items.title: FDG PET/MR for liver metastases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy and technical protocols with a proposed reporting framework.
items.authors: Asmundo L, Steffani S, Zanardo M, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: FDG PET/MR demonstrates high lesion-level diagnostic accuracy for the detection of hepatic metastases, with high summary sensitivity and specificity. However, substantial between-study variability in sensitivity, together with variability and frequent underreporting of technical parameters, highlights the need for standardized acquisition protocols and reporting frameworks to improve reproducibility, comparability, and clinical translation.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic performance of FDG PET/MR for detecting hepatic metastases from extrahepatic primary malignancies, together with acquisition protocols, reconstruction parameters, and technical heterogeneity.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: A systematic search was conducted through September 2026. Eligible studies evaluated FDG PET/MR for hepatic metastases and reported diagnostic performance data and/or technical protocol information. Summary estimates of sensitivity and specificity were obtained using a bivariate random-effects model. A structured qualitative assessment of PET and MR acquisition, reconstruction parameters, and image interpretation strategies was also performed.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Fifteen studies involving 861 patients met the inclusion criteria. Eight studies (53%) provided sufficient data for the diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis, whereas all contributed to the qualitative technical assessment. The meta-analysis demonstrated a summary sensitivity estimate of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89-0.97) and a summary specificity estimate of 0.99 (95% CI, 0.92-1.00) for detecting hepatic metastases. Sensitivity showed substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 0.83), whereas specificity showed low heterogeneity (I² = 0.21). Technical assessment revealed marked variability in PET acquisition, MR protocols, reconstruction parameters, and reporting, with frequent underreporting of voxel size, filtering, and motion correction. Hepatobiliary contrast agents were used in only a minority of studies, and dedicated PET motion correction was rarely implemented.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: FDG PET/MR demonstrates high lesion-level diagnostic accuracy for the detection of hepatic metastases, with high summary sensitivity and specificity. However, substantial between-study variability in sensitivity, together with variability and frequent underreporting of technical parameters, highlights the need for standardized acquisition protocols and reporting frameworks to improve reproducibility, comparability, and clinical translation.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion

sections.text: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States, and accurate pretreatment evaluation is essential for risk stratification, treatment planning, and detection of recurrent disease. This evidence-based review summarizes imaging recommendations for patients with established endometrial cancer undergoing pretreatment assessment, surveillance, or evaluation for suspected recurrence. MRI pelvis without and with intravenous contrast is usually appropriate for assessment of local tumor extension across histologic subtypes and grades. For aggressive histologic tumor types, or when metastatic disease is suspected, CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast and FDG-PET/CT are usually appropriate for evaluation of nodal and distant metastases. Routine imaging surveillance is usually not appropriate for asymptomatic patients with treated low- or intermediate-risk disease, whereas CT may be appropriate in selected asymptomatic high-risk patients. MRI pelvis, CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and FDG-PET/CT are usually appropriate for suspected recurrence. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision process support the systematic analysis of the medical literature from peer reviewed journals. Established methodology principles such as Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE are adapted to evaluate the evidence. The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method User Manual provides the methodology to determine the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where peer reviewed literature is lacking or equivocal, experts may be the primary evidentiary source available to formulate a recommendation.

sections.text: Biliary tract cancers, comprising gallbladder cancer and intrahepatic and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, are uncommon but aggressive malignancies that are often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Accurate staging is critical because patients with localized disease may be candidates for curative resection, whereas those with unresectable or metastatic disease are triaged to systemic and palliative therapy. This document reviews the evidence for imaging in five clinical scenarios: locoregional staging of gallbladder cancer, locoregional staging of cholangiocarcinoma, staging of distant metastatic disease, posttreatment evaluation, and surveillance. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen are the mainstays of locoregional assessment, whereas CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and FDG-PET are used for distant staging and follow-up.
