items.title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinical value of quantitative Na[18F]F PET/CT parameters to monitor therapeutic response in patients with benign metabolic bone diseases: A systematic review.
items.authors: van Schaik L, Huisman SA, Appelman-Dijkstra NM, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: Quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT provides high diagnostic accuracy for tracking regional turnover and treatment response in benign MBDs. However, clinical adoption is hindered by a lack of harmonized EARL-compliant protocols, unstandardized outcome metrics and a reliance on small, unadjusted cohorts.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT is increasingly used to evaluate treatment responses in metabolic bone diseases (MBDs), where conventional serum biomarkers and structural imaging fail to show local dynamic changes. The performance and utility of Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT in these diseases, however, has not been fully explored. We systematically evaluated the contemporary use of quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT for measuring MBD treatment responses.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Current review was prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261413536) and follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases were searched for clinical studies using quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT in MBDs. Risk of bias was assessed via QUADAS-2, ROBINS-I and QUIPS. Results were synthesized narratively.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Thirteen studies (n=14-72 patients; 358 total cases) met inclusion criteria, focusing on chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD, n=9 studies) and fibrous dysplasia/McCune-Albright syndrome (FD/MAS, n=4 studies). Two longitudinal studies evaluated therapeutic response: denosumab in FD/MAS yielded comparable reductions in total lesion metabolic activity across moderate (-64.9%) and high doses (-67.0%), while turnover-guided therapy in CKD-MBD significantly reduced bone kinetic flux (Ki). Remaining literature comprised cross-sectional and observational cohorts. Here, PET kinetic (Ki, FUR) and volumetric metrics (TV, TA, TLF) correlated strongly with bone formation rates and circulating biomarkers. Ki and background-adjusted uptake ratios (SUVR) discriminated bone turnover states with high accuracy (ROC AUC up to 0.98), outperforming serum parathyroid hormone in CKD-MBD. Reporting of reconstruction settings was highly variable; only one study explicitly noted EARL scanner accreditation and none documented compliance with EARL Standard 1 or 2. Risk of bias was primarily driven by small cohort sizes, attrition and unadjusted confounding.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: Quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT provides high diagnostic accuracy for tracking regional turnover and treatment response in benign MBDs. However, clinical adoption is hindered by a lack of harmonized EARL-compliant protocols, unstandardized outcome metrics and a reliance on small, unadjusted cohorts.

items.title: Companion animal nuclear medicine: A translational evidence map for dogs and cats.
items.authors: Becker S, Tually P, Currie GM

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Companion animals occupy an increasingly important clinical and societal space, with dogs and cats often managed as family members and receiving advanced diagnostic and therapeutic care. Many veterinary nuclear medicine procedures are adapted from human practice, while naturally occurring canine and feline diseases provide opportunities for comparative and translational insight.

sections.text: Companion animals occupy an increasingly important clinical and societal space, with dogs and cats often managed as family members and receiving advanced diagnostic and therapeutic care. Many veterinary nuclear medicine procedures are adapted from human practice, while naturally occurring canine and feline diseases provide opportunities for comparative and translational insight. This review mapped and synthesised the literature on nuclear medicine imaging and radionuclide therapy in dogs and cats, with emphasis on clinically mature applications and relevance to human nuclear medicine. A PRISMA-aligned systematic evidence map with focused narrative synthesis were undertaken. MEDLINE via PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection were searched, with supplementary Google Scholar searching, reference-list screening and citation mining. Because of heterogeneity in species, indication, radiopharmaceutical, protocol, comparator and outcome reporting, formal meta-analysis was not performed. A total of 228 articles were included. The literature was predominantly imaging-focused, with 176 articles addressing imaging alone, 34 therapy alone and 18 both imaging and therapy. Feline nuclear medicine was dominated by thyroid disease, particularly thyroid scintigraphy and radioiodine therapy for hyperthyroidism. Canine nuclear medicine was broader, including oncology PET/CT, osteosarcoma imaging and therapy, renal and hepatobiliary functional scintigraphy, portosystemic shunt imaging, neurology/behavioural imaging, thyroid carcinoma and radiosynoviorthesis. PET/CT was most prominent in canine oncology, while conventional scintigraphy remained important where functional information could not be replaced by structural imaging. Companion animal nuclear medicine is clinically useful and translationally relevant. Its most mature model is feline thyroid scintigraphy and radioiodine therapy, while its most dynamic future directions lie in canine oncology, molecular imaging and radiotheranostics. Closer collaboration between veterinary specialists and human nuclear medicine professionals may improve companion animal care while informing broader development of molecular imaging and targeted radionuclide therapy.

items.title: PSMA-directed radioligand therapy and radium-223 in prostate cancer bone metastases.
items.authors: Sathekge M

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Bone metastases are a major cause of pain, skeletal complications, marrow compromise and mortality in advanced prostate cancer. The therapeutic biology of skeletal disease is heterogeneous: malignant epithelial cells expressing prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) coexist with osteoblasts, osteoclasts, reactive mineralising bone and variable marrow infiltration.

sections.text: Bone metastases are a major cause of pain, skeletal complications, marrow compromise and mortality in advanced prostate cancer. The therapeutic biology of skeletal disease is heterogeneous: malignant epithelial cells expressing prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) coexist with osteoblasts, osteoclasts, reactive mineralising bone and variable marrow infiltration. Radium-223 dichloride is a bone-seeking alpha emitter with randomised evidence of overall-survival benefit in selected men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), whereas PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy delivers radiation to PSMA-expressing tumour deposits in bone and soft tissues. Their mechanistic complementarity has motivated sequential and concurrent strategies, but complementary localisation does not itself establish clinical synergy. This review critically integrates ALSYMPCA, ERA-223, PEACE-3, VISION, TheraP, PSMAfore, RALU and AlphaBet, together with radiobiology, molecular imaging, marrow and skeletal toxicity, dosimetry and evolving therapeutic sequencing. The final 133-patient retrospective RALU report describes the safety and outcomes observed after radium-223 followed by lutetium-177-PSMA in selected heavily pretreated patients; AlphaBet reports preliminary safety and antitumour activity with concurrent lutetium-177-PSMA-I&T and radium-223 in a single-arm early-phase study. Neither provides randomised evidence of an incremental survival benefit for dual-radionuclide treatment. Conversely, PEACE-3 establishes an overall-survival benefit for radium-223 combined with enzalutamide under contemporary bone-protective practice, whereas ERA-223 underscores the fracture hazards of inappropriate combinations. Future trials must integrate lesion-level imaging, whole-body disease phenotype, marrow reserve, patient-reported outcomes, competing systemic treatments and personalised radiation exposure. The most defensible clinical strategy is evidence-weighted selection of radionuclide therapy according to disease distribution and treatment history, with concurrent dual-radionuclide approaches restricted to appropriately governed trials.

items.title: Risk Stratification of Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS 3) Lesions in the Peripheral and Transition Zones Using Clinical and Quantitative MRI Markers.
items.journal_full: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
items.authors: Kaur T, Chahine R, Seiberlich N, et al.

conclusion.label: Data conclusion
conclusion.text: mADC combined with PSAD showed a significant increase in discrimination in the TZ, suggesting improved PI-RADS 3 stratification; independent validation is required before clinical implementation.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) 3 lesions often undergo biopsy despite a low positive predictive value (< 25%) for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa), defined as International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group ≥ 2.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To determine whether mean apparent diffusion coefficient (mADC), alone or with prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based metrics, improves zone-specific PI-RADS 3 classification for csPCa detection.

sections.label: Study type
sections.text: Retrospective, single-center.

sections.label: Population
sections.text: One hunderd and seventy-one males (71 ± 8 years) with 191 PI-RADS 3 lesions who underwent multiparametric MRI and targeted biopsy.

sections.label: Field strength/sequence
sections.text: 3 T, T2-weighted turbo spin-echo imaging, single-shot echo-planar diffusion-weighted imaging, and fat-suppressed dynamic contrast-enhanced T1-weighted gradient echo sequences.

sections.label: Assessment
sections.text: mADC, PSA, PSA density (PSAD), prostate volume, and body mass index were analyzed.

sections.label: Statistical tests
sections.text: Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses assessed associations with malignancy and diagnostic performance.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: mADC was significantly lower in cancers than non-cancers in 133 PZ lesions (885 ± 165 vs. 1068 ± 168 × 10-6 mm2/s) and 58 TZ lesions (670 ± 127 vs. 832 ± 179 × 10-6 mm2/s). In the PZ, mADC alone, and with PSAD showed no significantly different area under the curve (AUC, 0.79 vs. 0.80, p = 0.28). A combination of mADC and PSAD would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance. In the TZ, combining mADC with PSAD yielded significantly higher AUC than mADC alone (0.88 vs. 0.77, difference: 0.109 [95% CI: 0.010-0.208]). This combination would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance in 58 of 82 non-cancers (71%) while missing one csPCa in the PZ, and 27 of 35 noncancerous lesions while missing one csPCa in TZ.

sections.label: Data conclusion
sections.text: mADC combined with PSAD showed a significant increase in discrimination in the TZ, suggesting improved PI-RADS 3 stratification; independent validation is required before clinical implementation.

items.title: Prospective evaluation of an optimized low-dose CT enterography protocol for patients with Crohn's disease.
items.authors: Chen H, Tang B, Li J, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: On the GE Revolution 256-detector-row CT platform, the optimized CTE protocols reduced radiation exposure by approximately 50%, while Group C additionally achieved a protocol-defined 33.3% reduction in weight-normalized iodine dose. Based on the observed dose and image-quality findings, Group B can reasonably be recommended when radiation reduction is the primary goal, whereas Group C may be considered when both radiation and iodine reduction are desired. These findings do not establish equivalence or non-inferiority in image quality or diagnostic performance.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate an optimized CT enterography (CTE) strategy combining reduced radiation exposure and iodine administration in patients with Crohn's disease (CD), with subjective image quality as the primary endpoint.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This prospective single-center randomized study enrolled 102 patients with CD who underwent CTE between February and October 2025. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio using a computer-generated random sequence, with allocation concealed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes opened by a research nurse not involved in patient enrollment, image evaluation, or clinical data collection. No stratification or blocking was used. The three protocols were: a standard-dose protocol (Group A), a low-dose protocol using 100 kVp and 70% adaptive statistical iterative reconstruction-V (ASIR-V) (Group B), and a combined low-dose, low-contrast protocol using the same acquisition settings with a reduced iodine dose (320 mgI/kg, corresponding to 1.0 mL/kg of contrast medium) (Group C). The primary endpoint was subjective image quality assessed using a 5-point Likert scale. Secondary endpoints included objective image quality, bowel wall enhancement, and radiation dose metrics. Diagnostic performance for disease activity and luminal stenosis was evaluated as an exploratory analysis in patients with an eligible endoscopic reference standard; the study was not designed or powered for diagnostic non-inferiority or equivalence testing.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in baseline characteristics (all p > 0.05). For the primary endpoint, mean subjective image quality scores were 4.3 ± 0.5, 4.5 ± 0.6, and 4.5 ± 0.5 in Groups A, B, and C, respectively, with no significant between-group difference (p = 0.27); the between-group differences were 0.2 points (95% CI, -0.1 to 0.5) for Group B versus A, 0.2 points (95% CI, -0.1 to 0.5) for Group C versus A, and 0.0 points (95% CI, -0.3 to 0.3) for Group C versus B. Compared with the standard protocol, the estimated effective radiation dose was reduced by 53.2% in Group B and 50.0% in Group C (both p < 0.001), with no significant difference between the two optimized protocols. Both optimized protocols showed lower image noise and higher signal-to-noise and contrast-to-noise ratios than the standard protocol (all p < 0.05), whereas no statistically significant between-group differences were detected in bowel wall attenuation (all p > 0.05). For the exploratory diagnostic analysis, 76/102 patients had an eligible endoscopic reference standard (Group A, 25/31; Group B, 28/38; Group C, 23/33). Diagnostic accuracy for disease activity was 88.0% (95% CI, 70.0-95.8%) in Group A, 89.3% (95% CI, 72.8-96.3%) in Group B, and 87.0% (95% CI, 67.9-95.5%) in Group C; the corresponding between-group differences were 1.3 percentage points (95% CI, -16.8 to 19.4) for B versus A, -1.0 percentage points (95% CI, -19.4 to 17.4) for C versus A, and 2.3 percentage points (95% CI, -16.6 to 21.2) for B versus C. For luminal stenosis, diagnostic accuracy was 84.0% (95% CI, 65.3-94.1%), 89.3% (95% CI, 72.8-96.3%), and 87.0% (95% CI, 67.9-95.5%), respectively; the absolute differences were 5.3 percentage points (95% CI, -12.1 to 22.7) for B versus A, 3.0 percentage points (95% CI, -15.2 to 21.2) for C versus A, and 2.3 percentage points (95% CI, -16.6 to 21.2) for B versus C. The confidence intervals for between-group differences were wide and included values that could be clinically relevant; because the study was not powered to establish diagnostic non-inferiority or equivalence, the absence of statistically significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence of diagnostic equivalence or non-inferiority.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: On the GE Revolution 256-detector-row CT platform, the optimized CTE protocols reduced radiation exposure by approximately 50%, while Group C additionally achieved a protocol-defined 33.3% reduction in weight-normalized iodine dose. Based on the observed dose and image-quality findings, Group B can reasonably be recommended when radiation reduction is the primary goal, whereas Group C may be considered when both radiation and iodine reduction are desired. These findings do not establish equivalence or non-inferiority in image quality or diagnostic performance.

items.title: Anatomy-informed CT Spatial Phenotype Associated with Extrapancreatic Perineural Invasion in Resected Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
items.authors: Chen C, Yu J, Shen Y, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Higher PROPHET risk was associated with shorter survival (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.95; 95% CI: 1.53, 2.47; nominal P < .001). Conclusion PROPHET provides a CT-visible tumor-vessel spatial phenotype associated with pathologically confirmed EPNI.

sections.text: Purpose To develop and evaluate an interpretable CT spatial phenotype associated with extrapancreatic perineural invasion (EPNI) in resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Materials and Methods This multicenter study included training, internal testing, neoadjuvant testing, retrospective external testing, prospective external testing, and The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) sets. The Preoperative Risk of Perineural High-risk Extension in Tumors (PROPHET) model and threshold were locked before testing. Performance was assessed with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and threshold metrics. Six radiologists compared unaided and assisted readings. A stratified Cox model related PROPHET risk to survival, adjusting for age, sex, tumor size, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, nodal category, and differentiation. Results Among 1854 patients (median age, 63 years; 1131 male), AUCs were 0.92 (95% CI: 0.86, 0.96) in prospective external testing, 0.85 (95% CI: 0.75, 0.93) in retrospective external testing, 0.90 (95% CI: 0.83, 0.95) after neoadjuvant therapy, 0.99 (95% CI: 0.98, >0.99) in internal testing, and 0.80 (95% CI: 0.68, 0.93) in TCIA. TCIA sensitivity and specificity were 24 of 30 (80%) and two of 19 (11%). Assistance increased mean sensitivity to 93% from 82% and reduced reading time to 3.02 minutes from 3.64 minutes per patient (both Holm-adjusted P < .001). Higher PROPHET risk was associated with shorter survival (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.95; 95% CI: 1.53, 2.47; nominal P < .001). Conclusion PROPHET provides a CT-visible tumor-vessel spatial phenotype associated with pathologically confirmed EPNI.

items.title: 177 Lu-PSMA Therapy in Recurrent High-Grade Glioma : A Pilot Study With Dosimetric Insights.
items.authors: Karlberg AM, Vindstad BE, Berntsen EM, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: 177 Lu-PSMA therapy was feasible and well-tolerated. Radiologic stabilization was observed in a subset of patients, but strategies to increase tumor dose delivery may be needed to improve efficacy.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: Patients with recurrent high-grade glioma have poor prognosis and limited treatment options. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility and potential clinical benefit of 177 Lu-PSMA therapy in this patient population.

sections.label: Patients and methods
sections.text: Eligible patients were selected for treatment based on positive 68 Ga-PSMA-PET findings. 177 Lu-PSMA (7.4 GBq/200 mCi) was administered at 6-8-week intervals and continued as long as well-tolerated. The safety, tolerability, and efficacy of 177 Lu-PSMA were assessed in each treatment cycle using PET/MRI, SPECT/CT, blood tests, neurological tests, and patient-reported outcome measures.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Ten patients were enrolled (WHO grade 4 glioblastoma, n=6; WHO grade 4 astrocytoma, n=1; WHO grade 3 astrocytoma, n=3). 68 Ga-PSMA-PET before treatment demonstrated tumor uptake in 9 patients (median SUV max : 6.4, IQR: 4.2-9.0). Six patients received treatment (20 cycles total; range: 1-7 per patient). Median absorbed dose per cycle was 0.9 Gy (IQR: 0.8-1.1) for tumors, 2.6 Gy (IQR: 1.9-3.2) for kidneys, and 1.7 Gy (IQR: 1.5-2.2) for parotid glands. No CTCAE grade 3-4 toxicities occurred. The most common patient-reported symptoms were fatigue, transient xerostomia, and nausea. Median survival from treatment initiation was 187 days (range: 87-756) and the median progression-free survival was 45 days (range: 41-335). MRI (RANO 2.0) demonstrated stable disease in half of the patients during all or part of the treatment course.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: 177 Lu-PSMA therapy was feasible and well-tolerated. Radiologic stabilization was observed in a subset of patients, but strategies to increase tumor dose delivery may be needed to improve efficacy.

items.title: Measuring prostate cancer lesion size on serial MRI during active surveillance: A multi-centre observational study.
items.authors: Pakpoor J, Englman C, Adebusoye B, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Serial MRI assessment of PCa lesion size is subject to substantial variability, particularly for larger lesions and lesions with indistinct boundaries. The benefits of consistent readers and measurement methods warrant further confirmation in larger prospective studies to support reliable clinical decision-making during active surveillance.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To assess the intra- and inter-reader reliability of measurements of prostate cancer (PCa) lesions on serial multiparametric MRI scans, and to assess how lesion characteristics and measurement methods influence measurements over time in an international two-centre setting.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Twenty patients with low- or intermediate-risk PCa undergoing active surveillance were included. A total of three MRI scans were evaluated for each patient: one baseline and two serial follow-up scans. Five consultant radiologists from two institutions independently measured the size of the index lesion at each time point by four methods: maximum diameter, biaxial diameters, ellipsoid volume, and planimetry. Measurements were repeated after a four-week 'wash-out' period. Variability was assessed using strip plots and Bland-Altman analysis.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Graphical presentation of inter-reader and intra-reader reliability enabled examination of variability between methods, readers and reads. Variability increased with lesion size and was greatest for lesions with poorly defined margins. Smaller, well-delineated lesions demonstrated greater consistency over time and across readers. Estimates of percentage change showed greater variability than absolute measurements, particularly for volumetric methods. Small differences in the underlying absolute measurements are amplified when expressed relative to baseline values.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Serial MRI assessment of PCa lesion size is subject to substantial variability, particularly for larger lesions and lesions with indistinct boundaries. The benefits of consistent readers and measurement methods warrant further confirmation in larger prospective studies to support reliable clinical decision-making during active surveillance.

items.title: Imaging classification of pancreatic cystic lesions: a radiologist's guide.
items.authors: Boraschi P, Cervelli R, Donati F

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are increasingly encountered in clinical practice owing to the widespread use of high-resolution cross-sectional imaging. These lesions comprise a heterogeneous group of entities ranging from benign cysts to pre-malignant neoplasms and invasive cancers, making accurate characterization essential for appropriate patient surveillance and therapeutic management.

sections.text: Pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are increasingly encountered in clinical practice owing to the widespread use of high-resolution cross-sectional imaging. These lesions comprise a heterogeneous group of entities ranging from benign cysts to pre-malignant neoplasms and invasive cancers, making accurate characterization essential for appropriate patient surveillance and therapeutic management. Imaging plays a pivotal role in lesion detection, differential diagnosis, and assessment of malignant potential. This review presents a practical imaging-based classification of PCLs founded on lesion morphology, relationship to the pancreatic ductal system, enhancement patterns, and associated imaging features. Using a stepwise diagnostic approach, pancreatic cystic lesions are categorized according to their increasing risk of malignancy into non-neoplastic cysts, serous cystic neoplasms, mucinous cystic lesions, and cystic degeneration of solid pancreatic tumors. Characteristic imaging findings, relevant differential diagnostic considerations, and imaging features associated with increased malignant potential are comprehensively reviewed, with particular emphasis on the role of MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) in lesion characterization. A structured pattern-recognition flowchart is proposed to facilitate routine image interpretation and enhance diagnostic confidence. In addition, a practical reporting template is presented to promote standardized assessment and effective communication within multidisciplinary teams. Emerging techniques, including diffusion-weighted imaging, quantitative MRI biomarkers, radiomics, artificial intelligence, and molecular analysis of cyst fluid, are discussed as promising tools for improving diagnostic accuracy and refining risk stratification. By emphasizing readily recognizable imaging features and a systematic diagnostic workflow, this review provides radiologists with a practical and clinically applicable framework for the evaluation, diagnosis, risk assessment, and multidisciplinary management of pancreatic cystic lesions.

items.title: Preoperative risk stratification for anastomotic leakage after gastrectomy: a model based on dual‑energy CT extracellular volume fraction and sarcopenia.
items.authors: Ren T, You H, Liu X, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: A concise model integrating tumor location, DECT-derived ECV, and sarcopenia showed favorable performance for preoperative AL risk stratification after gastrectomy. This internally validated model may help preoperative AL risk stratification, but multicenter external validation and impact analysis are required before implementation.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To develop a purely preoperative risk stratification model for anastomotic leakage (AL) after radical gastrectomy using clinical, dual-energy CT (DECT), and body composition variables available before surgery.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective study included 439 patients with gastric cancer who underwent radical gastrectomy. Preoperative clinical, DECT, and body composition data were collected. A domain-based predictor selection strategy was used, followed by Firth penalized logistic regression to account for the low event rate. Internal validation was performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples, with an additional full-pipeline bootstrap sensitivity analysis. Model performance was assessed by discrimination, calibration, decision curve analysis (DCA), and risk stratification.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: AL occurred in 27 patients (6.15%). The final model included cardia tumor location (OR = 4.44), higher ECV (OR = 1.09 per 1%), and sarcopenia (OR = 3.66). The model showed good discrimination, with an apparent AUC of 0.853 and a bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.843. Full-pipeline bootstrap sensitivity analysis yielded an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.833. Calibration was acceptable, with a Brier score of 0.050, and DCA suggested potential net benefit. Observed AL rates increased stepwise across low-risk (< 3%), intermediate-risk (3%-10%), and high-risk (≥ 10%) groups: 1.23%, 5.13%, and 22.78%, respectively. The high-risk group comprised 18.0% of the cohort but accounted for 66.7% of all AL events.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: A concise model integrating tumor location, DECT-derived ECV, and sarcopenia showed favorable performance for preoperative AL risk stratification after gastrectomy. This internally validated model may help preoperative AL risk stratification, but multicenter external validation and impact analysis are required before implementation.

items.title: Contrast-enhanced CT-based multimodal modeling for overall survival prediction after resection of retroperitoneal liposarcoma: a bicentric retrospective study.
items.authors: Fan P, Zhang J, Luo W, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: RDCS estimates OS after complete RPLS resection using preoperative CT-derived imaging signatures and postoperative clinicopathologic information. RDCS may complement established postoperative prognostic tools, but its application in surveillance and clinical management requires prospective validation and clinical impact assessment.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: Postoperative risk estimation in retroperitoneal liposarcoma (RPLS) remains challenging because conventional clinicopathologic models capture only part of its biological heterogeneity. We aimed to develop and externally evaluate a postoperative prognostic model integrating preoperative CT features with postoperative clinicopathologic information to estimate overall survival (OS) after RPLS resection.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This bicentric retrospective study included 367 patients who underwent complete RPLS resection between 2009 and 2021. Institution 1 provided the training cohort (n = 128) and internal validation cohort (n = 55); Institution 2 provided the external test cohort (n = 184). A radiomics signature was constructed from three-dimensional tumor features. A deep-learning signature was derived from the largest axial tumor section using an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-101 trained with Cox partial-likelihood loss. Clinical variables underwent univariable and multivariable Cox regression analysis. The retained clinicopathologic variables and imaging signatures were integrated into a combined model termed RDCS.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: During follow-up, 71, 30, and 107 patients died in the training, internal validation, and external test cohorts, respectively. The corresponding RDCS C-indices were 0.775, 0.704, and 0.725, each higher than those of the individual radiomics, deep-learning, and clinical models. Calibration curves showed agreement between predicted and observed survival. Decision-curve analysis suggested potential clinical utility within the evaluated thresholds. In a separate exploratory comparison in the external primary-tumor subset (n = 82), C-indices were 0.746 for RDCS and 0.590 for the official Sarculator application.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: RDCS estimates OS after complete RPLS resection using preoperative CT-derived imaging signatures and postoperative clinicopathologic information. RDCS may complement established postoperative prognostic tools, but its application in surveillance and clinical management requires prospective validation and clinical impact assessment.

items.title: A pivotal Phase 2 study of derazantinib for previously-treated, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 aberrations: FIDES-01.
items.authors: Borad MJ, Droz Dit Busset M, Javle MM, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: In previously chemotherapy treated, FGFR-inhibitor-naïve patients with iCCA harboring FGFR2 fusions, mutations, or amplifications, derazantinib showed clinically meaningful efficacy with durable objective responses, and a manageable safety profile.

sections.label: Background aims
sections.text: To evaluate safety and efficacy of FGFR1-3 kinase inhibitor derazantinib, in advanced intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) harboring FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements (FGFR2F), mutations (FGFR2M), or amplifications (FGFR2A), previously treated with chemotherapy.

sections.label: Approach results
sections.text: Open-label, non-controlled Phase 2 trial. Patients with advanced iCCA, ≥1 prior chemotherapy, and FGFR2F (Substudy 1) or FGFR2M/FGFRA (Substudy 2), received once-daily oral derazantinib 300 mg until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, consent withdrawal or investigator decision to stop. Efficacy was assessed by central radiology review using RECIST v1.1. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR; Substudy 1) and 3-month progression-free survival (PFS3; Substudy 2). Other endpoints were PFS, ORR (Substudy 2), disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DOR), and overall survival (OS). In Substudy 1, ORR and DCR were 22.3% (23/103 partial responses) and 75.7%, respectively; median (95% CI) PFS was 8.1 (5.5,8.3) months, DOR was 6.5 (4.6,9.2) months, and OS was 17.2 (12.5,22.4) months. In Substudy 2, PFS3 was 63% (27/43), ORR was 9.3% (3 partial, 1 complete response), DCR was 69.8%, and OS was 11.9 (8.4,15.9) months. There were no Grade 4 or 5 drug-related events. FGFR inhibitor class-specific toxicities included drug-related hyperphosphataemia (38%, Grade 3: 3%) and dry eye (36%). Nail disorders (10%, any grade or causality), stomatitis (5%), retinal events (5%), and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (1%) were infrequent.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: In previously chemotherapy treated, FGFR-inhibitor-naïve patients with iCCA harboring FGFR2 fusions, mutations, or amplifications, derazantinib showed clinically meaningful efficacy with durable objective responses, and a manageable safety profile.

items.title: US Markers in the Noninvasive Assessment of Hepatic Steatosis in Metabolic Dysfunction-associated Steatotic Liver Disease.
items.authors: Sugimoto K, Moriyasu F, Dioguardi Burgio M, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Performance was similar across models in identifying steatosis grade S2 or greater (AUC, 0.89-0.90; all P ≥ .47) and for grade S3 (AUC, 0.89-0.90; all P ≥ .72), but an improvement in risk reclassification was observed for model 3 compared with model 1 (≥S2 steatosis: NRI, 0.58 [95% CI: 0.20, 0.94] [P = .002]; S3 steatosis: NRI, 0.71 [95% CI: 0.26, 1.14] [P = .002]). Conclusion Liver US-derived AC performed better than NLV and hepatorenal ratio in determining steatosis grade in participants with MASLD; when these markers were combined, reclassification of steatosis grade improved.

sections.text: Background Attenuation coefficient (AC) is an established US marker for assessing patients with liver steatosis. However, improvements in diagnostic performance are warranted. Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic performance of AC, normalized local variance (NLV), hepatorenal ratio, and their combinations for liver histopathologic steatosis in participants with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Materials and Methods This secondary analysis of the prospective Innovative Liver Elasticity, Attenuation, and Dispersion Ultrasound Study (iLEAD) (June 2019 to March 2023) included participants with biopsy-proven MASLD who underwent multiparametric liver US; AC, NLV, and hepatorenal ratio were measured. The diagnostic performance of each imaging marker and their combinations for determining steatosis grade were assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with the DeLong test, and reclassification improvement was also assessed using the category-free net reclassification improvement (NRI). Results A total of 102 participants (mean age, 52 years ± 16.1 [SD]; 51 male) were evaluated. AC showed the highest diagnostic performance for determining steatosis grade across all grades (AUC for grade ≥S1, 0.93 [95% CI: 0.87, 0.99]), compared with NLV (0.88 [95% CI: 0.77, 0.99]; P = .47) and hepatorenal ratio (0.85 [95% CI: 0.71, 0.98]; P = .30). Four models were constructed for identifying steatosis grades: model 1, AC only; model 2, AC plus NLV; model 3, AC plus hepatorenal ratio; model 4, AC plus NLV plus hepatorenal ratio. Models 2-4 showed no evidence of a difference in performance from model 1 for identifying grade S1 or higher (AUC, 0.93-0.98; P = .16, .15, and .07, respectively), but an improvement in risk reclassification was observed for model 4 (NRI, 1.18 [95% CI: 0.54, 1.77]; P < .001) compared with model 1 (reference). Performance was similar across models in identifying steatosis grade S2 or greater (AUC, 0.89-0.90; all P ≥ .47) and for grade S3 (AUC, 0.89-0.90; all P ≥ .72), but an improvement in risk reclassification was observed for model 3 compared with model 1 (≥S2 steatosis: NRI, 0.58 [95% CI: 0.20, 0.94] [P = .002]; S3 steatosis: NRI, 0.71 [95% CI: 0.26, 1.14] [P = .002]). Conclusion Liver US-derived AC performed better than NLV and hepatorenal ratio in determining steatosis grade in participants with MASLD; when these markers were combined, reclassification of steatosis grade improved.

items.title: Advances in the management of renal cell carcinoma.
items.authors: Lewis AR, Lyon TD, Gupta S, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer, with 435 000 patients newly diagnosed worldwide each year. In addition to morphology and histology, molecular subtyping has advanced the diagnostic classification of RCC.

sections.text: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer, with 435 000 patients newly diagnosed worldwide each year. In addition to morphology and histology, molecular subtyping has advanced the diagnostic classification of RCC. Contemporary diagnosis relies on cross sectional imaging in the form of computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging and selective biopsy. For localised disease, nephrectomy remains the standard of care, with partial nephrectomy being an option for smaller tumours. Ablation or stereotactic radiation is appropriate for selected patients. Adjuvant pembrolizumab provides improved disease-free and overall survival in high risk clear cell RCC. In metastatic disease, the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitor based combinations has extended overall survival, providing a durable response in some patients. Despite these advances, primary and secondary resistance, along with the lack of predictive and prognostic biomarkers, remain a challenge.

items.title: Sacituzumab tirumotecan versus treatment of physician's choice in previously treated endometrial cancer (TroFuse-005/ENGOT-en23/GOG-3095): a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial.
items.authors: Lorusso D, Martin-Babau J, Backes F, et al.

conclusion.label: Interpretation
conclusion.text: Sac-TMT significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival versus TPC in patients with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer previously treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy. These findings support sac-TMT as a new standard of care for patients with endometrial cancer who have received chemotherapy and immunotherapy and have few effective treatment options.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Therapeutic options for patients with endometrial cancer who progress after platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy are scarce, and prognosis is poor. Sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT) is a trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2-directed antibody-drug conjugate with a unique, bifunctional linker that maximises delivery of a belotecan-derived topoisomerase I inhibitor payload to tumour cells. This study aimed to compare sac-TMT with the treatment of physician's choice (TPC) in patients with endometrial cancer who had been previously treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: In this randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial, patients were recruited from 242 gynaecological oncology centres across 31 countries and regions. Participating centres were selected based on established expertise in gynaecological oncology and an adequate volume of potentially eligible patients. Eligible patients were female and aged 18 years or older with histologically confirmed advanced or recurrent endometrial carcinoma or carcinosarcoma, who had received up to three previous lines of therapy, including systemic platinum-based chemotherapy and anti-programmed death 1 or anti-programmed death ligand 1 therapy. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) via central interactive response technology to receive intravenous sac-TMT (4 mg/kg on days 1 and 15 of each 28-day cycle) or TPC (intravenous doxorubicin 60 mg/m2 every 3 weeks or intravenous paclitaxel 80 mg/m2 on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle). Investigators and patients were not masked to treatment; radiologists performing blinded independent central review were fully masked. Randomisation was stratified by mismatch repair status (deficient vs proficient), trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2 expression by immunohistochemistry (TROP2 EPR20043 Formulation Locked Assay [Roche Tissue Diagnostics, Tucson, AZ, USA]; low [0% to <50% of tumour cells with moderate (2+) or strong (3+) membrane staining intensity] vs medium-high [≥50% tumour cells with moderate (2+) or strong (3+) membrane staining intensity]), number of previous lines of systemic therapy (≤2 vs 3), and baseline disease status per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (version 1.1) by blinded independent central review (measurable vs non-measurable). Dual primary endpoints were progression-free survival per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (version 1.1) assessed by blinded independent central review and overall survival, analysed in the intention-to-treat population. The data cutoff date was March 23, 2026. Progression-free survival and overall survival were evaluated as dual primary endpoints using a graphical multiple-testing approach with prespecified alpha allocation. Progression-free survival was assessed every 8 weeks through to week 56, then every 12 weeks thereafter; overall survival was assessed continuously. The safety analysis included all randomly assigned patients who received at least one dose of study treatment. For progression-free survival, missing radiographic assessments were handled using prespecified censoring rules; no imputation was performed for missing overall survival or safety data. The trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06132958) and is ongoing.

sections.label: Findings
sections.text: Between Jan 5, 2024, and Sept 17, 2025, 776 patients were randomly assigned to sac-TMT (n=386) or TPC (n=390). 384 (99%) of 386 patients in the sac-TMT group and 367 (94%) of 390 in the TPC group received at least one dose of study treatment. At data cutoff, median follow-up was 14·0 months (IQR 11·0-16·9). Median progression-free survival was 7·2 months (95% CI 5·6-7·6) in the sac-TMT group and 3·9 months (3·7-5·3) in the TPC group (hazard ratio 0·59 [95% CI 0·50-0·70]; p<0·0001) and median overall survival was 19·0 months (16·1-not reached) in the sac-TMT group and 12·1 months (11·0-15·2) in the TPC group (0·68 [0·55-0·84]; p=0·0001). 265 (69%) of 384 patients in the sac-TMT group and 210 (57%) of 367 in the TPC group had a grade 3 or higher adverse event. Serious adverse events were reported in 133 (35%) patients in the sac-TMT group and 117 (32%) patients in the TPC group. Treatment-related adverse events led to death in three (<1%) patients in the sac-TMT group and three (<1%) in the TPC group.

sections.label: Interpretation
sections.text: Sac-TMT significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival versus TPC in patients with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer previously treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy. These findings support sac-TMT as a new standard of care for patients with endometrial cancer who have received chemotherapy and immunotherapy and have few effective treatment options.

items.title: Development and external validation of a CT-based clinicoradiological model for preoperative differentiation of pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma from ductal adenocarcinoma.
items.authors: Li Y, Kuang T, Zins M, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The CT-based clinicoradiological model showed good external discrimination but substantial miscalibration, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification rather than individual probability estimation. Further recalibration and prospective validation in unselected, prevalence-representative populations are required before clinical use.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To develop and externally validate a CT-based clinicoradiological model for preoperative differentiation of pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma (PASC) from pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This dual-center retrospective study included 397 patients with surgically confirmed PASC or PDAC and preoperative contrast-enhanced CT. In the development cohort, patients with PASC were matched 1:2 to patients with PDAC by age, sex, and tumor location. At the second center, consecutive eligible patients with PASC and PDAC identified during prespecified diagnosis-specific study periods constituted the external validation cohort. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression followed by multivariable logistic regression was used for model development.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: In the development cohort, the integrated model achieved an AUC of 0.919. In the external cohort, discrimination was preserved (AUC, 0.846; 95% CI, 0.781-0.910), but calibration was poor (slope, 0.445; 95% CI, 0.309-0.603). Calibration-in-the-large was 0.152 (95% CI, -0.358 to 0.656), with an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.03. The integrated model outperformed the clinical-only model (ΔAUC, 0.179; p < 0.001), whereas incremental discrimination beyond the imaging-only model was not demonstrated (ΔAUC, -0.004; p = 0.85). Decision curve analysis in the development cohort suggested potential net benefit across selected threshold probabilities.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The CT-based clinicoradiological model showed good external discrimination but substantial miscalibration, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification rather than individual probability estimation. Further recalibration and prospective validation in unselected, prevalence-representative populations are required before clinical use.

items.title: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms in adults: An update on the role of CT and MRI for risk stratification.
items.authors: Nguyen TTL, Barat M, Marchese U, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) are characterized histologically by an inner mucin-producing columnar epithelium supported by a dense ovarian-type stroma. MCNs account for approximately 10% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms.

sections.text: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) are characterized histologically by an inner mucin-producing columnar epithelium supported by a dense ovarian-type stroma. MCNs account for approximately 10% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice, as MCNs may harbor high-grade dysplasia or progress to invasive carcinoma. Establishing reliable imaging criteria for risk stratification is critical to identify patients who are candidates for surgery. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging play pivotal roles in lesion characterization and assessment of features associated with high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Current guidelines recognize several imaging features as high-risk characteristics for MCNs, including large tumor size, mural nodules, and main pancreatic duct dilatation. However, other potential predictors of malignancy remain poorly defined and are not sufficiently emphasized. The strongest MCN-specific evidence, as demonstrated in multivariable analyses, supports larger cyst size, mural nodules, main pancreatic duct dilatation, and, in selected cohorts, elevated serum cancer antigen 19-9. Male sex has also been associated with malignancy in retrospective surgical cohorts, whereas pancreatic head/neck location, calcification, wall/septal thickening, age, and signal heterogeneity on T2-weighted images remain less consistently validated. Importantly, most malignancy-prediction literature is based on resected, pathologically confirmed MCNs and is therefore vulnerable to selection and verification bias and cannot be directly extrapolated to all incidentally detected presumed MCNs. This article presents a transparent literature search methodology and an evidence-based synthesis of predictors of malignancy that clearly distinguishes MCN-specific multivariable evidence from lower-level or extrapolated data. It also provides a comparison of key guidelines. Unlike previous reviews, this article directly addresses the evidence gap between resection-based cohorts and the broader population of incidentally detected presumed MCNs. It also clarifies when imaging findings should prompt further evaluation rather than independently determine management.

items.title: Normal variants, pitfalls, and interpretation challenges of somatostatin receptor PET.
items.authors: Imperiale A, Mouissi I, Huon M, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Somatostatin receptor (SSTR) PET has become a central imaging tool in neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), with established roles in detection, staging, restaging, and selection of patients for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). Despite its high sensitivity and target specificity, interpretation is not always straightforward.

sections.text: Somatostatin receptor (SSTR) PET has become a central imaging tool in neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), with established roles in detection, staging, restaging, and selection of patients for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). Despite its high sensitivity and target specificity, interpretation is not always straightforward. Physiological SSTR expression, focal variants of normal biodistribution, technical and administration-related artifacts, inflammatory conditions, and benign or malignant non-neuroendocrine lesions may all generate uptake that mimics NET involvement. Conversely, small lesion size, partial-volume effects, high physiological background, and genuinely low or absent receptor expression may reduce lesion conspicuity and lead to false-negative or underestimated disease. Interpretive challenges have also become more relevant as SSTR PET is increasingly used for quantitative, longitudinal, and theranostic assessment. Somatostatin analogue treatment can modify normal-organ biodistribution and lesion-to-background contrast, while liver and spleen uptake may vary substantially across serial examinations and should not necessarily be considered stable reference tissues. In addition, inter-lesional differences in receptor expression may have practical implications when SSTR PET is used to assess suitability for PRRT, because intense uptake in part of the disease does not necessarily imply adequate target expression across all clinically relevant lesions. This review summarizes the principal physiological variants and false-positive and false-negative findings encountered on SSTR PET and discusses contemporary pitfalls related to biodistribution, receptor heterogeneity, quantitative interpretation, and theranostic decision-making. Accurate interpretation requires integration of molecular, anatomical, and clinical information rather than reliance on isolated uptake intensity or a binary positive/negative classification.

items.title: Preoperative MRI-based clinicoradiological scoring system for perineural invasion prediction and risk stratification in intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma: A multicenter study.
items.authors: Hu SA, Yan YH, Shu JJ, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: This MRI-based scoring system offers a noninvasive tool to preoperatively identify high-risk PNI patients, potentially guiding extended resection, neoadjuvant therapy, and intensified surveillance.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a strong predictor of early recurrence and poor survival in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC). However, PNI can only be confirmed by postoperative histopathology, and preoperative risk stratification tools remain lacking.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: A total of 190 intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma patients from three centers were retrospectively allocated into training, internal, and external validation cohorts. Continuous variables were dichotomized via the Youden index. Independent predictors from multivariate logistic regression were assigned integer scores, calculated by dividing each β coefficient by the minimum β, to construct a simplified scoring system. Performance was validated using AUC, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Using the optimal Youden cutoff , patients were risk-stratified to evaluate recurrence-free survival via Kaplan-Meier and Cox analyses.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Elevated platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (>144.43), perihilar location, and disrupted arterial enhanced edge integrity were identified as independent PNI predictors. Each was assigned 1 point to construct a 3-point scoring system. The system demonstrated favorable discrimination with AUCs of 0.870, 0.859, and 0.807 in the training, internal, and external validation cohorts, respectively. Calibration and DCA confirmed excellent agreement and clinical utility. High-risk patients (score ≥ 2) exhibited significantly shorter RFS across the training (hazard ratio [HR] = 4.150, 95 % CI: 2.343-7.350; P < 0.001), internal validation (HR = 3.801, 95 % CI: 1.589-9.093; P = 0.001), and external validation (HR = 3.311, 95 % CI: 1.397-7.848; P = 0.004) cohorts.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: This MRI-based scoring system offers a noninvasive tool to preoperatively identify high-risk PNI patients, potentially guiding extended resection, neoadjuvant therapy, and intensified surveillance.

items.title: Deep learning classification of benign and malignant adnexal lesions on pelvic MRI.
items.authors: Mokry T, Bischoff A, Netzer N, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: Despite the recent introduction of O-RADS MRI to standardize MRI assessment of adnexal lesions, diagnostic imaging remains challenging. Artificial intelligence might provide help in radiological decision support. Therefore, we trained deep convolutional neural networks (CNN) for detection and classification of benign and malignant adnexal lesions.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Two radiologists (R1/R2) retrospectively assigned MR-O-RADS scores on multiparametric MRI performed in 144 patients (median age 50.2 ± 14.3 years) prospectively included between 11/2016-12/2024 after diagnosis of indeterminate adnexal lesions on transvaginal ultrasound. R1 manually three-dimensionally segmented ovaries/adnexal lesions. Histopathology or 2-year-follow-up served as gold standard. Transverse T2WI, T1WI, T1WI fat-saturated, T1WI post-contrast, DWI and ADC maps were used for further analysis. nnU-Net was trained in 5-fold-cross-validation using three designs: D1) T2WI only at full resolution, D2) all 6 sequences at full resolution, D3) T2WI only downsampled by half in-plane. Prediction performance and specificity of malignant vs. benign entities was evaluated using ROC-AUC methods and the McNemar test for clustered data.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The dataset included annotations of 237 ovaries (130 benign and 67 malignant histopathologies, 40 lesions with negative 2-year-follow-up). R1/R2/D1/D2/D3 models achieved ROC-AUCs of 0.96/0.96/0.86/0.86/0.84 (95%CI 0.93-1.00/0.93-1.00/0.81-0.92/0.78-0.93/0.77-0.91), respectively. Cluster-adjusted AUC of R1/2 was significantly higher than D1-D3 models (all p < 0.001). Youden index specificity/sensitivity was 0.95/0.91,0.94/0.93,0.88/0.73,0.90/0.76,0.87/0.76, while it was 0.95/0.91,0.48/0.91,0.39/0.91,0.42/0.91 at the closest operating point to sensitivity ≥ 90%, with specificity of R1/2 being significantly higher than D1-3 models (all p < 0.001). Subanalysis in cases with full agreement between all CNN models demonstrated similar relationships. Subset analysis in frequent histopathologies showed AUCs of 1.0/0.99 (95%CI 1.00-1.00/0.98-1.00) for radiologists and 0.98 (95%CI 0.96-1.00) for model D2.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: Deep learning models achieved overall validation set performance at AUC ≥ 0.84, lower than the radiologists, however in frequent histopathologies D2 achieved AUC = 0.98, not statistically different from R1/2, suggesting that training with more examples especially of infrequent histopathologies may further increase performance.

items.title: Incorporating visceral adipose tissue into dual-region deep learning radiomics on CT improves preoperative lymph node metastasis prediction in gastric cancer: A multicenter study.
items.authors: Miao S, Xiong Z, Yang H, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The DR-DLR model improved LNM prediction, with its high-risk phenotype linked to immune-related molecular alterations, supporting its value for preoperative risk stratification.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) is associated with tumor progression in gastric cancer (GC), but its added value for predicting lymph node metastasis (LNM) remains unclear.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: This study aimed to construct a DR-DLR model that incorporates CT-based features from both VAT and tumor, with the goal of predicting LNM in GC patients, while investigating its biological relevance.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: 855 GC patients were retrospectively collected across three clinical centers, divided into a primary cohort, one internal test cohort, and two independent external validation cohorts. An Attention Residual Transformation Network (ARTNet) extracted imaging representations from CT images. Feature representations and clinical variables were integrated using a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to build the DR-DLR model. Model performance, generalizability, prognostic value, and biological relevance were evaluated using internal/external testing, radiologist comparison, survival analysis, and radiogenomics analysis.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Incorporation of VAT-derived features improved predictive performance compared with tumor-only models. The DR-DLR model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.898 (95 % CI: 0.817-0.946), 0.834 (95 % CI: 0.743-0.897), and 0.848 (95 % CI: 0.775-0.901) in the internal and two external test cohorts, respectively. It outperformed junior and senior radiologists in LNM assessment. Overall survival was shorter in high-risk patients than in low-risk. Radiogenomics analysis revealed that the high-risk phenotype was associated with activation of immune-related pathways and increased infiltration of CD4 + T cells, plasma cells, dendritic cells, and mast cells.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The DR-DLR model improved LNM prediction, with its high-risk phenotype linked to immune-related molecular alterations, supporting its value for preoperative risk stratification.

items.title: ENZARAD (ANZUP 1303): Phase III Trial of Enzalutamide With Androgen Deprivation Therapy and Radiation Therapy in High-Risk Localized or Locally Advanced Prostate Cancer.
items.journal_full: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
items.authors: Williams S, Sweeney CJ, Thomas H, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The use of enzalutamide rather than NSAA in addition to radiotherapy and ADT for 2 years showed no significant MFS-CI or overall survival improvement at 8 years.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: The effects of adding enzalutamide to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and radiotherapy for high-risk localized or locally advanced prostate cancer were unknown.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This is an open-label, phase III trial of definitive prostate radiotherapy with 24 months of ADT and 1:1 random assignment to either enzalutamide (160 mg once daily for 24 months) or an older nonsteroidal antiandrogen (NSAA) for 6 months. The primary end point was metastasis-free survival on conventional imaging (MFS-CI) with computed tomography and/or 99mTc-bone scintigraphy. Radiation to pelvic lymph nodes was required for cN1 disease but optional for cN0.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 802 participants were randomly assigned. After a median follow-up of 92 months, 207 MFS-CI events were reported (98 enzalutamide, 109 NSAA) with 8-year MFS-CI rates of 74% versus 72% (hazard ratio [HR], 0.88 [95% CI, 0.67 to 1.15]; P = .34). Prespecified subgroup analyses noted that enzalutamide was associated with a possible MFS-CI benefit in the subgroup undergoing planned pelvic nodal radiotherapy, n = 324 (HR, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.29 to 0.76]; Padjusted = .004). Grade 3 to 5 adverse events were reported in 185 participants in each arm.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The use of enzalutamide rather than NSAA in addition to radiotherapy and ADT for 2 years showed no significant MFS-CI or overall survival improvement at 8 years.

items.title: TheraPb Phase 1b: First-in-Human Dose-Escalation and Optimization Study of 212Pb-ADVC001 in PSMA-Positive Metastatic Androgen Pathway Modulation-Resistant Prostate Cancer.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Hansen AR, Pattison DA, Goh JC, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: 212Pb-ADVC001 was well tolerated up to 200 MBq, including at weekly dosing, and showed encouraging anti-tumor activity in pretreated mAPM-R. Two RP2D, 160 and 200 MBq, are under evaluation in phase 2.

sections.text: [212Pb]Pb-ADVC001 (212Pb-ADVC001) is a prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy with high linear energy transfer derived predominantly from the alpha-emission of its 212Pb payload which, upon decay, delivers potent ionizing radiation directly to the tumor. TheraPb (NCT05720130) is a first-in-human dose-escalation and optimization study evaluating 212Pb-ADVC001 in metastatic androgen pathway modulation-resistant prostate cancer (mAPM-R, formerly metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer). Phase 1 results, including available long-term safety and efficacy outcomes, are presented. Methods: Participants with progressive mAPM-R previously treated with ≥1 androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor and ≥1 taxane chemotherapy (unless contraindicated/declined) were enrolled. Escalating doses of 60-200 MBq 212Pb-ADVC001 were administered at prespecified intervals every 6, 4, 2, or 1 week(s) for up to 6 doses across 7 dose-schedule cohorts (interval 3 + 3 design). The primary objective was to determine the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) with primary endpoints of dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) and adverse events (AEs). Secondary endpoints included prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response, overall response rate (ORR), and radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS). Results: Twenty-two participants were enrolled, with a median follow-up of 14.1 months (IQR 8.8-17.1). No DLTs were observed and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. The most common treatment-related AEs (TRAE) were dry mouth (18/22 participants [82%], all grade 1-2) and nausea (14/22 participants [64%], all grade 1-2); there were no grade 4-5 or serious TRAEs. The selected RP2D are 160 and 200 MBq. At these dose levels, 12/15 (80%) participants had a PSA decline of ≥50% and the median rPFS from C1D1 was 11.2 months (95% CI 2.0-not estimable) as of data cutoff. ORR was 100%, with centrally confirmed objective responses in all 5 Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST)-evaluable participants treated at the RP2D. Conclusion: 212Pb-ADVC001 was well tolerated up to 200 MBq, including at weekly dosing, and showed encouraging anti-tumor activity in pretreated mAPM-R. Two RP2D, 160 and 200 MBq, are under evaluation in phase 2.

items.title: CT features of extra-pancreatic nerve plexus invasion predict mortality in early-stage pancreatic cancer.
items.authors: Truong K, Herrington T, Pavlovic A, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Preoperative CT detection of EPNI, especially PPC2 pathway involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology, identifies high-risk PDAC patients.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Extra pancreatic nerve plexus invasion in pancreatic adenocarcinoma is associated with aggressive disease, but the prognostic significance of specific pathways or morphologies remains unknown. Findings Plexus pancreaticus capitalis 2 involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology in EPNI of pancreatic adenocarcinoma are associated with decreased overall survival. Clinical relevance Identifying high-risk EPNI features on CT may facilitate early prognostic stratification and inform surgical and neoadjuvant treatment planning in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: The presence of extra-pancreatic nerve plexus invasion (EPNI) in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is known to correlate with aggressive disease, however, it is unknown whether specific pathways or morphologies carry different prognostic implications. This study evaluates whether distinct CT-defined patterns of EPNI predict mortality in PDAC.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective, single-center study included 89 patients with pathologically confirmed PDAC who underwent preoperative pancreatic protocol multidetector CT (MDCT) followed by surgical resection. Patients were identified from an institutional database and required available preoperative CT and histopathology. Two blinded, experienced radiologists reviewed MDCT images to assess EPNI, which was categorized by anatomic pathway and morphologic pattern. Overall survival was compared between EPNI-positive and EPNI-negative groups and among EPNI subtypes using log-rank testing, with stratification by tumor stage. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, and surgical margin were performed.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 89 patients (M/F: 54/35), median age: 66 years (IQR, 60-70 years), were evaluated. CT evidence of EPNI was present in 65 patients (73%) and was associated with decreased overall survival (p < 0.001). This association remained significant in Stage I tumors (p < 0.001). PPC2 pathway involvement (p < 0.001) and mass-with-stranding morphology (p < 0.001) were each associated with reduced overall survival. PPC2 (p = 0.003) and mass-with-stranding (p < 0.001) remained significant in stage I tumors.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Preoperative CT detection of EPNI, especially PPC2 pathway involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology, identifies high-risk PDAC patients.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Extra pancreatic nerve plexus invasion in pancreatic adenocarcinoma is associated with aggressive disease, but the prognostic significance of specific pathways or morphologies remains unknown. Findings Plexus pancreaticus capitalis 2 involvement and mass-with-stranding morphology in EPNI of pancreatic adenocarcinoma are associated with decreased overall survival. Clinical relevance Identifying high-risk EPNI features on CT may facilitate early prognostic stratification and inform surgical and neoadjuvant treatment planning in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

items.title: Remibrutinib versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis (REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2): two randomised, phase 3 trials.
items.authors: Wiendl H, Bermel R, Airas L, et al.

conclusion.label: Interpretation
conclusion.text: Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Remibrutinib is a highly selective, potent, covalent, CNS-penetrant, oral BTK inhibitor. We assessed the efficacy and safety of remibrutinib in adult patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2 are two identical, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active comparator-controlled, parallel-group, event-driven, phase 3 trials conducted at 407 centres in 46 countries. Patients aged 18-55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis, an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 0-5·5, and evidence of recent disease activity were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily via interactive response technology. Randomisation was stratified by geographical region, MRI cohort participation, and multiple sclerosis subtype. Patients, site investigators, and trial team were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint was annualised relapse rate (ARR), defined as the number of confirmed multiple sclerosis relapses per patient-year with up to 30 months of follow-up, and assessed in all randomly assigned patients. These trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05147220 and NCT05156281) and are ongoing, not recruiting.

sections.label: Findings
sections.text: Between Dec 13, 2021, and Dec 30, 2025, 2632 patients were screened and 2007 patients were randomly assigned. REMODEL-1 included 1000 patients (remibrutinib 502, teriflunomide 498; mean age 38·2 years, 666 [66·6%] female, 334 [33·4%] male) and REMODEL-2 included 1007 patients (remibrutinib 504, teriflunomide 503; mean age 39·0 years, 675 [67·0%] female, 332 [33·0%] male). ARR was significantly lower with remibrutinib than with teriflunomide: 0·073 versus 0·112 (rate ratio [RR] 0·648 [95% CI 0·453-0·927]; p=0·018) in REMODEL-1 and 0·080 versus 0·116 (RR 0·688 [0·487-0·972]; p=0·034) in REMODEL-2. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (132 [13·1%] of 1006 with remibrutinib vs 137 [13·7%] of 1001 with teriflunomide), nasopharyngitis (92 [9·1%] vs 123 [12·3%]), diarrhoea (84 [8·3%] vs 109 [10·9%]), and alopecia (58 [5·8%] vs 135 [13·5%]). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were less frequent with remibrutinib (31 [3·1%]) versus teriflunomide (58 [5·8%]). The safety profile of remibrutinib was consistent with that in other indications, including no liver safety concerns.

sections.label: Interpretation
sections.text: Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis.
