items.authors: Ren Y, Cui C, Zhang Z, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The diagnostic efficacy of the modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI scoring system was comparable to that of the standard O-RADS MRI risk stratification system, facilitating the distinction between benign and malignant adnexal neoplasms.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question How can a modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI scoring system be developed, and can this scoring system accurately classify adnexal masses? Findings The modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI system demonstrates excellent diagnostic performance and reliable risk stratification of adnexal masses by evaluating key imaging features. Critical relevance statement The modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI scoring system contributes to the risk stratification of adnexal masses, particularly for patients who cannot undergo contrast agent administration. This system provides a reliable tool to optimize treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: To develop a modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI scoring system and validate its diagnostic performance.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: The modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI scoring system was developed by incorporating the significant signs from the standard O-RADS MRI system. This study retrospectively enrolled the 176 adnexal masses in cohort A. MRI imaging features were compared between benign and malignant tumors within this cohort. The diagnostic performance of the two scoring models was assessed by estimating the area under the curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). In addition, 352 adnexal lesions from cohorts B and C were included to further evaluate the diagnostic ability of the modified scoring system.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: In cohort A, the papillary projections exhibiting the sea anemone sign were highly indicative of borderline lesions (p = 0.001). Diffusion restriction in solid components significantly distinguished benign from malignant masses (p = 0.001). The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value of cystic components yielded a cutoff of 1.74 (p < 0.05). The DeLong test revealed no statistically significant difference in AUCs between the two systems in cohort A (p > 0.05). The NRI and IDI for the modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI scoring system were -4.13% and -0.04, respectively (all p > 0.05). In cohorts B and C, the AUCs were 0.933 and 0.910.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The diagnostic efficacy of the modified non-contrast O-RADS MRI scoring system was comparable to that of the standard O-RADS MRI risk stratification system, facilitating the distinction between benign and malignant adnexal neoplasms.

sections.text: Purpose To compare the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of three MRI protocols for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) according to prebiopsy risk. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 390 male patients who underwent prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) between January 2019 and April 2024 for suspected csPCa, followed by biopsy. Patients were stratified by Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator score into low-risk (<4%), intermediate-risk (4%-9%), and high-risk (≥10%) groups. Three datasets were generated from each examination: mpMRI (T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI], and dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging), unenhanced MRI (multiplanar T2-weighted imaging and DWI), and short MRI (axial T2-weighted imaging and DWI). Overall, 1170 datasets were randomly assigned to 10 expert radiologists (117 examinations each). Diagnostic performance for grade group 2 or greater cancer and clinical utility metrics were compared across risk groups. Results Among the 390 patients (median age, 66 years [IQR, 61-71 years]), csPCa prevalence was 34.4% (134 of 390). In low-risk patients, short MRI demonstrated the highest sensitivity (95% [21 of 22]), with no significant differences among protocols (all P ≥ .21) and greatest potential for safe biopsy avoidance (84 biopsies avoided per missed csPCa). In intermediate-risk patients, mpMRI showed higher sensitivity (83% vs 72% for unenhanced MRI and 62% for short MRI; P = .012 for mpMRI vs short MRI) and higher biopsy efficiency (1.11 vs 0.85 for mpMRI vs unenhanced MRI). In high-risk patients, protocol-related differences were minimal (all P ≥ .12). Conclusion mpMRI was associated with improved sensitivity and biopsy efficiency in intermediate-risk patients, whereas protocol differences were limited in low- and high-risk groups; these findings support risk-adapted selection of MRI protocols.

items.authors: Jokar N, Pashazadeh A, Juweid ME, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion

sections.text: Targeted alpha therapy (TAT) has moved from a largely experimental approach into clinically relevant radiopharmaceutical therapy, although evidence varies across radionuclides and products. Alpha particles combine high linear energy transfer with a tissue range of only a few cell diameters. This permits dense, localized energy deposition but creates challenges in dosimetry, radiopharmaceutical production, quality control, contamination control, patient management, waste disposal, and regulation. This review examines evidence for safe clinical implementation and distinguishes established practice from emerging concepts and institution-specific choices. Radium-223 has the strongest clinical and regulatory foundation; actinium-225, lead-212, thorium-227, astatine-211, and bismuth-213 agents are at different stages of development. Particular attention is given to alpha recoil and daughter-radionuclide redistribution, Medical Internal Radiation Dose (MIRD)-based and small-scale dosimetry, route-dependent radionuclidic impurities, good manufacturing practice, prevention of internal contamination, renal and salivary-gland toxicity, marrow risk, and jurisdiction-specific regulatory requirements. Technologies already entering specialist workflows, including quantitative imaging, Monte Carlo transport, and voxel dosimetry, are distinguished from proof-of-concept automation and more aspirational artificial-intelligence applications. Evidence supports carefully governed TAT in selected indications and trials, but routine use remains limited by radionuclide supply, product-specific dosimetry, organ toxicity, manufacturing standardization, long-term safety data, and regulatory heterogeneity.

items.authors: Kassar M, Hu J, Rauscher I, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Conclusion: By adopting a physician-inspired assessment workflow, the VQA framework shows advantages in integrating imaging and laboratory data for clinical decision support compared with conventional machine learning. The preliminary results indicate that VQA-based approaches warrant future evaluation for survival prognostication in patients with mCRPC who are receiving PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

sections.text: Large language models show great promise for clinical decision support but generally lack medical imaging integration. Therefore, vision-language models have been proposed, but there is little evidence on their performance, particularly compared with conventional machine learning. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is a well-established treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but it is still not known which patients will be good long-term responders. Therefore, this study proposes a physician-inspired visual question answering (VQA) framework that emulates the structured integration of PSMA-directed imaging and clinical data used in routine clinical assessment for overall survival prognostication. Methods: As a proof of concept, we conducted a retrospective, multicenter study across 2 academic institutions that included 110 patients with mCRPC who were treated with either [177Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T or [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. Our VQA approach incorporates a 3-dimensional image encoder, the domain-specific language model RadBERT, and a cross-modal transformer to process baseline and interim (after 2 cycles) PET and SPECT images, clinical data, and clinical query. The model was trained to predict 24-mo survival, and performance was compared with state-of-the-art approaches. External validation was performed with the [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 cohort. Results: The VQA model outperformed all state-of-the-art approaches while showing accuracy comparable to the query-free attention multimodal fusion model. Specifically, it achieved 81.8% accuracy (95% CI, 0.52-0.95) when integrating SPECT or PET images with prostate-specific antigen measurements. External validation of the VQA showed 71.9% accuracy (95% CI, 0.53-0.86) after few-shot fine-tuning, with further improvement over all state-of-the-art approaches in survival stratification. The VQA approach showed the closest calibration with the ground-truth survival distribution, with no significant differences observed (log-rank test, P = 0.76). Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed the highest area under the curve (0.75) among the evaluated models. Together, these findings suggest that the VQA approach demonstrated adaptability across different PSMA ligands while maintaining slightly improved yet comparable overall survival prognostic performance. Conclusion: By adopting a physician-inspired assessment workflow, the VQA framework shows advantages in integrating imaging and laboratory data for clinical decision support compared with conventional machine learning. The preliminary results indicate that VQA-based approaches warrant future evaluation for survival prognostication in patients with mCRPC who are receiving PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

items.title: Brain-Specific Quantification of Somatostatin Receptor Expression: SUVmax and SUVRsss as Quantitative Correlates of the Krenning Score in Meningioma.
items.journal_full: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
items.authors: Marulanda-Corzo V, Farid M, Hill T, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Brain-only PET evaluation may provide an alternative to liver- and spleen-based visual grading and reduce the need for whole-body imaging in selected settings. Receiver-operating-characteristic curve-derived SUV thresholds correspond to Krenning scores used for eligibility for treatment with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, supporting further evaluation of quantitative PET parameters for theranostic decision-making for patients with meningioma.

sections.text: Somatostatin receptor type 2 is highly expressed in meningiomas and can be quantified using [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET. The Krenning score, originally developed for [111In]In-octreotide scintigraphy, remains the standard visual grading system for somatostatin receptor expression and is widely used to guide eligibility for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. However, visual grading may not optimally translate to intracranial disease. This study evaluated the relationship between brain-specific quantitative PET parameters-SUVmax and SUV ratio normalized to the superior sagittal sinus (SUVRsss)-and the Krenning score in meningioma. Methods: This single-institution retrospective study included 44 patients (70 meningiomas) who underwent clinical vertex-to-thigh [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT. Quantitative parameters (SUVmax, SUVRsss, lesion size) were extracted from coregistered PET and MR images. Spearman rank correlation analysis was performed to assess associations between imaging variables and Krenning score. Differences in quantitative PET parameters across Krenning categories were evaluated using Kruskal-Wallis test and Holm-Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test. Receiver-operating-characteristic curve analysis using the Youden J index identified optimal cutoffs for clinically relevant thresholds (Krenning score of <3 vs. ≥3 and 3 vs. 4). Results: SUVRsss and SUVmax were strongly correlated with the Krenning score (SUVRsss: Spearman ρ = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.55-0.82; SUVmax: Spearman ρ = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.64-0.85; P < 0.0001). PET parameters differed significantly across Krenning categories (all P < 0.001). SUVRsss optimal thresholds were 9.00 (area under the curve [AUC], 0.86; 95% CI, 0.74-0.96) for Krenning scores of 2 versus 3 and 29.84 (AUC, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.93-1.00) for Krenning scores of 3 versus 4. SUVmax optimal thresholds were 7.20 (AUC, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.84-0.99) and 30.70 (AUC, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.95-1.00), respectively. Conclusion: SUVRsss and SUVmax are complementary quantitative correlates of Krenning scores 2-4 in [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET-visible, MRI-measurable meningiomas. Brain-only PET evaluation may provide an alternative to liver- and spleen-based visual grading and reduce the need for whole-body imaging in selected settings. Receiver-operating-characteristic curve-derived SUV thresholds correspond to Krenning scores used for eligibility for treatment with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, supporting further evaluation of quantitative PET parameters for theranostic decision-making for patients with meningioma.

items.authors: Garabedian N, Zaragori T, Tabouret E, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion

sections.text: Evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas derives mainly from small, single-center studies. The French national multicenter MELUTE study aimed to consolidate these data using a standardized regimen within a compassionate-use program approved by a national multidisciplinary tumor board. Methods: In this retrospective multicenter cohort study, patients with refractory meningiomas treated with [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in 18 French centers between July 2022 and December 2024 were included. Treatment consisted of 7.4 GBq every 8 wk for up to 4 cycles. Clinical data (demographics, histologic World Health Organization grade [WHO], prior treatments, number of cycles, toxicity, progression, survival status as of October 1, 2025) were collected. Baseline [68Ga]Ga-DOTATOC PET and brain MRI scans obtained before and after treatment were centrally reviewed. The primary endpoint was 6-mo progression-free survival (PFS) assessed using volumetric Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology Group criteria. Secondary endpoints were PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Results: Sixty-nine patients were included (mean age, 65.1 ± 13.2 y; 52% female): 13 WHO grade 1, 42 WHO grade 2, 8 WHO grade 3, and 6 without histology. Most had prior surgery (86%) or radiotherapy (93%); 32% received prior systemic therapy. Twelve patients (17%) did not complete 4 cycles; only one discontinuation was toxicity-related. Six-month PFS was 70% (95% CI, 58.7-80.4%). Median PFS was 14.6 mo (95% CI, 13.3-18.5 mo), and median OS was 27.6 mo (95% CI, 24.2 mo to not reached). Grade 3 adverse events, mainly lymphopenia, occurred in 16%. Meningioma WHO grade independently predicted PFS, whereas higher Karnofsky performance status and corticosteroid use were protective; worse OS was associated with higher baseline tumor growth rate and prior systemic therapy. Conclusion: MELUTE demonstrates promising efficacy and favorable safety of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas with limited therapeutic options.

conclusion.label: Conclusion

However, because chronological age and Fontan duration were nearly collinear, this cross-sectional study cannot determine whether these imaging gradients reflect duration of Fontan physiology, chronological maturation, or both. sections.label: Background
sections.text: This study aimed to characterize sonographic hepatic findings across pediatric, adolescent, and adult Fontan patients and to examine their cross-sectional relationships with time since Fontan completion and chronological age. As a secondary objective, we explored a composite score integrating complementary sonographic findings.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: In this retrospective cross-sectional analysis of a prospectively established single-center Fontan cohort, hepatic ultrasound findings from 153 patients were evaluated, including gray-scale imaging, Doppler assessment, and shear-wave elastography performed according to institutional acquisition protocols. Individual sonographic findings were analyzed as the primary imaging outcomes. Cross-sectional associations with time since Fontan completion were assessed using sex-adjusted regression models; additional models simultaneously included chronological age, time since Fontan completion, and sex to examine their closely related contributions. A secondary exploratory 5-point composite score integrating five complementary sonographic domains was evaluated descriptively.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Longer time since Fontan completion was associated cross-sectionally with greater IVC diameter, liver size, shear-wave velocity, structural abnormality, and hepatic nodularity in sex-adjusted analyses. Chronological age and time since Fontan completion were nearly collinear (r = 0.970). When both variables and sex were included simultaneously, associations with IVC diameter, liver size, shear-wave velocity, and structural classification were attenuated and no longer statistically significant, whereas hepatic nodularity remained associated with time since Fontan completion (OR = 1.22/year; 95% CI 1.03-1.45; p = 0.024). Complete composite-score data were available in 101 patients; mean scores were 0.81 ± 0.88, 2.15 ± 1.26, 3.18 ± 0.80, and 4.27 ± 0.80 across < 5-, 5-<10-, 10-<20-, and ≥ 20-year post-Fontan categories, respectively. In 15 patients with serial examinations, scores were higher at the later examination in 10 and unchanged in five (p = 0.004). In a stratified subset of 40 independently reread examinations, interobserver agreement was high for liver size (ICC = 0.922) and IVC diameter (ICC = 0.947), whereas agreement for qualitative sonographic findings was lower (κ = 0.202-0.369).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Sonographic vascular, morphologic, structural, elastographic, and nodular abnormalities differed across patients examined at increasing intervals after Fontan completion. However, because chronological age and Fontan duration were nearly collinear, this cross-sectional study cannot determine whether these imaging gradients reflect duration of Fontan physiology, chronological maturation, or both. Hepatic nodularity showed the most robust association with time since Fontan completion in simultaneous models. The composite score provides a secondary exploratory framework for integrating complementary sonographic findings but requires prospective longitudinal and external validation. The limited interobserver agreement for qualitative findings further emphasizes the need for standardized image interpretation and supports the exploratory status of the composite score.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To evaluate whether post-chemoradiotherapy neoadjuvant chemotherapy Vesical Imaging-Reporting and Data System (nacVI-RADS) is associated with pathological complete response (pCR), and to assess its diagnostic performance and inter-reader agreement in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective study included 73 patients with non-metastatic cT2-4aN0-2 M0 bladder cancer who underwent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy followed by radical or partial cystectomy between 2009 and 2024. Two radiologists independently assigned post-chemoradiotherapy nacVI-RADS scores on MRI. For the primary diagnostic analysis, scores were dichotomized as < 3 and ≥ 3. The reference standard was bladder pCR, defined as ypT0 on pathological assessment.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: pCR was achieved in 46 of 73 patients (63%). The pCR rate was higher among patients with nacVI-RADS < 3 than among those with nacVI-RADS ≥ 3 for both readers (reader 1: 77% vs. 39%, p = 0.002; reader 2: 74% vs. 39%, p = 0.008). The sensitivity and specificity of nacVI-RADS < 3 for identifying pCR were 78% and 59% for reader 1 and 80% and 52% for reader 2, respectively. Inter-reader agreement was excellent (κ = 0.845; 95% CI, 0.687-0.962).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Post-chemoradiotherapy nacVI-RADS < 3 was associated with pCR and showed moderate diagnostic performance with excellent inter-reader agreement in patients with MIBC. Post-chemoradiotherapy nacVI-RADS may provide useful complementary information for response assessment. Larger prospective multicenter studies are warranted to validate these findings.

sections.text: The ureter is an important conduit between the kidney and the bladder and is frequently imaged to rule out cancer in the upper genitourinary tract. However, while malignancy can occur, a spectrum of other pathologic ureteral findings can exist, and these can be divided into congenital, intrinsic, and extrinsic abnormalities that range from postoperative and neoplastic conditions to inflammatory disease. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the ureter, including the ureteral anatomy, ureteral imaging strategies, and various ureteral conditions and their associated imaging features. It is important to identify congenital genitourinary variants, as these are frequently linked to further imaging recommendations, such as nuclear medicine renography and fluoroscopic voiding cystourethrography. Intrinsic abnormalities can be iatrogenic, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic. Intrinsic ureteral strictures are most commonly iatrogenic, usually resulting from prior surgery or radiation therapy. Ureteral infections include tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, and Escherichia coli infection, which have varying imaging manifestations. Inflammatory conditions include ureteritis cystica and pseudodiverticulosis. Ureteral masses are rarely benign and are most commonly urothelial carcinomas. Processes in the abdomen and pelvis, including mass effect from pregnancy, ureteral compression from advanced pelvic floor prolapse, and rarely, ureteral obstruction from vaginal devices, also can affect the ureter. The ureter can be injured during pelvic surgery or trauma. It also may be involved by deep pelvic endometriosis, mass effect from extrinsic lesions, or reactive change from inflammatory processes. Radiologists need to have a clear understanding of the patient's history and the range of possible ureteral conditions to establish the optimal differential diagnosis.

items.title: Saroglitazar improves hepatic steatosis and liver enzymes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome and MASLD: A multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
items.authors: Samala N, González-González J, Jenders RA, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: In women with PCOS and MASLD, saroglitazar significantly improved hepatic steatosis, liver enzymes, lipid profile, and FibroScan AST score. These findings support further evaluation of saroglitazar in larger studies in women with PCOS.

sections.label: Background and aims
sections.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the leading endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is common in women with PCOS, but they are underrepresented in MASLD therapeutic trials. We evaluated the safety and efficacy of saroglitazar, a novel peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors α/γ agonist, for the treatment of hepatic steatosis in women with PCOS and MASLD.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: In this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2A trial, 60 women (18-45 y) with PCOS and MASLD were randomized 1:1 to either saroglitazar 4 mg or placebo for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was relative (percent) change in hepatic fat content, measured by MRI proton density fat fraction. Primary analysis was performed in the per-protocol population (saroglitazar: 25; placebo: 23).

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Participants in the saroglitazar group showed a significant reduction in percent hepatic fat content at 24 weeks from baseline compared to placebo ([least squares mean±SE]: -14.81±5.52 vs. 1.96±5.75, p =0.041). When controlled for baseline HbA1c imbalance, the beneficial effect of saroglitazar was more pronounced ([least squares mean±SE]: -18.93±4.83 vs. 6.43±5.04, p <0.009). A higher proportion in the saroglitazar group achieved ≥30% reduction in magnetic resonance imaging-proton density fat fraction (36.0% vs. 8.7%; p =0.025). Saroglitazar also significantly reduced aminotransferase levels, lipid parameters, and the FibroScan AST score. Adverse events were comparable between the groups, and none were serious. One pregnancy in the saroglitazar arm resulted in uneventful maternal and neonatal outcomes.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: In women with PCOS and MASLD, saroglitazar significantly improved hepatic steatosis, liver enzymes, lipid profile, and FibroScan AST score. These findings support further evaluation of saroglitazar in larger studies in women with PCOS.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question What is the added value of post-mortem MRI in forensic cases, in the absence of international guidelines and standardised indications? Findings Additional findings were observed in post-mortem MRI examinations indicated for soft tissue injuries caused by penetrating force and in cases of suspected strangulation. Critical Relevance Statement The criminal investigation can be optimised by using post-mortem MRI in addition to post-mortem CT, either by showing additional findings on post-mortem MRI not seen on CT, or by excluding findings with higher certainty.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: In the Netherlands, post-mortem radiology aids forensic investigation, using a full-body post-mortem computed tomography (PMCT) scan and a post-mortem magnetic resonance imaging (PMMRI) scan in specific cases. Application of PMMRI varies between countries and institutions in the absence of international guidelines. This study analyses current use and added value of PMMRI in a single forensic imaging institution in the Netherlands.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: All post-mortem cases scanned between July 2024 and July 2025 were included, except non-accidental injury protocol cases. The (contra-)indications for additional PMMRI scans in addition to PMCT were recorded. On the same day as image evaluation, added value was scored by the forensic radiologist and consultant using the following options: additional finding, exclusion of a finding, confirmation of PMCT and no added value.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: PMMRI was conducted in 47.4% of all cases, indicated by suspected strangulation, penetrating injuries, blunt force trauma and lesions seen on PMCT. In suspected strangulation, PMMRI neck showed additional findings or exclusion of findings in 31/46 cases, while PMMRI brain had the lowest added value in 13/25 cases. PMMRI thorax and abdomen showed additional findings in 14/20 and 4/9 cases of penetrating trauma, respectively. Additional findings were found in 10/15 PMMRI brain scans and 6/8 PMMRI thorax scans, based on PMCT.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Application of PMMRI in addition to PMCT is currently used in a targeted manner. In cases of strangulation and penetrating injuries, additional or excluded findings were found. Therefore, adding PMMRI in these specific cases can be of added value.

items.title: Prostate cancer screening with MRI: insights from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group.
items.authors: Brembilla G, Messina E, Barret T, et al.

conclusion.label: Abstract opening — no stated conclusion
conclusion.text: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer (PCa) remains controversial due to uncertain long-term benefits, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment of indolent disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has transformed the diagnostic pathway of PCa and is increasingly explored as a screening tool.

sections.text: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer (PCa) remains controversial due to uncertain long-term benefits, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment of indolent disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has transformed the diagnostic pathway of PCa and is increasingly explored as a screening tool. This special report from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group provides an overview of current evidence and insights into the potential role of MRI in PCa screening. MRI-based screening strategies appear to improve detection of clinically significant PCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies and diagnoses of non-significant disease, though long-term outcome data, including mortality impact and interval cancer rates, remain limited. Biparametric MRI is particularly suited for screening due to its shorter acquisition time, reduced operational complexity, and lower costs compared with multiparametric MRI. Two main implementation approaches have emerged: MRI-first pathways, which maximise detection but require substantial resources, and risk-stratified strategies, in which MRI is used after initial assessment (e.g. PSA), potentially offering greater feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Evidence from large trials supports integrating MRI into screening pathways, particularly as a reflex test after PSA screening, although uncertainties remain regarding optimal protocols, interpretation thresholds, follow-up strategies, and long-term outcomes. Key barriers include limited MRI capacity, economic considerations, and the need for standardisation and quality assurance. Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance efficiency. Overall, MRI has the potential to improve the balance between benefits and harms in PCa screening, but further evidence is required to define its optimal implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can prostate MRI be effectively integrated into population-based prostate cancer screening pathways? Findings MRI-based screening improves detection of csPCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies; biparametric MRI should be the protocol of choice to enhance feasibility, although optimal implementation and long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Clinical relevance MRI may overcome key limitations of PSA-based screening by enhancing the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer while reducing harms such as overdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsies.

items.title: Test order, timing, and multidisciplinary review predict management change in sequential fluoroscopic and MR defecography.
items.authors: Almeida RR, Boatright C, Stankiewicz A

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Sequential multimodality defecography changed management in approximately one-quarter of patients. Its value was greatest when MRD followed FLD, especially when examinations were performed closely together. MRD after FLD detected a higher frequency of second-test abnormalities, particularly cystocele. The association between multidisciplinary review and management change suggests that the clinical impact of sequential defecography depends not only on the added imaging findings but also on how they are integrated into treatment planning.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To determine whether sequential fluoroscopic defecography (FLD) and MR defecography (MRD) change clinical management of patients with pelvic floor dysfunction and to identify factors associated with management change.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: Multi-institutional retrospective study including adults who underwent both FL and MR defecography within 3 years, without interval surgery. Primary outcome was management change attributed to the second examination. Clinical information, test order & timing, multidisciplinary review, and imaging variables were compared between patients with and without management change. Univariate analyses were performed overall and by first-modality subgroup. Multivariable logistic regression was performed in the overall cohort.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Of 46 patients, 24 underwent FLD first and 22 underwent MRD first. Management changed after second examination in 23.9% (11/46). FLD-first order (adjusted OR, 72.70; 95% CI, 2.77-1909.81; p = 0.010), shorter interval between examinations (adjusted OR per 30 days, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.68-1.00; p = 0.038), and wider MR resting anorectal angle (adjusted OR per degree, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.02-1.20; p = 0.016) were independent predictors of management change. MRD after FLD showed more frequent new second-test abnormalities than FLD after MRD (16/24 [66.7%] vs. 5/22 [22.7%], p = 0.0037), particularly new cystocele detection (41.7% vs. 0%, p = 0.0006). In the FLD-first subgroup, multidisciplinary review was associated with management change (5/5 [100%] vs. 5/19 [26.3%], p = 0.0059).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Sequential multimodality defecography changed management in approximately one-quarter of patients. Its value was greatest when MRD followed FLD, especially when examinations were performed closely together. MRD after FLD detected a higher frequency of second-test abnormalities, particularly cystocele. The association between multidisciplinary review and management change suggests that the clinical impact of sequential defecography depends not only on the added imaging findings but also on how they are integrated into treatment planning.

items.title: Impact of VI-RADS quality score on VI-RADS diagnostic performance for muscle invasion: the role of tumor size and reader experience.
items.authors: Joo Y, Cho SW, Tse JR, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The VI-RADS quality scoring system demonstrated good inter-reader agreement. Optimal image quality improved diagnostic performance in small tumors and for the less experienced reader; however, because only one less experienced reader was included, this finding requires external validation.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Does image quality, assessed by the VI-RADS quality score, influence diagnostic performance of VI-RADS for detecting muscle invasion in bladder cancer? Findings Higher image quality improved PPV and accuracy of VI-RADS, particularly in tumors < 3 cm and for the less experienced reader, while having limited impact in larger tumors. Clinical relevance Ensuring optimal MRI image quality enhances the reliability of VI-RADS interpretation, particularly in small tumors and non-specialized settings, and supports standardized imaging as a prerequisite for accurate bladder cancer staging.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To evaluate the inter-reader agreement of the Vesical Imaging Reporting and Data System (VI-RADS) quality scoring system and to assess its impact on the diagnostic performance for detecting muscle invasion.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective study included 587 patients who underwent multiparametric bladder MRI before surgery. Three radiologists (two specialists and one non-genitourinary radiologist) independently assessed VI-RADS category and quality scores. Inter-reader agreement was evaluated using weighted kappa statistics. Associations between image quality, VI-RADS categorization, and tumor characteristics were analyzed using multivariable models. Diagnostic performance for muscle invasion was assessed at predefined VI-RADS thresholds and compared across quality groups and tumor size subgroups.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: A total of 7/587 (1.2%), 284/587 (48.4%), and 296/587 (50.4%) scans were VI-RADS quality score 0, 1, and 2, respectively. Inter-reader agreement for the final quality score was substantial (k = 0.628-0.702). Higher VI-RADS quality scores were associated with increased T2-weighted image VI-RADS scores (odds ratio [OR], 2.95; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-7.43; p = 0.021). In tumors < 3 cm, particularly for the less experienced reader, higher image quality was associated with increased positive predictive value (PPV) and accuracy at the VI-RADS ≥ 3 threshold (PPV: 51.0% vs 22.7%, p = 0.004; accuracy: 81.6% vs 71.7%, p = 0.023). No significant differences in diagnostic performance were observed across VI-RADS thresholds in tumors ≥ 3 cm.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The VI-RADS quality scoring system demonstrated good inter-reader agreement. Optimal image quality improved diagnostic performance in small tumors and for the less experienced reader; however, because only one less experienced reader was included, this finding requires external validation.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Does image quality, assessed by the VI-RADS quality score, influence diagnostic performance of VI-RADS for detecting muscle invasion in bladder cancer? Findings Higher image quality improved PPV and accuracy of VI-RADS, particularly in tumors < 3 cm and for the less experienced reader, while having limited impact in larger tumors. Clinical relevance Ensuring optimal MRI image quality enhances the reliability of VI-RADS interpretation, particularly in small tumors and non-specialized settings, and supports standardized imaging as a prerequisite for accurate bladder cancer staging.

items.title: Estimation of glomerular filtration rate by standard renal CT imaging.
items.authors: Huitfeldt Sola K, Genberg H, Webster-Ford J, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Renal function can be estimated with high precision from clinical renal CT.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Accurate GFR assessment is critical, but current methods are either labor-intensive or imprecise. Can renal CT imaging provide a reliable alternative? Findings CT-derived eGFR showed the strongest correlation with iohexol clearance (R² = 0.77), with lower error compared to creatinine- and cystatin C-based estimates. Critical relevance statement Routine CT imaging can provide precise estimates of kidney function, supporting donor evaluations, chemotherapy dosing, and critical care decisions when accurate renal function is essential.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To develop and evaluate a method to predict glomerular filtration rate (GFR) from clinical renal CT.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: Medical records of adult living kidney donors operated between 2013 and 2022 and patients considered for neoadjuvant cisplatin prior to cystectomy between 2019 and 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Inclusion criteria were (1) renal CT obtained at 100 or 120 kVp before and 5-15 min after contrast administration, and (2) iohexol clearance test within 2 months of imaging. The iohexol clearance test was performed on the same day as the cystatin C and creatinine measurements. Estimated GFR values included cystatin C-based eGFR (eGFRcystatin C), creatinine-based eGFR using the Cockcroft-Gault formula (eGFRCockcroft-Gault), and eGFR using the Revised Lund-Malmö formula (eGFRLMR18), which is based on both creatinine and cystatin C. Manual and automatic segmentations of the renal pelvis and bladder were performed in both the excretory and unenhanced phases.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: In total, 139 patients were included in the analysis (mean age 52 ± 13 years; 60% women). Multivariate linear regression analysis combining the segmentation-derived variable with body surface area and age gave an adjusted R-square of 0.77 to mGFRiohexol (p < 0.001). GFRCT had the strongest relationship to mGFRiohexol with a mean absolute error of 12.8 mL/min, compared with 15.6 mL/min for eGFRCockcroft-Gault, 14.2 mL/min for eGFRcystatin C, and 13.0 mL/min for eGFRLMR18. Manual and automatic segmentations had similar performance. Patients evaluated for cisplatin treatment had greater variation in CT-estimated split renal function than donors.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Renal function can be estimated with high precision from clinical renal CT.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Accurate GFR assessment is critical, but current methods are either labor-intensive or imprecise. Can renal CT imaging provide a reliable alternative? Findings CT-derived eGFR showed the strongest correlation with iohexol clearance (R² = 0.77), with lower error compared to creatinine- and cystatin C-based estimates. Critical relevance statement Routine CT imaging can provide precise estimates of kidney function, supporting donor evaluations, chemotherapy dosing, and critical care decisions when accurate renal function is essential.

items.title: Quantitative ultrasound-derived estimated fat fraction for detection and grading of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in a pediatric population.
items.authors: Wang Y, Du L, Yang C, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: USFF shows high diagnostic performance (AUC > 0.94) for pediatric MASLD, but its 3.13% underestimation and wide non-parametric limits of agreement warrant caution. USFF may serve as a practical tool for categorical steatosis grading in children with suspected MASLD, and the proposed thresholds require external validation before clinical use.

sections.label: Background
sections.text: Pediatric metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) prevalence is approximately 10%, but ultrasound fat quantification lacks validation. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of quantitative ultrasound-derived estimated fat fraction (USFF) against magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) in children with suspected MASLD.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This prospective single-center study enrolled 65 children aged 6-18 years with suspected MASLD. USFF, tissue attenuation imaging (TAI), tissue scatter distribution imaging (TSI), hepato-renal index (EzHRI), and shear wave elastography (SWE) were measured on a Samsung R10 Prestige platform; 3.0 T MRI-PDFF served as reference. Steatosis was graded using pediatric PDFF thresholds. Diagnostic performance was assessed by ROC analysis with DeLong comparisons and internally validated by bootstrap resampling; agreement by Bland-Altman analysis; inter-operator reproducibility assessed in a randomly selected 30-child subset.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Among 65 children (48 boys; median age 11.2 years), 20 were classified as S0, 29 as S1, and 16 as S2-3. USFF AUCs were 0.941 (≥S1) and 0.960 (≥S2), higher than EzHRI and SWE, and similar to TAI (0.903, 0.957) and TSI (0.900, 0.880). USFF strongly correlated with MRI-PDFF (ρ = 0.906) but systematically underestimated PDFF (mean bias - 3.13%; non-parametric limits of agreement - 14.51% to + 4.24%). In an exploratory analysis, younger children (<12 years) showed larger bias (-4.00% vs - 1.82%, p = 0.029) with similar AUC point estimates.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: USFF shows high diagnostic performance (AUC > 0.94) for pediatric MASLD, but its 3.13% underestimation and wide non-parametric limits of agreement warrant caution. USFF may serve as a practical tool for categorical steatosis grading in children with suspected MASLD, and the proposed thresholds require external validation before clinical use.

items.title: Periprostatic adipose tissue imaging in prostate cancer: Imaging phenotypes, task-specific spatial strategies, and multicompartment integration-a critical review.
items.authors: Huang J, Zhang Y, Yang O, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusions
conclusion.text: PPAT imaging is best regarded as a set of spatially defined, task-specific phenotypes rather than a single biomarker. Current evidence positions PPAT as a candidate adjunct to established clinical and intraprostatic imaging information. Clinical adoption will require reproducible definitions and measurements, task-matched assessment of incremental value, independent external evaluation, and prospective evidence of decision impact.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To appraise how periprostatic adipose tissue (PPAT) is defined, sampled, and evaluated in prostate cancer imaging, with emphasis on spatial strategy, intended clinical use, evidence maturity, and imaging-tissue correspondence.

sections.label: Method
sections.text: We conducted a structured critical review with evidence mapping, supported by PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science searches through August 29, 2026, supplemented by prespecified Google Scholar and citation searches. Two reviewers independently screened records. Reports were mapped by imaging strategy, spatial target, clinical task, evaluation design, reproducibility, cohort overlap, and imaging-tissue correspondence.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: The formal evidence set comprised 113 reports, including 63 clinical imaging reports. Strategies comprised morphometry / computed tomography (CT) attenuation (48 reports), tissue-property / compositional imaging (4), PPAT-focused radiomics (4), and interface / multicompartment modelling (7). Quantitative reproducibility was reported in 19/63 clinical reports. Only two reports underwent independent external evaluation, and neither evaluated a PPAT-only model. Biological and translational evidence supported PPAT as a heterogeneous tumour-adjacent compartment, whereas direct spatially matched imaging-tissue validation remained uncommon. Clinical evidence spanned prebiopsy risk refinement, upgrading or active-surveillance reclassification, local extension and surgical planning, prognosis, treatment-related outcomes, and nodal and metastatic assessment; most reports lacked independent evaluation.

sections.label: Conclusions
sections.text: PPAT imaging is best regarded as a set of spatially defined, task-specific phenotypes rather than a single biomarker. Current evidence positions PPAT as a candidate adjunct to established clinical and intraprostatic imaging information. Clinical adoption will require reproducible definitions and measurements, task-matched assessment of incremental value, independent external evaluation, and prospective evidence of decision impact.

items.title: Reproducibility and diagnostic performance of ADC for assessing response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer: a multi-ROI comparison analysis from the phase-Ib NABUCCO trial.
items.authors: Greidanus J, Bernabei C, Chupetvloska K, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Despite analyzing different measurement techniques for ADC values, none was simultaneously reproducible and predictive, nor provided insights into the biology of the tumor. While ADC shows promise in MIBC, there is an urgent need for more standardized, robust imaging biomarkers.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question Non-invasive biomarkers are urgently needed to guide bladder-preserving strategies in MIBC. Findings DWI-MRI shows promise, but standardized robust imaging biomarkers are essential for reliable response assessment. Critical relevance statement Standardized or AI-assisted ROI segmentation could improve ADC reproducibility and diagnostic accuracy in multicenter studies.

sections.label: Objective
sections.text: MRI is increasingly used to assess treatment response in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), but only qualitatively. This study evaluates the reproducibility and predictive value of quantitative apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), thought to be a non-invasive surrogate for tumor cell density, in patients with MIBC receiving neoadjuvant immunotherapy.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: MRI data from 35 patients, enrolled in the Phase-Ib NABUCCO trial, were analyzed. ADC maps were derived from pre- and post-treatment MRI scans. Three independent radiologists assessed multiple regions of interest (ROIs) to evaluate inter-observer agreement and predictive performance for pathological complete response (pCR). ADC values were normalized using muscle tissue as a reference. Additionally, we analyzed the correlation between ADC and cell densities, derived from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) data.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: ADC measurements from the whole-tumor ROI (n = 25) demonstrated the highest reproducibility (0.98, 95% CI = [0.95-0.99]), but lacked predictive value (AUC = 0.31, 95% CI = [0.12-0.53], p = 0.109). The most hypointense ROI (n = 22) showed the strongest predictive value for pCR (AUC = 0.80, 95% CI = [0.57-1], p = 0.025), though with limited reproducibility. The difference between baseline and follow-up ADC values in the hypointense region (n = 20) again showed the highest diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.80, 95% CI = [0.58-0.98], p = 0.015). Although muscle normalization is proposed to reduce scanner variability, it did not improve predictive performance in this cohort and occasionally reduced reproducibility. No significant correlation was found between whole-tumor ADC and cell density.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Despite analyzing different measurement techniques for ADC values, none was simultaneously reproducible and predictive, nor provided insights into the biology of the tumor. While ADC shows promise in MIBC, there is an urgent need for more standardized, robust imaging biomarkers.

sections.label: Key points
sections.text: Question Non-invasive biomarkers are urgently needed to guide bladder-preserving strategies in MIBC. Findings DWI-MRI shows promise, but standardized robust imaging biomarkers are essential for reliable response assessment. Critical relevance statement Standardized or AI-assisted ROI segmentation could improve ADC reproducibility and diagnostic accuracy in multicenter studies.

items.title: MRI for restaging pancreatic cancer.
items.authors: Zamboni GA, Omboni F, Panozzo I

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Findings Different MRI sequences and techniques have been suggested as possibly improving this assessment, reflecting on better patient management. Critical relevance statement We summarize the available evidence on MRI for restaging pancreatic carcinoma after neoadjuvant treatment.

sections.text: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a tumor with a dismal prognosis, as the majority of patients are diagnosed when the tumor is not resectable. Neoadjuvant treatment has significantly improved prognosis, but assessing treatment response can be challenging for radiologists. Given the fibrotic nature of the primary tumor, differentiating between residual viable tumor and fibrotic response can be difficult. MRI can have a role in reassessing the primary tumor and disease spread. In this review, we discuss MR techniques that can be used for this assessment, including routinely used sequences (e.g., DWI) and sequences that are not yet routinely included in pancreatic protocols (e.g., T1 mapping, ECV imaging, and USPIO contrast for nodal staging). KEY POINTS: Question Imaging assessment of the response of pancreatic adenocarcinoma to neoadjuvant treatment is difficult and still has limited accuracy. Findings Different MRI sequences and techniques have been suggested as possibly improving this assessment, reflecting on better patient management. Critical relevance statement We summarize the available evidence on MRI for restaging pancreatic carcinoma after neoadjuvant treatment.

items.title: Ultrasonography in disaster medicine: a narrative review.
items.authors: Amiot F, Tazarourte K, Gorincour G, et al.

conclusion.label: Closing lines — abstract has no labeled conclusion
conclusion.text: Findings Across 63 studies, FAST reached 92.1% pooled sensitivity for hemoperitoneum, lung ultrasound 90-97% versus 60-69% for radiography; management changed in up to 44%. Critical relevance statement This review critically appraises ultraportable ultrasound across all four disaster domains, showing that radiation-free bedside imaging accelerates triage, conserves scarce CT capacity, and extends radiological expertise through tele-guidance, while exposing an evidence base still lacking prospective outcome data.

sections.text: This narrative review aimed to critically appraise the diagnostic accuracy, clinical impact, and operational feasibility of ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) across the four domains of disaster medicine. A literature search was conducted following the SANRA and PRISMA-trAIce guidelines. Records were identified through an AI-assisted literature-discovery tool (the Undermind Deep-Search platform, interrogating the Semantic Scholar corpus) run on 15 June 2025, rather than through an independent structured multi-database search. Candidate references were screened manually against pre-specified eligibility criteria by a single reviewer, with the search parameters independently verified by the senior author. Of 71 records identified, 63 met the inclusion criteria. The included studies comprised 32 original studies, 10 systematic or scoping reviews, 20 narrative or operational papers, and one guideline. In CBRN scenarios, lung ultrasound demonstrated sensitivities of 90-97% for COVID-19 pneumonia versus 60-69% for chest radiography while minimizing healthcare worker exposure. For blast and ballistic injuries, FAST showed a pooled sensitivity of 92.1% (95% CI: 87.8-95.6) and specificity of 98.7% (95% CI: 96.0-99.9) for intra-abdominal hemorrhage. In natural disasters, ultrasound altered management in up to 44% of patients. Post-disaster applications included vascular access, tube confirmation, and complication monitoring. Ultraportable POCUS demonstrates diagnostic utility and operational feasibility across multiple disaster domains. However, evidence quality varies significantly, and standardized protocols remain lacking. Prospective studies linking ultrasound deployment to improved patient outcomes are needed. KEY POINTS: Question When disasters disable conventional imaging, how does ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography perform for diagnosis, triage, and procedural guidance across the four domains of disaster medicine? Findings Across 63 studies, FAST reached 92.1% pooled sensitivity for hemoperitoneum, lung ultrasound 90-97% versus 60-69% for radiography; management changed in up to 44%. Critical relevance statement This review critically appraises ultraportable ultrasound across all four disaster domains, showing that radiation-free bedside imaging accelerates triage, conserves scarce CT capacity, and extends radiological expertise through tele-guidance, while exposing an evidence base still lacking prospective outcome data.

items.title: Limited incremental value and cross-cohort transferability of CT radiomics for survival prediction after TACE in hepatocellular carcinoma.
items.authors: Bartnik K, Tsevegmed B

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The evaluated models showed no consistent incremental value for OS prediction within these TACE cohorts and limited frozen-model discrimination in the clinically distinct HCC-TACE-SEG cohort. These findings do not support clinical use of these models or establish a general limitation of CT radiomics.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: To evaluate whether pretreatment CT radiomics adds information for overall survival (OS) prediction among patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), and assess frozen imaging-model performance in an independent cohort.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective study included 221 WAW-TACE and 98 HCC-TACE-SEG patients with pretreatment arterial and portal venous CT. Incremental value of a tumor-radiomics Random Survival Forest score (R1) beyond cohort-specific clinical Cox models (C0) was evaluated within each cohort using 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times. External validation was restricted to frozen WAW-trained R1 models (Top-K = 5, 10, 15) applied to HCC-TACE-SEG without refitting; the combined C0 + R1 model was not externally validated.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: WAW-TACE included 162 deaths and HCC-TACE-SEG 86 deaths. In WAW-TACE, C0, R1 Top-K = 15, and C0 + R1 achieved C-indices of 0.646 ± 0.043, 0.593 ± 0.049, and 0.639 ± 0.045, respectively. Corresponding HCC-TACE-SEG estimates were 0.496 ± 0.087, 0.530 ± 0.072, and 0.495 ± 0.094. Thus, R1 did not consistently improve cohort-specific clinical reference models. In frozen external application, Top-K = 5, 10, and 15 achieved C-indices of 0.463 (95% CI 0.397-0.532), 0.535 (0.468-0.608), and 0.528 (0.460-0.598), respectively.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The evaluated models showed no consistent incremental value for OS prediction within these TACE cohorts and limited frozen-model discrimination in the clinically distinct HCC-TACE-SEG cohort. These findings do not support clinical use of these models or establish a general limitation of CT radiomics.

items.title: Machine learning-assisted monitoring of radiofrequency ablation in hepatic tumors using spectral traces.
items.authors: Abdlaty R, Basyouny M, Abbass M

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Overall, HSI is neither a contact nor destructive modality for quantitative RFA assessment. Despite classifier-dependent variability necessitating standardized or ensemble strategies, these findings support its prospective integration into real-time surgical guidance, pending in vivo validation.

sections.label: Purpose
sections.text: Accurate intraoperative assessment of radiofrequency ablation (RFA) margins in hepatic malignancies remains a significant clinical challenge.

sections.label: Methods
sections.text: This study investigates the efficacy of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for objective, spatially resolved discrimination of ablated tissue, viable tumor, and normal parenchyma in 10 ex vivo liver specimens. Analysis of visible-near-infrared (VNIR) reflectance revealed distinct spectral signatures, characterized by a consistent monotonic hierarchy (ablated < normal < tumor), enabling reliable tissue differentiation. Segmentation performance was systematically evaluated using four supervised classifiers: Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). The total delineated tissue area exhibited notable inter-method variability, ranging from 137,283 to 189,289 pixels (+ 37.9%), underscoring sensitivity to classifier architecture.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Nevertheless, all approaches maintained biologically coherent tissue distributions, with normal parenchyma predominating (44-56%), followed by tumor (25-39%) and ablated regions (17-20%). That is consistently indicating the necessity for monitoring ablative margins. SAM, SVM, and LDA classifiers achieved class-specific detection errors around 3.5% and 18%. LDA attained the highest overall accuracy (94.5%), demonstrating the potential of HSI for reliable, intraoperative image-guided tissue characterization. Dimensionality reduction across 462 spectral bands identified an optimal discriminative window within 643-698 nm, supporting the development of streamlined multispectral systems.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Overall, HSI is neither a contact nor destructive modality for quantitative RFA assessment. Despite classifier-dependent variability necessitating standardized or ensemble strategies, these findings support its prospective integration into real-time surgical guidance, pending in vivo validation.

items.title: Predicting advanced-stage recurrence in resected hepatocellular carcinoma using preoperative gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI radiomics.
items.authors: Kang JG, Han K, Ryu L, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: The preoperative radiomics model outperformed staging systems and was comparable to the postoperative clinicopathological model in predicting advanced-stage recurrence, relying entirely on noninvasive data.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: To develop and validate a preoperative gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI-based radiomics model for predicting the time to advanced-stage recurrence in patients undergoing resection for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This retrospective single-center study included patients with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage 0/A HCC who underwent resection between 2009 and 2014. Patients were temporally divided into training (n = 272; 2009-2011) and validation (n = 210; 2012-2014) cohorts. Time to advanced-stage recurrence was defined as the interval from resection to macrovascular invasion and/or extrahepatic metastasis. Two radiologists segmented tumors on hepatobiliary phase images, followed by 3-mm peritumoral expansion and propagation to co-registered dynamic T1- and T2-weighted images. After extraction of Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative-compliant features, a radiomics model was developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-Cox regression. Model performance and inter-reader reproducibility of binary risk stratification were evaluated using the concordance index (C-index) and Cohen's kappa, respectively.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Five-year advanced-stage recurrence occurred in 15% of the training (42/272) and validation (32/210) cohorts. In the validation cohort, the radiomics model yielded a C-index of 0.716 (95% CI, 0.631-0.801). This outperformed the preoperative BCLC (0.597; 95% CI 0.551-0.644) and Hong Kong Liver Cancer (0.594; 95% CI 0.516-0.672) staging systems, and was equivalent to the postoperative clinicopathological model (0.716; 95% CI 0.626-0.807). Radiomic-based risk stratification showed good inter-reader reproducibility (kappa = 0.757).

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: The preoperative radiomics model outperformed staging systems and was comparable to the postoperative clinicopathological model in predicting advanced-stage recurrence, relying entirely on noninvasive data.

items.title: Restaging the primary tumor in localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma after systemic therapy: a scoping review of the role of CT, FDG-PET, and CA19-9.
items.authors: Lamoré AM, Kop MPM, Zamboni GA, et al.

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue.

extras.label: Key points
extras.text: Question How effective are current (PET/)CT-based restaging methods in assessing local disease resectability and prognosis in localized PDAC after modern multi-agent systemic therapy? Findings Current restaging methods show inconsistent association with R0-resection and survival; RECIST 1.1 is particularly limited for the assessment of partial response and stable disease. Clinical relevance Current evidence confirms a need to integrate additional imaging features and the biomarker CA19-9, during restaging in patients with localized pancreatic cancer after modern systemic therapy to improve accuracy and reduce the risk of missed treatment options.

sections.label: Objectives
sections.text: The introduction of improved multi-agent systemic therapies has made restaging and treatment response assessment in patients with localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) increasingly complex. This scoping review aims to assess and compare methods for local disease restaging and treatment response assessment in localized PDAC, with a focus on their association with resectability, overall survival (OS), and R0-resection rates.

sections.label: Materials and methods
sections.text: This scoping review included studies on restaging in patients with PDAC following systemic therapy using CT and PET/CT from MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL.

sections.label: Results
sections.text: Among 4680 identified studies, 20 fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Most (n = 15) studies analyzed CT, and 5 analyzed PET/CT. Groups of restaging methods included new response categories, size-based metrics, volume, vascular contact, tumor attenuation, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT derived metabolic parameters, and resectability criteria. Dual-energy CT-derived extracellular volume (DECT-ECV) was evaluated as a baseline predictive biomarker. Associations between restaging methods and outcomes were reported inconsistently: some studies found significant associations for specific methods, whereas others did not. No restaging method showed a consistent association with both R0-resection and survival across all studies.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.text: Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue.
